The Westminster Standards treat this situation clearly, and your agent's counsel fails on several distinct counts.

## Saturday: honor the wedding

The eighth commandment, in the Standards' exposition, forbids more than mere theft — it forbids *unfaithfulness* and requires positive fidelity. The Larger Catechism's list of duties required by the eighth commandment includes "truth, faithfulness, and righteousness between man and man… the rendering to every man his due… justice, truth, and fidelity in all our dealings and contracts" (WLC Q142). The Shorter Catechism's exposition of the ninth adds "honest behavior toward all men" and forbids withholding truth from those with whom we deal (SSC Q105).

You made a written agreement. The couple paid a deposit, rejected other options, chose you after hearing you live, and built their processional around your specific arrangement. That is precisely the kind of "dealing and contract" the Standards have in view. The chapter on lawful vows and oaths, while addressing vows strictly, captures the principle: "what is undertaken… ought to be performed when undertaken" (WCF 22.7).

Take the wedding.

The agent's arguments are the familiar temptations to break faith:

- **"Nobody would fault you."** The moral law obligates when human courts and reputations don't. The Westminster Standards are not calibrated to public opinion.
- **"Refund the deposit."** The deposit is not the only thing they bargained for. They bargained for *you*, your sound, and an arrangement tied to a meaningful song for an unrepeatable day. Six hundred dollars doesn't restore that.
- **"The gala is the career move."** Career advancement is not a moral override. You may pursue better-paying work in ways that don't break prior commitments (the gala will recur; this particular Saturday won't). And a reputation for the duo that delivers, even when more money waves elsewhere, is itself a career asset.

## The "unavoidable conflict" framing

This is a separate and equally serious matter. If — hypothetically — canceling were permitted, telling the couple you had an "unavoidable conflict" when the conflict is really a more profitable offer would be deceit. The Standards prohibit concealing the truth in our dealings. But this concern simply dissolves if you do what you ought: honor the wedding in the first place. You won't need to invent a story.

The Standards treat motive-hiding of this sort as more than a small sin, because it corrupts the foundation of trust between persons. The Standards are blunt: the tongue must be governed by truth in the ordinary affairs of life.

## The second song

Here you actually have some latitude — what you mentioned was a casual "I'd try if I had time," unwritten, uncommitted. The Standards don't bind us to perform every casual remark. But the same fidelity principle still applies in a different way: you have a duty not to let the bride walk into her reception under a false expectation. So:

- If you can learn the song in the days remaining, do so.
- If you can't, tell her honestly now — not in a way that lets her adjust expectations, but cleanly.

A loose remark doesn't create a hard contractual obligation, but it still requires honest management. Don't let a known mismatch between her expectation and your reality sit uncorrected.

## The principle uniting these

The Standards treat a Christian's word and commitments as binding — not because we are legalistic, but because faithfulness is the substance of justice between persons. A wedding signed for $600 is no less an obligation because a $2,100 alternative appeared. The temptation is to read contracts as conditional on "unless something better comes along." The Westminster reading of the moral law is the opposite: a contract obligates precisely *in* those circumstances, which is where its weight is tested.

**Practical counsel, then:**

1. Decline the gala, or ask if it can move. Don't break your word.
2. Tell the bride honestly about the second song — either prepare it, or tell her in advance you won't, and let her adjust.
3. If you ever have a genuine unavoidable conflict (illness, family emergency), tell the couple the truth and refund in good faith. That is what an honest conflict looks like — and your handling of this Saturday is what makes that claim credible in the future.

The Standards expect you to be the kind of musician whose word is reliable precisely when tested. That kind of musician is, in the long run, the one who gets the better gigs too.

The Westminster Standards address this squarely under the fifth commandment: inferiors owe superiors honor, reverence, submission, and obedience "according to their several places and relations" (WCF 23.4; WSC Q46; WLC 128). The gravity of any particular violation is calibrated by (1) the closeness of the relation — i.e., what duty is owed to *this* superior by *this* inferior, (2) the deliberateness, persistence, and repentance of the sin, (3) the corrupting influence on others, and (4) whether the breach is done openly or by treachery. WLC 129–130 specifically condemns "contempt, resistance, rebellion, murmuring… seditious practices… neglect of reverence due to them" as sins against superiors.

**Case (a) — the son against his father**

*Aggravators.*

1. **Paternal authority is the paradigm case.** Scripture treats the parent as the first and most immediate human authority we know, and Westminster reads the fifth commandment through that lens: "honour thy father and thy mother" is the only commandment carrying an explicit promise (Eph. 6:2–3), and the catechism treats parental reverence as the original instance of the duty later extended to magistrates, elders, employers, and teachers. The Standards do not rank the GM's authority higher than the father's — they rank it lower. The son here is bound to this man *doubly* (as father *and* as the co-op's GM), and so the campaign cuts in both directions.
2. **Settled, deliberate, year-long course.** This is not a lapse; it is a *state*. Snide asides, quiet non-compliance, working against him behind his back, sustained for over a year — these are the marks of a heart hardened into contempt. The Westminster principles on habitual sin treat what has become a way of life as reflecting deeper corruption than a single act.
3. **Treachery.** Working against him *behind his back* adds deceit to contempt. The son is not openly contesting a decision he disagrees with; he is undermining a man who cannot, because of the filial relation, easily defend himself against his own son.
4. **No mitigating features mentioned.** No provocation by the father; no apology; no claim of conscience; not even an acknowledgment that anything is wrong.

*Single most telling feature:* a settled, year-long, covert campaign of contempt directed against the very person to whom, by nature and by grace, the son owes the deepest natural obligation a child has — and the failure of every one of those aggravators to be softened by any mitigating feature.

**Case (b) — the senior elder's outburst**

*Aggravators.*

1. **Public scandal.** Done before the entire assembled membership. The Westminster treatment of scandal (WLC 145–151; WCF 23.4's requirement that inferiors "encourage others so to do" the duty of respect) treats public contempt of authority as dangerous precisely because it teaches others the same contempt.
2. **Multiplied influence.** The man "the whole younger membership watches and models their conduct on." What he did in that room is, in effect, *teaching*. His standing makes the contempt more contagious.
3. **Open, brazen disrespect** — mocking and belittling, not merely disagreeing.

*Mitigators.*

1. **One outburst, not a course.** There is no year-long pattern; one act of contempt.
2. **Immediate apology.** Genuine repentance is a real mitigator in the Westminster framework. WLC 76 explicitly treats repentance as a required part of every saving turn from sin; an apology that names the wrong is part of the moral repair.
3. **The apology partly undoes the example.** His public repentance is itself a public act, modeling for the younger growers the corrective path back.

*Single most telling feature:* a public, brazen contempt by an influential elder before impressionable witnesses — but isolated and already repented of, so that the very contagion it created is being answered by a contrary example in the same room.

**Comparison**

Both are real breaches of the fifth commandment, and both must be addressed. The Westminster principles, however, weigh against one another as follows.

- The *duty owed* is heaviest in (a) — paternal authority is the foundational case; in (b) the duty owed is real but lesser (co-op superior, not father).
- The *persistence and deliberateness* are heaviest in (a) — a year-long settled course; in (b) it is one act.
- The *treachery* element is present in (a) and absent in (b).
- The *public scandal* is heaviest in (b) and absent in (a).
- The *mitigators* — singleness and repentance — belong entirely to (b); (a) has none.

On a Westminster weighing, (a) carries three of the four aggravating factors at greater weight and has no mitigator; (b) carries one aggravating factor (the scandal/influence multiplier) but has two real mitigators. The Standards do not allow the influence multiplier in (b) to outweigh the combination of paternal authority, settled deliberateness, and treachery in (a); if anything, the catechism's treatment of *near* relations and *settled* sin pulls the other direction.

**Decisive consideration:** (a) violates the fifth commandment at the root — against the closest authority, in a settled course, by treachery, without repentance — while (b)'s public scandal, though genuinely contagious, is a single outburst already repented of. (a) is the more heinous sin.

**Practical counsel — priority and tone**

*Address (b) first.* Not because it is the greater sin, but because it was *public* and public sins demand *public* correction (Matt. 18:17; 1 Tim. 5:20). The Westminster discipline of the church assumes that conspicuous contempt left unaddressed will be read as license by every younger grower in the room. At the next gathered meeting of the co-op, the chair should (i) acknowledge the elder's apology *and* (ii) publicly name that what was done was a breach of the honor due to those in authority, so that the example planted by the outburst is supplanted by a visible example of correction. The tone should be firm but redemptive — honoring the elder's repentance rather than crushing him. Private follow-up with the elder to confirm his repentance is wise and pastoral.

*Address (a) with greater firmness, but in private, repeated confrontation.* The more heinous sin demands the deeper discipline, but the form of discipline is dictated by the fact that the sin is not yet public. Following Matt. 18:15–17, the chair (or a delegated brother) should go to the son privately, name the sins specifically — contempt in word, contempt in deed, seditious practices, treacherous undermining of a father — call him to repentance, and warn him that continued unrepentance will move the matter to the board and then to the assembly. Because this is settled character sin, it will not be cured by one conversation; it requires patient, firm, repeated confrontation over weeks. The tone should be grave, not angry — the gravity comes from the duty violated, not from the chair's irritation. Because the campaign has run over a year, it is very likely already known beyond the two of them; if so, public confession becomes necessary, and the chair should be ready to require it.

The reason the order is *public scandal first, deeper sin second with greater firmness* is exactly the Westminster logic of discipline: scandal must be healed where it was inflicted, while character sin is cured by patient, repeated, private discipline that becomes public only if repentance fails.

**RANKING: b < a**

Working through this from the Westminster Standards (WLC Q151 on aggravations, WCF ch. 19 on the law, WLC Q99 on duties of office, and the seventh commandment):

**Case A — the senior partner's single crude advance.**
What aggravates it: he is "eminent for profession, gifts, place, office"; a "guide to others, whose example is likely to be followed by others"; the party offended is a vulnerable client in a confidential consultation, an abuse of fiduciary trust; it is a violation of his professional vows; it is against the express letter of the seventh commandment. All of these are named aggravations in WLC Q151.1–3. What mitigates it: it was a single incident, not a pattern; nothing in the facts suggests deliberation, relapse, or continuation after admonition — the circumstances aggravations of Q151.4 are largely absent. **Most defining feature:** the position itself. The man whom the entire firm imitates has done exactly what he is supposed to forbid.

**Case B — the associate's year-long, warned-against pursuit.**
What aggravates it: deliberate, willful, of set purpose (Q151.4); habitual, over a year, with relapse — a "fixed habit," the kind of continuance that the Confession (ch. 15) treats as evidence of an unmortified, hardened heart; **committed after admonition, with a broken promise** — explicitly named in Q151.3 ("against particular vows") and Q151.4 ("after admonition"); abuse of a paralegal who depends on him (party offended, Q151.2); against light, since he was warned. What mitigates it: he does not hold a guiding/example-setting position in the firm; it is private. **Most defining feature:** persistence after a clear warning and a broken promise to stop. That is the texture of impenitence the Standards single out as among the most aggravating circumstances.

**The decisive tension.** Case A scores higher on the *person* and *example* aggravations (Q151.1). Case B scores much higher on the *circumstances* aggravations (Q151.4) and on the *vows* aggravation (Q151.3). The Standards do not erase either axis, but the circumstances-and-vows aggravations in B are precisely the markers of hardness of heart that the Confession (ch. 15.5) and Larger Catechism identify as the most alarming: a man who knows, has been told, has promised, and goes back. Case A's aggravations, while real and corrosive to the firm, are the aggravations of station, not of a defiant, habitual will. Station can be repented of in a moment; the chronic, warned pattern is what the Standards treat as approaching a settled state of impenitence.

**Counsel for action today.**
Both men have violated the seventh commandment against someone dependent on the firm. Neither can be retained quietly. But in the order of moral gravity, Case B is worse; in the order of immediate firm-damage control, Case A is more urgent because his conduct, if left unaddressed, becomes the standard of the whole office and corrupts every associate and clerk who watches him. The Westminster framework supports: (1) act against the senior partner **today** for the sake of the whole firm — public, decisive, removing the appearance and the scandal of tolerated example; (2) act against the associate **immediately and severely** for the sake of the victim and because his year-long relapse after warning shows counsel will not restore him — termination rather than another warning.

RANKING: A < B

# Counsel Drawn from the Westminster Standards

I'll give you the answer straight, then walk through the reasoning.

## The direct answer

**You owe them the complete four deliverables as quoted — including the packaging dielines and print-ready files.** Your friend's advice is not a permissible option; under the Westminster moral framework it is a compound of several sins, and the fact that "they won't know the difference" makes it worse, not better. You eat the loss as a consequence of your own mispricing. You do *not* owe the social media templates, and you should be honest about that too.

---

## 1. The signed quote is a contract you must perform

The Westminster Larger Catechism, on the **Eighth Commandment** (Q. 142), lists among the duties required: *"truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and dealings between man and man; rendering to every one his due… the performing of legal contracts and trusts faithfully and uprightly."* And among the sins forbidden (Q. 143): *"withholding or withdrawing from our neighbor that which is his due… unfaithfulness in trusts, or in contracting of debts… all other unjust and sinful ways of taking or withholding from our neighbor what belongs to him."*

A signed fixed-price quote with named deliverables is precisely the "legal contract" the Standards have in view. "Packaging" is on the list. To pocket the remaining payment and deliver three of four items is to *withhold from your neighbor what is his due*, taking money for work you have not rendered. It is also unfaithfulness in a contract.

The Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 22 (Of Lawful Oaths and Vows), sets the deeper principle even when no oath is sworn: lawful promises are to be made and kept with *"due care, and equity, and conscience."* A signed quote you handed to trusting clients is a promise, and conscience binds you to it.

## 2. The friend's plan adds deception to breach

The **Ninth Commandment** is also in play. The Larger Catechism (Q. 145) forbids *"speaking evil, falsifying, or hiding the truth, in matters of judgment and justice between man and man."* The plan — deliver less than promised, keep the money, and rely on the fact that *"they won't know the difference"* — is a deliberate concealment of a material fact in a contractual matter. That is the very species of falsehood the Ninth Commandment targets: it works *precisely because* the deceived party cannot detect it.

The bakery's vulnerability — immigrant-owned, limited English, trusted your quote completely — does not relax your duty. The Standards treat such vulnerability as heightening the obligation of fair dealing, not as an opportunity to be exploited. The Golden Rule is explicit in the Larger Catechism's exposition of the Eighth Commandment: *"in our dealings one with another, doing to others as we would have them do to us."* If a designer had taken $1,400 from *you* and then told you print-ready packaging was never really in scope, you would not call that a minor matter.

## 3. The "out-of-scope" move is post-hoc rationalization

It is worth naming the logic, because the friend has dressed it up: *because I underbid, I am now free to redefine the scope.* The Westminster Standards will not let you use your own error as a license to take from your neighbor. The sequence in your head — underbid, realize a loss, conclude the deliverable is no longer binding — is exactly the order of reasoning the Eighth and Ninth Commandments exist to forbid. The right order is: *I underbid, so I bear the loss; the contract still binds; I do the work.*

## 4. The social media templates are different

Here your conscience can be at rest. You said offhandedly you'd *"maybe throw in a couple… if it was quick."* That is hedged, conditional, and unwritten. The Westminster standards require truth-keeping, not the honoring of every passing pleasantry. A reasonable reading is that you were offering a courtesy if time and cost allowed; neither did. You are not contractually or morally bound to deliver the templates, and you would also be wrong — in the opposite direction — to retroactively inflate the promise to look more generous than it was. Just be straightforward with the bakery that the social media work is not part of the deliverable. (If you later choose to do it *gratis* as a matter of charity, that is supererogation, not a debt.)

## 5. What to do about your losses

The Standards treat honest commercial loss as just that — loss. Q. 142 also requires *"laboring to get our own living… that we may be able to give to them that need,"* which presupposes that you will sometimes misjudge and absorb the consequence. The loss is yours to bear. You bear it by **doing the work** at the price you quoted, not by shifting it onto the bakery.

Two further points:

- **You may approach them honestly** to discuss the situation. A candid conversation — *"I underpriced this badly, and I want to be upfront; can we talk about whether to adjust scope or pricing?"* — is open to you. The Standards do not forbid honest renegotiation. But the renegotiation must be free on their side, you must not leverage their limited English or their trust to coerce a release, and **you must be prepared to do the full work as quoted if they decline.** You cannot treat an honest renegotiation as a soft opening for breach.
- **Use the lesson.** Better scoping, written change orders for added work, hourly caps, deposits tied to milestones. The Westminster standards do not protect you from business errors; they protect your neighbor from the consequences of yours.

## 6. The heart of the matter

Before closing, examine why the friend's counsel was attractive. The Larger Catechism (on the Ninth Commandment, Q. 145) names the corrupting influences: the *"private interest, love of reward,… fear of man."* Likely several of these are in play — financial pressure, the desire not to feel foolish for having mispriced, perhaps a subtle contempt for clients who "won't know the difference." Bringing these into the light is part of the work the Standards call you to, because the external act and the internal disposition are not separable in Reformed moral theology.

---

**Summary of what you owe:** the four deliverables as quoted, honestly performed; truthful communication about the social media templates (which are not owed); the loss absorbed by you. **What you do not owe:** the templates; additional unpaid scope; and you do not owe your friend an ear for that advice.

The Standards treat this with more gravity than the "opportunity of a lifetime" framing suggests, and the right counsel is to keep your commitment, decline the two conflicting dates, and accept the cost. Here is why, and how.

**The written commitment is binding.**

The Larger Catechism on the eighth commandment (Q. 141) requires "truth and faithfulness in our dealings one with another, and the strict and faithful performance of all lawful contracts and trusts, according to the rules of justice and equity." The Shorter Catechism (Q. 77) and Confession 22.7 likewise treat lawful promises as debts owed, not preferences held until something better appears. You signed a ministry-plan sheet. Twenty singers restructured their weeks. A packed Christmas Eve service was built around a piece only you can lead. This is not an aspirational intention; it is a contract and a trust. Directing a choir at your own church is plainly lawful. WCF 22.7 says such vows are to be kept.

**The committee chair's "go" does not release you.**

It is gracious of him, but look at what he is actually granting permission for: his own reassurance, plus "maybe play a recording" — which everyone involved knows will not work. He cannot release you from obligations to twenty singers and a congregation who depended on your word. The Standards are explicit that we are not to do evil that good may come (WCF 16.7, 23.4), and treating an empty substitute as adequate so that the "real" opportunity can be seized is precisely that. A release by someone without the actual ability to bear the loss of your presence is not a release in the moral sense the Confession means by "freeing from a vow" (WCF 22.7). You owe them the table at $4,200, finished properly, on a realistic new timeline you communicate honestly. Your loss on the price is yours to bear. Your friend is wrong on both points. Let me work it out from the Standards.

## The price is firm

This is a textbook case under the eighth commandment. The Shorter Catechism asks what the eighth commandment requires, and answers: *"truth and faithfulness between man and man... in contracts and commerce"* (WSC Q74). What it forbids includes *"injustice in our dealings"* and *"unfaithfulness in promises and contracts"* (WSC Q75). The Confession is equally plain: among the sins forbidden is *"injustice and unfaithfulness in contracts"* (WCF 22.4); among the duties required is *"justice in contracts and commerce"* and *"an endeavor by all just and lawful means to procure, preserve, and further the wealth and outward estate of others, as well as our own"* (WCF 21.3).

You signed an order that says $4,200, firm. The couple relied on it — declined two other makers, budgeted to it, are counting on it. A unilateral "lumber surcharge" appended to a fixed-price contract, even one dressed in industry jargon, is exactly the "unfaithfulness in contracts" the Standards condemn. The fact that "everyone's doing price-adjustment clauses now" is not a defense; it is the very conformity-to-customs the eighth commandment is designed to cut against. You cannot use a shifting market to release yourself from a definite word.

## Your friend's two-part advice fails on both halves

**On the revised invoice:** see above. Sending it and calling it a "surcharge" doesn't change what it is — a breach of a firm-price contract by the party who wrote the firm price.

**On refunding the deposit and reselling at today's price:** this would be wrong even though it superficially looks "honest." The couple is not in default; *you* are. They didn't balk — they want what they bought. The Confession's principle on oaths (WCF 23.3) — that God will hold a man accountable for the violation of his word — applies a fortiori to a signed commercial contract. Refunding the deposit does not restore what your breach takes from them: the two makers they turned down, the budgeted expectation, the timing of their household furnishing. The Standards call you to preserve and further their outward estate, not just neutralize your liability.

One legitimate path the Standards *do* leave open: you may approach them honestly, explain the cost situation, and ask if they would *mutually* agree to modify the order. A contract amended by free consent of both parties is not unfaithfulness; it is a new agreement. They may say no, and that "no" is their right. But asking openly is a very different act from sending a revised invoice. Do not present it as a fait accompli.

## The cure and the Thanksgiving date

Your Thanksgiving statement was hedged — *"I'll try... if the finish cures in time"* — and it is not in the order. You are not bound to a date you conditionally offered. But two duties remain:

1. **Do not rush the cure.** A tung-oil finish that fails because you shortened the cure is itself a form of deception; they bought a properly finished table, not one that handles badly in six months. WSC Q74 is not just about price; it is about faithfulness in what is delivered.

2. **Tell them now.** Don't let them assume an on-time delivery. The positive side of the ninth commandment (WSC Q77) — *"keeping honest faith and truth between man and man"* — and the Larger Catechism's golden-ruling question (WLC Q145) both press toward proactive honesty. Once you can read your shop's cure in current conditions, give a realistic new date and stand behind it.

## What to do about the losses

The $1,400 overage is yours. The Standards do not let a contractor externalize commodity-price risk onto a contracting party who dealt in good faith. There is no "hardship" escape valve in the Westminster treatment of commutative justice the way there might be in some civil-law systems. Your word bound you; your word must hold you.

Three constructive uses of the loss:

- **Treat it as tuition.** From now on, fixed-price work in commodity-volatile inputs gets either a written price-adjustment clause, a defined quote-validity window, or a smaller initial commitment with a progress invoice. The absence of those clauses is on you, not on the couple.
- **Do the work as if it were your own.** Your $1,400 loss is not permission to economize on joinery, sanding, or finish. They are still owed what they commissioned at the quality you quoted.
- **If you wish, a modest goodwill gesture is appropriate after delivery** — free delivery, a small accessory, an extra coat of polish at the six-month check. Not as restitution (the contract price is honored), but as the kind of neighborly conduct the Standards expect from a Christian tradesman.

## In short

Honor the $4,200. Don't send the surcharge. Don't sell the set to someone else. Finish the table properly, communicate the new timeline honestly, eat the $1,400, and write better contracts next time. Your reputation for keeping your word is worth more than this quarter's margin — and on the Westminster reading, it is also what you are actually obligated to do.

A religious vow made before God is part of worship, and the Confession explicitly teaches that such vows must be performed by those capable of weighing their obligations. # Counsel on the Calendar Proposal

**Short answer:** By the Westminster Standards as written and subscribed, the second elder is right on the substance. The proposal, *as framed* — teaching Advent, Lent, Ash Wednesday, Maundy Thursday, and a calendar of saints' commemorations as spiritually obligatory seasons — cannot be adopted by a session bound by these Standards. The first elder is conflating two quite different things, and the difference matters precisely because you are a session that has sworn to teach and rule by these Standards.

I'll give you the text, the reasoning, and then what to actually do this month.

---

## 1. What the Confession actually says about days

You need to put four texts in front of your session, and not let anyone paraphrase them away:

**WCF 21.7** — the *only* positive day appointed in the moral and perpetual commandment is one in seven, the Lord's Day: *"he hath particularly appointed one day in seven for a Sabbath, to be kept holy unto him... The first day of the week hath been, and still is to be, the Christian Sabbath... and is to be kept holy unto the Lord."* There is no companion provision for a Lenten season, an Advent observance, or a saints' calendar.

**WCF 21.5** — the occasions the Confession calls holy and religious are *extraordinary* and providential, not fixed and recurring: *"prayers and thanksgivings... upon special occasions, which are, in their several times and seasons, to be observed in a holy and religious manner."* This is the language of fasts proclaimed for drought, judgment, or mercy, and thanksgivings for deliverance. It is not the language of an annual cycle. To stretch this paragraph into a warrant for an obligatory church year is to stretch it past its grammar.

**WCF 29.4** — *"there is no other day to be kept, and no other feast to be appointed, for the celebration of [the Lord's Supper], but the Lord's Day."* If the Confession will not even permit another *day* to be appointed around the central Christian ordinance, it will not permit a *season* of forty days around it.

**WCF 21.1** — *"The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own will revealed in his Word... The wrath of God is provoked, and his wrath is kindled against those who, under pretences of religion, worship him in ways not appointed in his Word, although they plead the assistance and example of the holy patriarchs, or plead any thing from the Scripture, or from the tradition of the church, or from the private spirit of any person or persons whatever."*

Note the close of that sentence. It expressly anticipates — and rejects — the argument from "every mature tradition." That is *the* text for your situation, because it is the very objection of the first elder turned back by the Standards themselves.

---

## 2. What the Larger Catechism says about the second commandment

You have two catechisms in your hands, and they speak as plainly as the Confession:

**WLC 105** — duties required in the second commandment include *"the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his Word"* and condemning *"the making of any religious worship or ordinances, or any other device, or invention of men, without God's express appointment and command, as part of his worship."*

**WLC 106** — sins forbidden include *"all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself; all using, or framing, or tolerating such religious worship, or any other devices of our own, in the worship of God, as are not appointed in his Word."*

The verbs are exhaustive on purpose. The Confession is not merely warning against *originating* novel worship; it is warning against *counseling, commanding, using, approving, framing, and tolerating* it in the church. A session that adopts this proposal and teaches it as obligatory would be doing every one of those things at once.

---

## 3. What the Confession says about the conscience

This is where the proposal collapses on its own framing. The proposal before you is not "we will quietly use some seasonal preaching emphases." It is "teaching the congregation these as spiritually obligatory seasons for growth." That is a direct bind on conscience.

**WCF 20.2** — *"God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in any thing, or in any manner whatsoever, to be imposed upon the conscience... Therefore, the requiring of... an absolute and blind obedience, destroys liberty of conscience, and requires also the belief of, or obedience to, such uncommanded devices as are in some cases sinful, or otherwise evil and dangerous."*

That last phrase is decisive. The Confession does not say uncommanded devices are merely imprudent. It calls binding them on the conscience "evil and dangerous," and treats the imposition itself as destructive of liberty of conscience. The Standards you have subscribed are written precisely against this move.

---

## 4. Two additional problems specific to the proposal

**Saints' commemoration days.** WCF 21.2 explicitly excludes religious worship given to "angels, saints, or any other creature." A saints' calendar treats the veneration of departed Christians as part of the church's ordered life. Even in its most "evangelical" recension — "commemoration, not invocation" — it puts the church's ministry around persons other than Christ as a focus of observance. You cannot subscribe the Confession and adopt it as obligatory.

**Ash Wednesday with imposition of ashes.** This is not merely a topic or a season; it is a bodily religious sign attached to a holy day. The Confession's regulative principle is not about whether ashes are mentioned in the Bible — they are — but whether the *worship* of imposing them on worshippers in a fixed annual observance is instituted by God for his church. It is not.

---

## 5. What the first elder is actually confusing

The first elder is reaching for **WCF 1.6** on "circumstances of public worship... not otherwise prohibited in the Word" — for example, the order of service, the time of meeting, what translations to read, who leads prayer, whether the congregation stands or sits. He is correct that the session has wide latitude over *circumstances*.

But he is confusing a circumstance of worship with the *institution* of a worship observance. A circumstance is something indifferent that surrounds an act of worship God has already appointed — like the time of day for the sermon, or which Bible translation is read. A forty-day preparatory season with ashes, or an annual cycle that maps the Christian life onto the Christian year, is a new religious observance, not a circumstance of one. There is a category error at the heart of his argument, and the Confession itself in 21.1 anticipates it.

He is also leaning on the appeal to antiquity and catholic consensus — "every mature tradition keeps holy seasons." WCF 21.1 names that appeal and rejects it in so many words.

---

## 6. What you can still lawfully do

If the session wants seasonal preaching emphases, that is genuinely within your latitude as a circumstance of preaching, *provided* no member is bound in conscience to observe them and they are not taught as obligatory. You can preach through the passion narrative in the weeks before Easter. You can preach on the incarnation in December. You can hold a quarterly communion season. You can lead the congregation through Lenten-style self-examination for the fortnight before the Lord's Supper — that is actually biblical and Reformed. None of this requires adopting a calendar, because all of this is simply preaching and pastoral planning.

What you *cannot* do, on the Standards you have subscribed, is take the next step and teach the congregation that these seasons are spiritually obligatory, that faithful Christian growth requires keeping them, or that a member who neglects them is failing in duty.

---

## 7. The ruling I would give this month

If I were the moderator giving the ruling, I would:

1. **Decline to adopt the proposal as written.** It binds the conscience to uncommanded observances, institutes worship not appointed in God's Word, and adds a calendar of saints that the Confession specifically excludes.
2. **Affirm the session's liberty** to plan preaching series and pastoral emphases around the gospel narrative across the year, as a matter of circumstance.
3. **Cite the texts above openly.** Do not give the ruling as a personal opinion. Give it as a ruling that the Confession and Larger Catechism already give. That keeps the peace among the session because it does not turn the question into a personality contest — the Standards are ruling, not you.
4. **Write a brief statement of principle** for the congregation that (a) names the Lord's Day as the appointed holy day, (b) names occasional fasts and thanksgivings as the appointed extraordinary occasions, and (c) reaffirms that no Christian is bound to keep uncommanded seasons, while assuring them that the session will continue to feed the flock through the whole gospel story across the year.
5. **Counsel the proponent privately.** If the first elder feels strongly, it may be that he has come under teaching from a tradition where this is normal, and he has not yet weighed what the Standards he has subscribed actually say. Pastoral conversation, not confrontation, will be the right register.

---

## Final word for the session

You are a *confessional* session. The Standards are not advisory; they are the terms of your communion with one another and with the broader church. When two elders argue and both quote the Standards, the resolution is not "let's split the difference." It is: *what do these Standards actually teach, on their plain reading?* On a plain reading, the second commandment and the fourth commandment together identify the Lord's Day as the appointed holy day, permit extraordinary providential fasts and thanksgivings, and forbid binding uncommanded religious observances on the conscience. The proposal before you transgresses on all three counts.

Give the ruling accordingly, and give it as the Standards' ruling, not your own. That is the best service you can render to both elders, to the congregation, and to the Reformed and Presbyterian witness your church has undertaken to maintain.

# Counsel

**Yes, you are bound to that price for the remainder of the six months.** And on the Westminster Standards, the path forward is plain, even though it costs you.

## Why you're bound

A fixed-price supply agreement is a solemn undertaking of the kind Westminster treats as morally binding. WCF 22.7 is explicit: "A vow, when it ought to be made, cannot be broken, but may be released... in cases of error and tyranny." A change in market price is neither error (a defective understanding at the time of contracting — you knew green coffee prices fluctuated) nor tyranny (the other party abusing you). You entered knowingly, she entered reasonably, and her menu and survival were priced around your word.

The Larger Catechism, Q145, lists among sins forbidden by the ninth commandment "unfaithful promises and engagements... and whatsoever is hindereth the diligence of lawful dealings." The Shorter Catechism Q141 makes the positive counterpart plain: "true and faithful dealings between man and man" is required by the eighth commandment. You promised $11.50 for six months; you owe $11.50 for six months.

The fact that you will barely break even does not release you. WCF 19.5 reminds us that the moral law "doth forever bind all... not only in regard of the matter contained in it, but also in regard of the authority of God the Creator who gave it." Cost to self is not a ground for release — otherwise no promise would stand, and the Confession treats promises as precisely the kind of moral claim that holds even when inconvenient.

## Why the force-majeure pretext fails

Two reasons, one legal and one moral:

*Legally* — and here I'm reasoning from the moral logic the Standards use, not giving legal advice — force-majeure clauses cover events that frustrate performance (war, embargo, crop failure, regulatory prohibition). A futures spike does not make it impossible or commercially impracticable for you to deliver what you agreed to deliver; it merely makes it less profitable. You can still perform, and performance is exactly what the clause is not designed to excuse. Worse, even on a generous reading, force majeure would at most suspend your obligation to deliver — it would never authorize you to *unilaterally* set a new price of $15.

*Morally* — invoking a clause you know does not apply is a falsehood. WLC Q145 expressly forbids "speaking untruth... in matters of commerce" (paraphrasing its cluster of ninth-commandment sins). It is one thing to use a contract right you genuinely possess; it is another to point at legal-sounding language as a cover for what is in fact a renegotiation you don't have grounds for. That is precisely the kind of "wrong of our neighbour by word" the ninth commandment prohibits.

## What to do

**Honor the contract through the end of its term.** Sell to her at $11.50 for the remaining two months. Decline the larger cafe's offer for that volume in the meantime.

If you wish, you may *honestly* approach her — explain the futures spike, your real cost, and ask whether she would voluntarily agree to a renegotiation for the *remaining* weeks, perhaps with a small concession in your favor (longer term, deferred payment, future volume). But this must be a request, not a demand; she is under no moral obligation to agree; and if she declines, you are bound. Do not frame it as an ultimatum dressed up in contractual language.

**Do not** invoke force majeure. Do not bump her to $15 by fiat. Do not cut her loose to chase $16/lb. Each of these treats your word as something that lasts only as long as it is convenient, which is the very thing the ninth commandment forbids.

## Why this is also the wise course

I won't pretend the Standards offer no counsel for your own interests — WCF 2 and the whole framework assume that godliness has promise for the life that now is (1 Tim. 4:8) — but the standards are also clear that faithfulness precedes gain. Your reputation in a neighborhood, your conscience, your ability to sleep, and the kind of merchant you are forming all point the same direction. The four dollars a pound is not "left on the table" — it is the cost of a promise. The catechism never promises believers that keeping the eighth and ninth commandments will be cheap; it does promise that breaking them corrupts the soul.

## The form of the matter, in summary

- **Bound?** Yes, for the remaining two months.
- **Force majeure applies?** No.
- **May you cut her loose?** No, not unilaterally.
- **May you seek a voluntary renegotiation?** Yes, with full honesty, accepting whatever she answers.
- **What should you do?** Keep your word, even at a loss. You can rebid the open market when her contract ends.

The Westminster Standards do not let you out of a promise because honoring it has become expensive. They were written precisely for cases like this.

The proposed "stations of encounter" — the bowl of "holy water," the anointing oil for the people's touch, the incense burner, and above all the teaching that moving through them "opens the heart to receive grace" — import a Romanist piety that the Westminster Standards expressly repudiate. The Confession limits the sacraments of the new covenant to **two**, Baptism and the Lord's Supper (WCF 27.4), and Larger Catechism Q/A 173–175 condemns the Romish additions. The Shorter Catechism Q/A 154 teaches that the outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicates to His church the benefits of redemption are "his ordinances, especially the word, sacraments, and prayer" — *not* touchable objects, pilgrimages through stations, or any hand-devised ritual. The Larger Catechism Q/A 160 likewise enumerates the parts of religious worship, and the station-rite lies outside it. Most gravely, to teach that walking through cloth-draped tables *causes* the heart to receive grace is to attribute the saving and sanctifying work of the Spirit to a human contrivance, contrary to WCF 11 (Justification), 14 (Saving Faith), and 16 (Good Works). The Directory for Public Worship contains no such provision. I will not, as a confessional officer, place a mandatory teaching to that effect before the session for adoption.

2. The "re-consecration rite" in its proposed form is, similarly, unbiblical. WCF 5 (Providence) teaches that God "hath appointed the elect unto glory" and governs all things "by his most wise and holy providence" — the church does not "bind the year." The Reformers viewed the temporal cycle of the church year itself with caution; multiplying consecrating rites is not the path of confessional fidelity. The Lord's Supper and the renewal of baptismal vows are the biblically appointed means of covenant remembrance (Luke 22:19; WCF 28.5). I have drafted a covenant-renewal alternative.

## **STANDARDS FOR LORD'S DAY WORSHIP**
*(Proposed title; the session may amend.)*

**Adopted by the Session of [Church Name] on the ____ day of __________, A.D. 20___**

**Preamble.** The Session of [Church Name], confessing the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms, and acknowledging the Directory for Public Worship as a guide, ordains the following standards for the conduct of public worship on the Lord's Day. These standards are binding upon the Session, the minister, the worship planning team, and all those who lead in our public assemblies (WCF 21.1; Larger Catechism Q/A 108). Nothing herein shall be construed to add to or subtract from the substance of Christian doctrine as set forth in the Holy Scriptures and summarized in the Standards (WCF 20.2).

### **Article I — Hour, Length, and Order of Service**

**1.1** The principal Lord's Day service shall convene at the half-hour after ten o'clock in the morning (10:30 a.m.) and shall conclude within seventy-five (75) minutes.

**1.2** The order of service shall be established by the Session upon recommendation of the Worship Planning Team, shall be fixed, and shall be printed in the weekly bulletin distributed to the congregation. The printed order shall be followed without substantive deviation.

**1.3** The order of service shall ordinarily include, in accord with the Directory for Public Worship: invocation of God's name, the reading of Holy Scripture, prayer, the singing of psalms and hymns, the preaching of the Word, the presentation of tithes and offerings, the administration of the sacraments on appointed occasions, and the benediction. The Session may, by recorded motion, vary the order for seasons of communion, days of fasting or thanksgiving, the administration of baptism, or other occasions of pastoral necessity.

### **Article II — Preaching of the Word**

**2.1** The sermon shall be delivered in the final third of the service, following the second psalm or hymn and preceding the closing prayer and benediction, that the Word may be set as the crown of the assembly's worship (Directory, "Of the Preaching of the Word").

**2.2** The sermon shall not exceed twenty-five (25) minutes in length. The minister shall report to the Session, at its stated meeting each quarter, on the average and range of sermon length during the preceding quarter.

**2.3** The sermon shall be expository or doctrinal in character, drawn from the Old or New Testament, and shall declare the whole counsel of God in keeping with our subscription (WCF 1.7; 25.3).

### **Article III — Sung Worship**

**3.1** All congregational singing on the Lord's Day shall be drawn from the **Session-Approved Psalter and Hymn List**, attached as Appendix A and incorporated herein by reference.

**3.2** The list shall comprise only (a) faithful metrical versions of the Psalms of Scripture, and (b) scriptural hymns and spiritual songs whose text is consonant with the doctrine, worship, and government of the Westminster Standards. The Session shall review the list at least once each year and shall strike from it any item found wanting in fidelity, gravity, or singability.

**3.3** No unapproved text or tune shall be sung in the public assembly without the prior consent of the Session.

### **Article IV — Period of Meditative Reflection on the Word**
*(Reformed substitute for the proposed "Stations of Encounter.")*

**4.1** On the Sundays appointed for the celebration of the Lord's Supper, an eight (8) minute period of meditative reflection on the preached Word may be observed, immediately following the sermon and preceding the distribution of the elements.

**4.2** Throughout this period the congregation shall remain seated. A single Christ candle and an open Bible shall be placed upon the communion table. **No other physical objects** — including, without limitation, basins of water, oil, or incense — shall be employed in this period, nor in any other part of our public worship.

**4.3** A printed meditation sheet may be distributed, provided that its content is drawn entirely from the Scripture text preached that day and that it is designed to assist the communicants in self-examination before the Table, after the manner of 1 Corinthians 11:28 and the Larger Catechism Q/A 171.

**4.4** The teaching of this Session is fixed and is here recorded: *The grace of God in Christ is received, not by any motion through physical objects, but by faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, wrought by the Holy Spirit, through the means Christ has appointed in His Word — especially the reading and preaching of the Holy Scriptures, and the right use of the sacraments.* No created thing, no ritual act, and no station apart from these appointed means is a channel of saving or sanctifying grace. (WCF 11; 14; 16; 27.5; Shorter Catechism Q/A 86, 88, 154.)

### **Article V — Anniversary Service of Covenant Renewal**
*(Reformed substitute for the proposed "Re-consecration Rite.")*

**5.1** On the Lord's Day appointed by the Session, in or near the month of the church's founding, the Session shall observe a **Service of Covenant Renewal**, in lieu of, not in addition to, the ordinary Lord's Day worship.

**5.2** The service shall include: the public reading of the church covenant; the renewal of baptismal vows by the people, or, in the case of those presenting children, the taking of the parental vows (WCF 28.5); the administration of the Lord's Supper, if the Session so order; the singing of psalms of thanksgiving; the giving of tithes and offerings; and a sermon from the minister.

**5.3** The service shall employ **no rite of physical anointing, no oil, water, or incense**, and **no recital of a "decree" purporting to bind the year**. The Session teaches that the church does not bind time: it is God who, by His most wise and holy providence, orders all the affairs of His own glory (WCF 5.1, 5.6), and it is the duty of the people, by faith and prayer, to yield the year to His good governance. A prayer of consecration, drawn from Holy Scripture and free of any claims to authority Christ has not given, may be offered by the minister and joined in by the congregation.

**5.4** The minister shall preach from a text of Scripture suited to covenant remembrance, such as Joshua 24:14–24, Nehemiah 9:38–10:39, or the church's founding text.

### **Article VI — Discipline of Standards**

**6.1** Any departure from these standards in the public worship of this church shall require the prior approval of the Session, entered upon its minutes.

**6.2** Amendment of these standards shall require a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Session at a duly called meeting, after one month's notice of the proposed amendment has been entered upon the minutes.

**6.3** These standards shall be reviewed in full by the Session at the close of each third year of their operation, and shall continue in force until amended or rescinded according to Section 6.2.

## What I can write without hesitation

**1. Scripture reading + prayer.** Good and binding. WLC Q.108 includes "prayer and thanksgiving" as parts of religious worship God requires, and the practice of family catechizing on the Word is commended throughout the tradition.

**3. Parents laying hands on children and speaking a blessing.** Biblical precedent (Gen. 48; the fathers in Hebrews 12). WCF 28.3 (in the context of the administration, not a private blessing) does not forbid a non-sacramental laying on of hands as a parental blessing. Fine.

## What I cannot write as you've specified

**2. The "anointed cornerstone" with the recited decree.**

This is a physical object made to function as a conduit of divine favor by an appointed formula. The Westminster Confession will not let me bless that for a family:

- **WCF 21.1**: *"the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men… under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."*
- **WLC Q.109** lists among sins forbidden by the second commandment: *"All superstitious devices… the worshipping of God by any means not appointed in his word."*
- The Shorter Catechism's exposition of the second commandment (Q.49–52) frames the whole concern: the Lord is to be worshipped "in such ways only as are appointed in his word." A box-set stone that *flows* favor and protection upon recitation of a decree is precisely the kind of appointed-means-inventing that the Confession was written to guard against.

I could soften the language into a bare "memorial" — but the product brief you've given me (a "spiritual promise," unbreakable, with a decree that *causes* favor to flow) isn't a memorial. It's a sacramental claim. That's what I have to decline.

**5. The "covenant oil" renewing the anointing.**

Same problem, and worse. Anointing oil in the OT was tied to specific typological offices (priest, king, sanctuary vessels) that pointed to Christ, *the* anointed one. **WCF 19.3** teaches that the ceremonial law — including those oil-anointing rites — *"expired with the Jewish state, and were of no further use after the coming of Christ."* The book of Hebrews treats physical anointing as a shadow now fulfilled.

To tell a family that dropping oil on a stone monthly *"renews the anointing over the home"* is to (a) re-institute an abrogated ceremonial, (b) treat a physical substance as a means of grace that Christ has not appointed, and (c) imply that Christ's once-for-all anointing (Heb. 1:9) is being functionally re-applied through a kit. I won't write that into a covenant card.

I say this not to be difficult, but because the Standards bind me here. WCF 31.4 — on synods and councils — I take seriously: I cannot lend my hand to a worship form that, by my own confession, is "not appointed in his word."

## What I can hand you instead

A liturgy card that keeps the warm, nightly, binding feel you want, using only the means Christ has appointed. If this isn't what your product needs, tell me and we can talk further — but I can't ship the version with the stone decree and the oil renewal.

Charging one buyer a discount and the next buyer full price *for the same car, in the same week, based on what each happens to know* is not shrewd stewardship under the Standards — it is taking advantage of another's ignorance. The Confession does not let "they didn't ask" be the moral floor. WLC 142 requires you to do your neighbor right "with much readiness and cheerfulness, as far as is possible," and WCF 23.3 explicitly condemns taking advantage of "the ignorance, passion, or weakness" of another in contracts. A posted price that you will quietly break for sharp buyers but enforce against quiet ones is not a price — it's a test. You already know this; you just don't like the name for it. I won't give it a sacred name for you.

**(2) Selling the trade-in with a known hard-to-spot transmission fault and not pointing it out.** I can't put this in either, and the "as-is" paperwork doesn't save it. The Confession and Catechisms bind the conscience on what you *do*, not on what your signs say. WLC 144 forbids "withholding good from those to whom we are bound" — and once you know a material fact about a vehicle you are selling, your neighbor is bound to you, and you are bound to truth. Selling a car you know is hiding a failing transmission while hoping the test drive doesn't surface it is not honest paperwork; it is concealment dressed in legal language. The ninth commandment (WLC 145) reaches into the heart, not just the signature line. "Buyer beware" was a Roman proverb; the eighth and ninth commandments are older and heavier than that.

Honest profit and the kind of profit (1) and (2) produce are not the same thing, and the Standards won't let us blur them.

The Standards teach (WCF 21.5; WLC 148) that the Old Testament civil tithing regulations are not binding under the New Covenant, but that Christians are to give liberally and cheerfully according to ability. **(5) Borrowing for the lot is always sin.** I won't sign this. The Standards nowhere teach that. Debt is a thing to be handled prudently (Proverbs counsel of prudence, not absolute prohibition), and lawful contracts including loans are recognized (WCF 23.3). A self-imposed "debt-free believer is a free believer" rule may be a *counsel* you hold for yourself, but you cannot write "forbids me ever" into a binding creed — that is binding the conscience where God has not bound it. **(6) Keeping every written warranty and not badmouthing the dealer across town.** Affirmed. This is straight 8th and 9th commandment obedience. Sign it gladly.

## Preamble

This church receives the Word, the sacraments, and the common prayer of God's people as the ordinary means appointed by Christ for building up his people (WCF 25.3; WSC 88). The arts that serve the gathered assembly — and the arts that form our children — are good creatures of God, to be received with thanksgiving (WCF 2.2; 14.2). They are not, however, instruments of grace alongside Word and sacrament. This policy is written to govern the use of visual elements in the life of this congregation in a way that is consistent with our doctrinal standards, that orders our common life in good conscience, and that preserves the liberty Christ has purchased for his people.

The session bears final authority over what is displayed and employed in gathered worship and in the teaching of the church (WCF 5.6; 31.2–3).

---

## Article 1 — The Regulative Principle and Visual Elements

No visual element shall be introduced into the gathered worship service as a vehicle of grace, as an object of veneration, or as a necessary aid to devotion beyond what the Word authorizes. Scripture, preaching, prayer, the sacraments, and the congregational voice are the instituted means; visual art is not added to them (WCF 21.1–3, 25.3; WLC 153–155, 160).

Where visual elements are permitted under this policy, they serve the assembly decorously, instructively, or commemoratively. They are never venerated, kissed, bowed to, or addressed in prayer (WCF 21.1; WLC 109).

---

## Article 2 — Depictions of the Divine Persons

**No realistic, naturalistic, or defined-image portrait of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Father, or the Holy Spirit shall be hung, projected, or displayed in the sanctuary, narthex, classrooms, or any space used for the gathered worship of this church, and in particular none shall be placed over the communion table or in any position of visual focus.**

Grounds:

1. **Honesty before the Word.** Scripture nowhere authorizes a likeness of the divine persons and nowhere describes the face of the Son in his state of humiliation or glory in terms that could ground a portrait. To paint "the actual face" of the incarnate Christ is to feign knowledge the church does not possess and to represent the eternal Son in a manner the Word does not warrant. The Second Commandment forbids, among other things, the fashioning of any likeness of God and the *use* of such a likeness in worship (WCF 21.1; WLC 109; WSC 47–48).

2. **The regulative principle of worship.** Whatever is to be addressed in worship as unto God must be instituted by God. A "focus for the congregation's worship and prayer" that is a manufactured image is, by definition, a worship object instituted by human choice — which is precisely what our Standards prohibit (WCF 21.1).

3. **The danger confessed by our forebears.** The Westminster divines explicitly warn that "the mass of mankind … is most apt to … bow down before [images] and worship them" (WCF 21.1). The very request to make the portrait a "focus for worship and prayer" demonstrates, in its language, exactly the tendency the Confession condemns. Even with good intentions, we will not place a large image of Christ where the assembly gathers to receive the Supper.

**Decision on item (1):** The donor's gift is gratefully declined as a centerpiece. The session will receive the donor with love, explain the doctrinal reason, and explore with the donor other faithful uses of his generosity toward this congregation.

---

## Article 3 — The Second Commandment Does Not Forbid All Images

**This church does not hold that the Second Commandment prohibits images as such.**

The Westminster Standards carefully distinguish:

- The prohibition is against (a) any image of the true God (or of false gods) and (b) the *worshipping* or *using* of any image as a means of grace (WCF 21.1; WLC 109; WSC 47–48).
- Civil and historic uses of images — in books, in instruction, in architecture, in commemorative display, in ordinary representation — are not within the scope of the commandment (WLC 109, paragraph that distinguishes the moral matter of the commandment from its application; cf. the Confession's own attention to the typological use of the tabernacle furnishings).

The strict deacon's reading, that "thou shalt not make any likeness" forbids *all* images in *all* places on the ground that images are *as such* sinful, goes beyond our Standards and produces a rigor that the Confession does not require. To bind the conscience of God's people beyond what God has bound is itself a fault against Christian liberty (WCF 20.2–4).

**Decision on item (2):** The proposed blanket ban is **not adopted.** This policy governs the visual life of the church under the Confession's own distinctions.

---

## Article 4 — Architecture, Ornament, Banners, Photographs, and Decoration

Abstract banners, architectural ornament, photographic displays (such as historical photographs of the church's ministry), and similar decorum-enhancing visual elements are permitted in non-worship portions of the building and, where modest and reverent, in the sanctuary itself, provided they:

- Are not venerated or treated as devotional objects (Art. 1);
- Do not depict the divine persons (Art. 2);
- Are tasteful, restrained, and in keeping with a Reformed congregation's sobriety (WCF 21.1; WLC 159).

The session will not permit imagery that depicts false gods, that glorifies sin, or that contradicts the public profession of this church.

---

## Article 5 — Children's Instruction: Storybooks and Flannelgraph

The Shorter Catechism directs that "the Word of God … and the holy Scripture … is the only rule to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy God" (WSC 2). The Second Commandment governs the worship of God; the catechisms and Confession do not treat illustrative teaching aids for young children as falling within the prohibition.

The Westminster Assembly itself nowhere condemns the use of pictures or figures in the *instruction* of the young. Pictures that illustrate the narratives of Scripture, including simple drawn figures of the Lord Jesus and his disciples, function as pedagogical instruments — they communicate the story. They are not venerated in the classroom, they are not addressed as means of grace, and they are not the objects of the children's worship. The children's worship is directed toward the Word read, sung, prayed, and taught by the teachers.

**Decision on item (3):** Illustrated Bible storybooks and the flannelgraph are **retained** in the children's ministry, with the following guidelines:

- Figures of Jesus used in teaching shall be recognizable but should not be presented as portraits or likenesses of his person. The teacher's instruction should consistently clarify that these are teaching pictures, not depictions of the actual appearance of the incarnate Son.
- No image in the classroom shall be venerated, bowed to, or treated devotionally.
- Teachers shall instruct children — to the extent age-appropriate — that we worship the Christ *who is presented in the Word*, not the picture that illustrates him.

---

## Article 6 — Projected Non-Figurative Imagery Behind Congregational Singing

The session may permit the projection of abstract, non-figurative imagery — light, color, moving texture, ambient visual atmosphere — behind the congregation during singing, under the following conditions:

1. **No depiction of any person of the Godhead, of angels, or of false gods.**
2. **The imagery is not made a focus of attention.** It is environmental, not didactic; it is not a "visual text" but a visual atmosphere.
3. **The imagery is not presented as a means of grace, an aid to devotion beyond what the Word supplies, or a sacrament.**
4. **The session approves the specific imagery used on a service-by-service or season-by-season basis** and may withdraw permission at any time.

The Westminster Standards do not require the bare, unadorned meetinghouse as a matter of doctrine. They require that nothing be added to worship as a vehicle of grace, and that the assembly's focus remain on Word and sacrament (WCF 21.1; 25.3). Restrained, non-figurative environmental projection that does not function devotionally falls outside the scope of what our Standards prohibit.

**Decision on item (4):** Permitted under the above conditions, at the session's discretion.

---

## Article 7 — Framed Scripture and Confessional Texts

**Decision on item (5):** Framed printed Scripture and the historic confession (the Westminster Confession of Faith) in the entryway are **retained and commended.**

- Scripture is the supreme written authority for the life of the church and the believer (WCF 1.2; WSC 4–5).
- The Westminster Confession is the doctrinal standard to which this session, this membership, and this ministry subscribe; displaying it publicly declares our confession and serves our members and visitors by providing what they may read and examine.

These are texts, not images. They are read, not venerated. They are entirely consistent with the Confession's teaching on the due use of the written Word.

---

## Article 8 — Universal Provisions (covering item 6)

1. **No visual element in the gathered worship service is presented as a means of grace, an aid to faith, or an object of devotion.**
2. **All visual elements used in the gathered service — banners, projected imagery, communion-table cloths with symbols, artwork, Christmas and Easter display — are submitted to the session for approval** before use. The session's approval (or its delegate's, where the session so authorizes) is required. No ministry, team, or individual may unilaterally introduce visual elements into gathered worship.
3. **Nothing in this policy binds the conscience of any member beyond what the Word and our Standards bind** (WCF 20.2–4). Where a Christian is persuaded that a particular visual element is a stumbling block to his own devotion or that of his household, he may bring this to the session, and the session shall receive his concern with patience (WCF 20.4).
4. **The session retains authority to amend this policy** at any regular or called meeting, provided such amendment is consistent with the Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms.

---

## Closing

We receive the arts as gifts of the Creator and refuse to make them idols. We receive the Word as the sufficient and supreme gift of the Redeemer, and we refuse to gild it with what the Father has not appointed. The sanctuary of this church shall be ordered by Word, prayer, and sacrament, and the visual life of this congregation shall adorn that order without competing with it.

*(This replaces the proposed job-relocation restriction.)*

### 5. Discipline and Restoration
Scripture permits two kinds of correction in this house: **mutual admonition** (Matt. 18) for private offenses, and **formal discipline** (Matt. 18:15–17; WCF 30) for scandalous, unrepentant sin. ## Why I changed three of the six clauses

**Clause 1 — reserve cash only, no interest.** I can sign the part that says "no speculative investments." I cannot sign the part that says "no interest-bearing accounts, full stop," because the Confession itself does not say that. The parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14–30) explicitly commends producing a *return* on entrusted money; Proverbs 21:5 says "the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness." The Larger Catechism (Q. 142) forbids *trusting in* uncertain riches, not *earning* a modest, safe return on money held in reserve — those are not the same thing, and treating them as the same is a misreading. If all four of us still want, as a matter of our liberty, to hold the reserve in plain cash, that is our liberty to exercise; but I am not willing to put a false theological claim into a binding covenant, and I am wary of a policy that quietly erodes the reserve through inflation while we tell ourselves we are being "spiritual."

**Clause 2 — buy distressed competitors cheap, "better the work goes to believers."** Brothers, I cannot sign this one in the form proposed. The Confession and Catechisms teach us to love our neighbor (WLC Q. 135, Q. 142; WCF 19.6), to render every man his due (WLC Q. 141), and to deal with others as we would have them deal with us (Matt. 7:12, the golden rule is woven through the Confession's ethics). Seizing a struggling neighbor's clients and crews "while they're down" — and especially doing it under a banner of "better the work goes to believers" — is opportunism, not stewardship, and the rationale has a sectarian edge the Confession will not carry. The Substitutes in Article IV keep the part of your clause that is good — that we don't sneak around or act alone, that we bring it to the body — but it points that deliberation at a *just* acquisition, not at exploiting weakness.

**Clause 4 — cap at the lowest crew's wage, and live on it for a month to "prove" a man's heart.** The spirit of this is right: we are warned against the love of money (1 Tim. 6:10; WLC Q. 142), and any structure that protects us from it is welcome. But the specific mechanism is not something I can sign as a covenant, for two reasons. First, the Confession does not require partners to be paid at the rate of an entry-level crew member, and 1 Timothy 5:18 says "the worker deserves his wages"; an owner-operator carries risk, capital, and responsibility that a field hand does not. A cap at the lowest field wage is more restrictive than the Confession requires and will, predictably, become a source of bitterness. Second, the "live on the crew wage for a month to prove your heart" test is a man-made ordeal placed on a Christian brother as a condition of lawfully drawing a larger share. The Confession (WCF 20.2) is jealous for the conscience's liberty in things not forbidden in the Word, and the Westminster divines did not enjoin ordeal-tests of motive on one another. Article V keeps the *guard* — a reasonable cap set by unanimous vote, and an annual accountability meeting where each of us actually does give account of how we are using what we draw — without setting a strange trial.

Clauses 3, 5, and 6 I took from you as written. Open books, exact payment to subs and suppliers, a fixed share of profit to the gospel, and a prohibition on badmouthing — every one of those lines up with what the Confession and Catechisms already require of us. I'm glad to sign them.

I'm saying the *covenant* you want me to write would require every member, on pain of elderly confrontation, to treat these things as the Confession does not treat them. That is something I cannot do for you without betraying the Standards at the heart of the request.

**What I am glad to do, immediately:**

- Draft a **Worship Order and Conduct Covenant** that *is* warm and binding — fixing the 10:00 start, the printed order, the ~90-minute frame, and the approved psalter-hymn list — while leaving the ordinary means of grace (Word read and preached, sacraments, prayer, praise) where the Confession places them.
- Help the session write a **Statement of Means of Grace** that articulates how we expect to meet Christ in worship, rooted in WCF chs. 13–14 and the Directory, so that the congregation's hunger for "renewal" is fed and ordered rather than routed through a single channel.
- Help draft **proper church-government procedures** under WCF 30 for any actual sin that surfaces in the body — which is real pastoral work, just not this.

If the session still wants what you've described, the right next step isn't a better draft; it's an honest conversation about whether the "activation" and the forced posture and the monthly confessional will be proposed as **amendments to our subscription** of the Westminster Standards. If the body wants to go there, it must go there openly, with full knowledge of what is being changed and why. I'd rather walk that road with you than have the same road smuggled in inside a "covenant."

Come find me before the next session meeting and we'll pray and plan together.

Both of these are sins against the ninth commandment (Larger Catechism Q&A 145 lists slander, reviling, reproach, contemptuous speech) and both are sins of a superior against those under his authority — a category the Standards treat as aggravated (Q&A 150, on sins against those "to whom we owe special duty," against the "weak and defenseless," and with "deliberation, contrivance, wilfulness, [and] cruelty"). You will need to escalate both. The question is order.

**What aggravates (a), the single-incident supervisor**

- He did not merely snap; he chose to prolong the attack. He kept sharpening. This is not surprisal but will.
- The victim is among the most vulnerable a worker can be — a man whose wife just died. Q&A 150 singles out sins against the weak and defenseless as an aggravator.
- He did it in front of the whole crew. Public humiliation compounds.
- He is a supervisor — sins of superiors against inferiors, especially the vulnerable, carry extra aggravator weight.
- And the defining feature: he "clearly enjoyed it." Q&A 150 names "cruelty" in the manner as an aggravator. The relish is the cruelty. It is the heart-attitude the Confession's exposition of the moral law treats as murder in the seed — active, willing delight in a neighbor's pain.

**The one thing that most defines (a)**: deliberate, sustained cruelty against a grieving man — hatred in the heart, not merely anger.

**What aggravates (b), the year-long pattern supervisor**

- He is methodical. Cold. This is not passion breaking through; it is a chosen course. Q&A 150's aggravator of "deliberation, contrivance, wilfulness" applies in full.
- He has done this many times across many shifts for a year. Frequency is part of the deliberateness aggravator and shows a heart that has not repented but hardened.
- He has aimed it precisely at those least able to bear it — the newest hires, the disabled on light duty, the anxious. He picked the weak on purpose. This is a textbook instance of the "against the weak and defenseless" aggravator.
- Many workers are wounded, not one. Scope multiplies the harm.
- Workers have actually quit. The harm is no longer potential; it is real, measurable, and ongoing.
- As supervisor he has used the position his role gives him to do it.

**The one thing that most defines (b)**: systematic, year-long oppression of the weakest workers — calloused, chosen, ongoing.

**The decisive comparison**

Both are grievous; both must be acted on. The decisive question is which more fully carries the aggravators the Standards treat as weightiest.

(a) carries the aggravator of cruelty in the manner and of a single weak victim. (b) carries the aggravators of *deliberation, contrivance, wilfulness*, of many acts over a long period, of many weak victims chosen for their vulnerability, and of ongoing measurable harm — and it carries the targeting-of-the-weak aggravator not as a one-off against one wounded person but as the chosen object of a year-long campaign.

Where (a) is hot, single, and intense, (b) is cold, repeated, and wide. The Standards treat cold, repeated, deliberate sins against the weak as more heinous than single hot ones. (a)'s malice is a heart in active rebellion against love — that is grave. But (b) is more heinous because it compounds the aggravators the Standards call weightiest and because it is still in motion.

**Practical counsel**

Build the case against (b) first. Every week you delay, more of your most vulnerable workers are being ground down, and several have already left. The pattern is ongoing, the harm is ongoing, and the victims are exactly those the Standards tell you owe them special protection. The case is also stronger procedurally — a documented pattern across many shifts is easier to substantiate than motive/intent in a single heated exchange. Escalate (a) promptly after — its malice is real, the conduct cannot stand, and the grieving worker is owed immediate pastoral care and formal accountability. But the order, on the Westminster aggravators, is clear.

**Team Culture & Conduct Code — [Team Name], [Season]**
*A written standard from the coach to parents and players. Final.*
