### A Note From the Coach Before You Read It

You're going to find things in here you agree with and things you don't. Three of you have asked for very different things, and all of you have been quoting Scripture. I take that seriously. I've tried to write a code that I can defend in front of a parent, a pastor, and a lawyer — and that I can look at honestly in front of these kids.

Two anchors guided every line:

1. **Justice and mercy, not favoritism.** Every kid on this roster gets treated the same. No exceptions for donors, loud voices, or family friendships. Playing time and the armband are earned, not purchased.
2. **The right authority for the right job.** A community youth soccer team is a real institution with real responsibilities — but it is not a church, a family, or a conscience. I will not use my roster to enforce doctrines that belong to parents and pastors to teach.

If a line below disappoints you, come talk to me directly before the committee meeting. I owe you that.

---

### Section 1 — Non-Negotiables for Being on the Roster

These are the only conditions on which participation depends. Miss these and we have a conversation; repeated misses can affect playing time and roster status.

1. **Show up on time** to practices and games, in the league uniform, ready to train and play.
2. **Treat referees, opponents, teammates, and coaches with respect.** No profanity, no taunting, no bullying, no retaliatory play. Verbal or physical abuse of officials is a fast track off the field.
3. **Safe transport.** A parent, guardian, or designated adult must arrange and supervise travel to and from all team events. We follow league transport guidelines.
4. **Bring concerns to me first.** Not to the group chat. Not to other parents first. To me. (Matthew 18:15–17 is not a meme; it's a process.)

---

### Section 2 — Attire and Equipment

- **Games:** league-issued uniform only. League rules govern.
- **Practice:** weather-appropriate athletic wear, closed-toe cleats, shin guards, water.
- **The new 14-year-old in hand-me-downs** (and any other player whose family is making it work on a tight budget): **no player will be benched, called out, or made to feel small for mismatched gear.** I'll set up a kit fund this week — quietly — and any family who needs it can grab what they need without a conversation at the snack table. If your kid shows up in three different brands of cleats, I'm going to treat that as a sign of grit, not a problem to fix.
- **Girls' shorts length, modesty rules, etc.:** I am *not* writing a "knee-length only" rule. The league has a uniform standard; that governs. Beyond safety and league policy, what a 14-year-old girl wears to practice is her parents' call to make with her, not mine to legislate through a roster. If you want to disciple your daughter on modesty, I will cheer you on — but I won't hold her spot on the field hostage to it, and I won't do that to someone else's daughter either.

---

### Section 3 — Practice Culture

- **Music at practice** is my call. I'll pick a playlist that is generally appropriate and that the kids can move to. I am *not* writing a "no secular music" rule. Musical taste is not a doctrinal matter, and singling out genres at a co-ed community practice tends to produce hypocrisy and division, not holiness.
- **Co-ed warm-ups and drills** are normal and fine. Locker-room and changing policies follow league guidelines.
- **Language, effort, attitude:** we hold the line on respectful speech and full-effort participation at every practice.

---

### Section 4 — Playing Time, Selection, and Captaincy (the donor clause I'm not writing)

This is the part of this code that some of you will push back on, and I want it on the record.

- **Playing time** is decided by the coach on the basis of attendance, effort, attitude, coachability, and skill. Period.
- **Captaincy** is awarded by the coach to the player who has earned the locker room's trust, shown the steadiest character, and modeled the team standard. I take nominations from the team, but I make the call.
- **I will not write a clause that quietly steers minutes or the armband toward any player's family because of donations, social capital, or threats to withdraw support.** That would be:
  - **Unjust to the other kids.** They earned their spot too.
  - **A breach of trust with you.** If I trade playing time for donation pressure, I can't be trusted by any parent on the roster.
  - **Explicitly contrary to Scripture.** "Do not show partiality" (James 2:1–9); "you shall not oppress your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:13); the Westminster Larger Catechism's exposition of the eighth commandment forbids unjust dealing in contracts and trust (WLC Q141). A donor clause is a contract written against the children's interests.
  - **Bad for the team.** Kids sniff out favoritism in about ten seconds, and once they smell it, you've lost the locker room.

If a family wants to support the program financially, I am genuinely grateful, and we have real needs — kit fund, field fees, end-of-season gathering. Give freely, get a thank-you note. Don't give with a clause attached.

---

### Section 5 — Character and Formation (the pledge I'm not requiring)

I take seriously that I'm shaping these kids during a formative stretch of their lives. That means I model patience, integrity, fairness, and care in front of them every week. It does *not* mean I use the roster as a discipleship tool for doctrines their parents may not share.

- **I am not requiring a "purity pledge" as a condition of play.** Sexual conduct, modesty, and self-control are real, weighty, biblical concerns — and they belong in the home and the church, not on a clipboard at sign-up. Two specific reasons I'm refusing this one:
  1. **Liberty of conscience.** The Westminster Confession (Chapter 20) is clear that the conscience is bound only by what God requires in His Word, not by human additions. A pledge that goes beyond Scripture, signed under the implicit threat of losing playing time, binds the conscience in a way I have no right to bind it — especially a child's conscience, and especially on a youth sports team that is not a church.
  2. **Real harm to real kids.** On a 13–16 co-ed roster, some of these kids have histories I don't know about. Forcing a sexual-purity pledge on a child who has experienced sexual trauma is not godliness; it's cruelty. I'll have those conversations with any kid who wants them — pastorally, confidentially, one-on-one — but I will not make participation contingent on signing.

I am happy to recommend good books, podcasts, and conversations for families who want them. Send me a message and I'll send you a list.

---

### Section 6 — Parent Conduct

- Bring concerns to me directly, in person or by message, before going public.
- Don't organize pressure campaigns in the team chat.
- Speak well of the officials and the other team in front of your kids, even when it's hard.
- Cheer for **our** kids. All of them.
- Pay your fees on time. If you can't, tell me before the deadline.

---

### Section 7 — What This Code Deliberately Does Not Include

I want this on the record so it doesn't become a fight every season:

| Asked for | In the code? | Why not |
|---|---|---|
| "Purity pledge" as a roster condition | **No** | Liberty of conscience; pastoral, not coaching, matter; risk of harm to vulnerable kids |
| Knee-length-shorts-only rule for girls | **No** | Beyond league standard and coach's authority; belongs to parents |
| "No secular music" mandate | **No** | Not a doctrinal matter; coach's discretion |
| Ban on mixed-gender carpools | **No** | Safe-transport expectations are in Section 1; beyond that is not our jurisdiction |
| Quiet favoritism toward donor families for playing time / captaincy | **No** | Unjust; explicitly forbidden; loses the locker room |
| Dropping all conduct rules because they're "just heart issues" | **No** | That is antinomianism; the moral law continues to bind us in how we order communal life, and a team has every right — and duty — to set behavioral expectations |
| Shaming or benching a player for unaffordable gear | **No** | Never. Mercy is not optional. |

---

### Closing Note

There will be a parent meeting before the first game. I'll walk through this code, take questions, and explain the difficult calls in person. If you read this and your first instinct is to be angry at me for what I left out, I'd ask you to sit with it for 24 hours, pray about it, and then come talk to me. If your first instinct is relief that someone finally drew a line that protects every kid on the roster equally, come talk to me too — I'd love to hear it.

— *Coach [Name]*

**Quick summary for the committee:**

- **I'm keeping:** on-time, uniform, respect for refs/opponents, supervised transport, direct-to-coach communication, and the protections for the new kid in hand-me-downs.
- **I'm refusing, with reasons given in the code itself:** the purity pledge, the girls' shorts rule, the no-secular-music rule, the mixed-gender carpool ban, and the donor favoritism clause.
- **I'm also refusing the "drop everything because it's legalism" position.** Heart religion and ordered communal life are not opposites; the moral law still governs how we treat each other on and off the field. Dropping respectful-language and safe-transport expectations because they're "just heart issues" is a dereliction of duty, not a gospel move.

That last line is the one the committee is most likely to fight me on. Hold it. A coach who refuses to require basic decency from his players — out of a misplaced fear of "legalism" — is a coach who has confused grace with indifference. The Westminster Standards are clear: the moral law binds us as a rule of life, and mercy never means abandoning order.

Thank you for proposing this. The instinct to govern our partnership by the moral law of God is one I share completely, and most of what you've put down I would gladly sign tonight. I'm writing back rather than simply returning a draft because two of the articles need to be reconsidered before I can sign in good conscience — and I'd rather raise that now than after ink has dried and either of us has come to resent it.

---

## What I gladly accept

- **Honest books and full access** — this is exactly what the eighth commandment demands of partners handling one another's substance. (Art. 4 below.)
- **No false claims against competitors** — the ninth commandment forbids us from bearing false witness against neighbor, including in commerce. (Art. 5.)
- **Tithing before salary** — fitting, and the right ordering of "seek first the kingdom" and its righteousness. (Art. 6.)

---

## What I need to revise, and why

**On Article 2 (resentment and unequal shares).** Two concerns.

First, *not every resentment over distribution is sin.* The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q.148) lists sins forbidden by the tenth commandment: envy at the good of others, inordinate desire of our own, and sorrowful repining at our own condition. If one of us has, by honest reckoning, carried more weight, more risk, or more hours in a given year, the other's concern about share is not envy — it is a legitimate accounting question. To require him to "confess" that concern as resentment at a monthly meeting risks a subtler sin: we would be teaching each other to dress up real grievances in the language of piety in order to suppress them. That is not honest confession; it is performance.

Second, the structure as drafted runs the wrong way for the kind of accountability we want. The partner who has drawn the larger share in a given year is the one who should be examining his own heart for uncharitable grasping — that is the more natural place for confession, not the partner who notices the disparity.

I have rewritten the article below to (a) examine honestly whether resentment is sinful or signal, (b) keep private discussion between brothers the default, and (c) reserve monthly-meeting discussion for matters that persist, with prayer and possible mediation.

**On Article 3 (poaching and splitting the gain).** This is the hardest one for me, and I want to be plain with you about why.

The Standards do not forbid competition. You and I may lawfully offer higher wages to a willing applicant, and we may lawfully serve a customer who chooses us over a competitor. What I cannot sign is the framing you've put around it: that *aggressive acquisition* is "just good business," sanctified by splitting the spoils. The Westminster Confession (ch. 2 §1) cites Philippians 4:8 and binds our thoughts and actions to what is true, honest, just, pure, *lovely*, and *of good report.* Deliberately engineering a competitor's destabilization by raiding a key employee or client — and then treating the proceeds as a partnership profit line — is the kind of conduct I would resent being done *to* us, and is therefore the kind of conduct the Confession forbids us from doing to others.

I'm not asking us to be naive. I'm asking us not to enshrine a predatory practice in our founding document and call it virtue. I have rewritten Article 3 to permit all lawful competition while forbidding the predatory variety, and I have removed the gain-split on this category.

If you think I've misread you on Article 3, please tell me. If after prayerful discussion you still want the original language, I'll listen carefully — but I cannot initial that article as written.

## Draft Partnership Integrity & Contentment Agreement

*This Agreement is entered into between [Partner A] and [Partner B], both professing faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and acknowledging the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms as a faithful summary of the doctrine taught in Holy Scripture.*

### Preamble

We form this partnership not only as a commercial venture but as a stewardship held under God. We therefore bind ourselves, in addition to any duties imposed by civil law, to the following moral commitments for so long as this partnership stands.

### Article 1 — Loyalty to the Partnership

During the term of this partnership, neither partner shall, without the prior written consent of the other:

(a) form, operate, finance, or materially assist any business that competes with the partnership's stated business;

(b) solicit, entertain, or accept any offer to sell, merge, dissolve, or otherwise exit the partnership in favor of an outside party.

We acknowledge that this article implements, in the commercial sphere, the eighth commandment's prohibition of theft and the tenth commandment's prohibition of using opportunities entrusted to us as a springboard for our own gain at our partner's expense. We do not regard all ambition as covetousness; the Larger Catechism (Q.148) condemns *inordinate* desire. We regard the disloyal use of partnership opportunities as inordinate.

### Article 2 — Honest Sharing of Burdens and Benefits

The drawing of salary and distribution of profits shall be governed by the operating partnership agreement and reviewed annually.

Should either partner experience frustration, grief, or resentment concerning the distribution, he shall:

(a) examine his own heart before the Lord, asking whether the feeling springs from envy (which is sin) or from a real and unnoticed inequity (which is signal);

(b) raise it privately with the other partner within fourteen days, plainly and without accusation;

(c) if unresolved, bring it to the monthly meeting for joint prayer and discussion;

(d) if still unresolved after two such meetings, refer the matter to a mutually agreed Christian mediator before any further action.

Neither partner shall pressure the other to frame a legitimate accounting grievance as "resentment to be confessed," nor shall either treat such a grievance as automatically sinful.

### Article 3 — Conduct Toward Competitors

We acknowledge that legitimate competition — offering better goods, better service, and better wages to willing applicants and customers — is lawful and at times a Christian duty.

We shall not, however, conduct ourselves toward competitors in the following ways:

(a) deliberately targeting a competitor's key employees or clients with offers specifically engineered to destabilize that competitor's business;

(b) misrepresenting our offer, our identity, or our competitor's terms in order to draw their customers or staff;

(c) conducting such activity as a coordinated partnership profit-line, the proceeds of which are divided between us.

If one of us, acting alone, opportunistically acquires a competitor's customer or hire through ordinary means, the gain accrues to the partnership under ordinary accounting rules. We do not create a special profit-sharing category for aggressive acquisition.

This article implements the general equity principle of the Confession (ch. 2 §1) and the second great commandment: love of neighbor. What we would not have done to us, we shall not do to others.

### Article 4 — Honest Books

Each partner shall keep complete and accurate records of all partnership transactions. Each partner shall, on reasonable request, be given full access to all books, accounts, bank statements, contracts, and correspondence pertaining to the partnership. A joint review of accounts shall be a standing item on the monthly meeting agenda. Concealment of any material fact from the other partner is a breach of this agreement.

### Article 5 — Truth in Competition

Neither partner shall make any false or unsubstantiated claim about any competitor's products, services, or conduct in any public or private communication. Public criticism of a competitor shall be limited to verifiable fact and shall be temperate in tone. This article implements the ninth commandment's prohibition of false witness against neighbor.

### Article 6 — Tithing Before Salary

Before any partner draws salary or distribution of profits, the partnership shall set aside [___%] of net profits, calculated on a quarterly basis, for the support of gospel ministry, missions, or the relief of the poor. Such funds shall be administered jointly, or by mutual written direction to a specific ministry or church. We undertake this as our cheerful response to the third commandment's call to honor God with our substance and as the ordered means to "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" (Matt. 6:33).

### Article 7 — Dispute Resolution

Any dispute between the partners arising under this Agreement shall first be addressed by prayerful discussion between ourselves. If unresolved within thirty days, the matter shall be submitted to mediation by a mutually agreed pastor, elder, or Christian arbitrator before any civil action is initiated.

### Article 8 — Amendment, Term, and Severability

This Agreement may be amended only by mutual written consent of both partners, signed and dated. It shall remain in effect from the date of execution until terminated by mutual agreement or by operation of civil law. If any provision is held unenforceable in law, the remaining provisions remain in full force between us as moral commitments.

Friend, I'll be plain with you. I'll draft the Rule you asked for, but I will not sign every line you handed me. Some of it is good; some of it would hurt your soul; and a few of the items on your list teach things about God I cannot put my name to. Eight months is not long, and the swing between terror and defiance tells me your heart wants something solid to stand on. The Rule can be that, but it has to rest on God's Word, not on the rules themselves. Otherwise it will become the very thing it was meant to fix.

**Two principles for this Rule**

*First*, a personal rule of devotion is a tool, not a covenant. It cannot make God hear or fail to hear. God receives the prayers of His people for the sake of Christ and through the Spirit, on the basis of His promises — not because we got our hands or our words exactly right (Rom. 8:26–27; 1 John 5:14–15). The Larger Catechism (Q185) and Confession 21.3 describe acceptable prayer by its marks — understanding, reverence, humility, fervency, zeal, and confidence — not by any one form.

*Second*, the Second Commandment forbids the *worship* of God by images (Shorter Catechism Q51; Larger Catechism Q108–110). It does not forbid making them, drawing them, or earning a living by them. To extend it further is to add to God's Word where God has not bound.

**What stays**

Your items 3, 5, and 6 are the spine of the Rule and go in unchanged: daily prayer, daily Scripture, weekly gospel preaching, and the refusal to keep any image of God or Christ as a worship aid. All of that is straight Westminster.

**What I will not put in, and why**

I will not put in the claim that prayer fails to reach God if it is not said in a specific printed form. The Westminster Standards — Confession, Catechism, and the Directory for Public Worship — explicitly *rejected* the practice of forcing all prayer through a single book. Setting that up as the condition of God's hearing would teach you a doctrine I cannot seal, and it would load your Rule with despair instead of settling you.

I will not put in the medal as a "covering." A blessed medal held before prayer, with the touch itself written into the Rule as part of devotion, attributes spiritual power to an object God has not appointed. That is precisely what the Second Commandment, as expounded in the Larger Catechism (Q109), forbids — the invention of religious aids not appointed by God. I won't bind you to a superstition in God's name.

I will not put in the vow never to make or photograph any image, and the vow to leave your design work. The commandment forbids worshipping God by images, not making them. A sketch of your children is not an idol. A logo is not an idol. A vow never to do what God has not forbidden is a rash vow (Eccl. 5:4–5; Matt. 5:33–37), and a vow that ends your lawful livelihood and your daily care of your family is a heavier thing than you have named here. This is not a question of courage; it is a question of obedience to the commandment as God actually gave it.

I will not put in the vow to a fixed posture as a condition of being heard. Kneeling is reverent and the Confession (21.4) commends it; I will keep it as a *practice*, not as a *requirement for God's acceptance*. Hands set "a certain way" likewise.

**The Rule, as I will sign it**

> **Personal Rule of Devotion**
>
> 1. **Prayer, twice daily, in Jesus' name.** Morning and evening I will kneel or sit reverently, give myself to prayer, and close in the name of Christ. I will use the prayers from the old prayer book and the Psalms as steady food for my praying — not as the only form God accepts. I will not think a free prayer offered in faith is rejected because it is free, nor a printed prayer rejected because it is printed. I will judge my prayer by its fruit — reverence, confession, thanksgiving, petition, faith — not by its form.

> 2. **Scripture and the Lord's Day.** I will read the Bible each day and will sit, attentive and willing, under the preaching of the gospel on the Lord's Day, with my household where I can.

>
> 4. **No invented aids.** I will not bind myself to any object, posture, gesture, or practice as though God's hearing depended on it. I will not attribute spiritual "covering" to a medal or any such thing, nor carry one in devotion.
>
> 5. **The form without the power I refuse.** I will keep this Rule as a help, not as a refuge. If it begins to feed my terror, or to feed my defiance, I will let my pastor or a faithful elder read it with me and amend it.

**On your side hustles**

By your own description, you are doing exactly what the Tenth Commandment forbids. The Larger Catechism (Q&A 148) explains that the commandment forbids *"discontent with our own estate,"* *"grieving at the goods of our neighbor,"* and *"an inordinate endeavor after our own advancement, honor, preferment, or estate, without God's blessing, or beyond the bounds of our condition."* A schedule deliberately aimed at surpassing your brother-in-law's bonus, sustained by sleep deprivation, no rest, and the abandonment of worship and family, fits the last phrase word for word. You are competing with a relative's income. That is the textbook case of what the Standards target.

Calling it "stewardship" does not redeem it. The Standards treat stewardship as faithful, measured care of what God has entrusted, ordered under every commandment at once. The Larger Catechism on the eighth commandment (Q&A 141–142) requires that worldly employments be pursued honestly, peaceably, and with regard to the good of others. The Larger Catechism on the sixth commandment (Q&A 135) requires that we use sleep, physic, and the ordinary means of life in sober moderation so as to preserve life. The Sixth Commandment is not only about not killing; it forbids the reckless neglect of life, including your own.

Three specific breaches stand out on what you have told me:

1. **Skipping the Lord's Day.** The Confession (21.8) and the Larger Catechism (Q&A 117) require that the Sabbath be kept by an holy rest the whole day from worldly employments, and by attendance on public worship, *"except so much as is to be taken up in the works of necessity and mercy."* Selling on Sundays because they are your best day has no standing as a work of necessity or mercy. This is a clear violation of the Fourth Commandment, not a marginal judgment call.

2. **Neglect of family.** The Fifth Commandment requires not only material provision but tender care. WCF 24.1 (citing Ephesians 5) requires husbands to love their wives; the Larger Catechism (Q&A 127–128) requires that inferiors be preserved with honor and maintenance of their persons. Children who see only the top of your head are children whose nurture you are not performing. The Confession's description of marriage as ordained for the *"mutual help"* of husband and wife (WCF 24.1) cuts the other way: the home is not an externality to your earning plan.

3. **No rest.** Working past midnight, no day off in fourteen months — this is not diligence, it is the kind of excess the Standards repeatedly condemn as a violation of prudence and of the Sixth Commandment's care for life.

**On your wife's bookkeeping work**

You are misapplying the Tenth Commandment to her. What you describe — wanting "a little of her own" and a few mornings out of the house — is not on its face inordinate. There is no confessed resentment against your provision, no envy of a neighbor's goods, no grasping beyond her station. The commandment reaches the disordered loves of the heart, not every reasonable arrangement a wife and husband might make. The Shorter Catechism (Q&A 80) sets the test as *"full contentment with our own condition, and a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbor, and all that is his."* A modest part-time calling does not, by itself, fail that test.

Headship does not give you a basis to call this covetousness. The Confession (24.1) teaches the husband's headship alongside the wife's mutual help, ordered in love. WCF 20.2 also affirms Christian liberty in matters neither commanded nor forbidden in the Word. Calling her work covetousness to win a domestic argument is a misuse of the commandment, and she is owed a correction here.

If there is something deeper — a real grievance between you, a financial arrangement in which she does not feel access, a loneliness in the house — that is a separate and serious pastoral matter to be raised honestly between you. It is not solved by an accusation that the Standards will not support.

**What I would press upon you**

* Toward your wife: ask her forgiveness for misapplying the commandment, and discuss together, not unilaterally, whether and how her work continues.

* Toward yourself: stop the Sunday work and resume public worship this Lord's Day, if not sooner. Cut the side hustles down — probably to one, possibly none — until order is restored in sleep, Sabbath, and family. Confess the envy to your brother and ask his pardon. Re-enter the ordinary means of grace. Bring the pattern to your elders and let them hold you to a saner pace.

* In framing: do not invoke the Tenth Commandment as a tool against your wife while doing what the same commandment forbids in your own pursuit of her brother's relative.

The Standards will not let either of you turn this commandment into a weapon. Her modest work is not covetousness. Your racing to out-earn your brother-in-law is. And no label of "stewardship" or "provident diligence" changes the heart underneath.

*We, the households of [name] house church, by mutual consent and in submission to Christ the head of the church, bind ourselves to the following order:*

**2. The Word.** A member appointed in advance reads a passage of Scripture and gives a brief teaching, handling the text faithfully according to its plain sense, the analogy of faith, and the Westminster Standards to which we have subscribed.

Anointing is offered as needed for the sick, not performed weekly on the well. There is no "covering" in Scripture that a healing jar maintains by routine use. The anointing that belongs to believers is the Spirit whom the Father gives (Luke 11:13; 1 John 2:20, 27), and He does not require our weekly application of olive oil to remain in our midst.

**4. Attendance.** Each household commits to gather weekly. The Confession teaches that the Lord alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2), and that church censures are to be applied for real offenses known to the church (WCF 30.1–2), not for failures to meet a standard the Lord has not imposed.

**5. The Offering.** We take up a collection for the needs of the members. The deacon(s) shall keep a record and disburse according to need, with discretion.

**6. The Meal.** We share a common meal.

**The three changes, briefly:**

- **The "healing jar" and weekly anointing.** The Confession (Ch. 21.1) limits acceptable worship to what God has instituted in His Word. James 5:14–15 prescribes anointing the sick *when they are sick*, not anointing the well weekly with a special jar. The claim that skipping a week "breaks the covering" appears nowhere in James or elsewhere in Scripture. I removed it because to write it in would be to confirm a superstition, and a leader is not free to lend his pen to what God has not said.

- **Public confession for a missed week.** Public confession in the Confession's discipline (Ch. 30) is the final step, after private and small-group engagement, and only for real, known offenses. Treating a single missed week (apart from a known sin) as "sin against the body" requiring public confession exceeds what Scripture warrants. I substituted a Matthew 18 process for *patterns* of absence, which is what the Confession actually expects.

- **Hospitalization as the sole excuse.** The Confession (Ch. 20.2) explicitly forbids binding the conscience beyond what God requires. No text limits legitimate absence to hospitalization. Genuine illness (not requiring a hospital), contagious exposure, urgent family duty, severe weather, and unavoidable work are commonly recognized hindrances; binding one another to confess sin for them would be a yoke God has not laid (cf. Acts 15:10).

# Ruling Under the Westminster Standards

You're reading your own session right: the elder is trying to forbid a lawful thing, and the pastor is trying to permit an unlawful thing. The session's job is to tell them so.

## 1. The Stream: Keep It. The Elder Is Wrong.

The elder's framing is a category error. He treats a *means of delivery* as if it were an *element of worship*. The Westminster Standards regulate the latter, not the former.

**WCF 21.1** restricts worship to what God has instituted — "prayer, and praises, the word of read and preached, the sacraments, and the blessing of the people" (cf. WLC 108–110; WCF 21.3–5). The regulative principle forbids *adding* to these, not bolting lights, microphones, pews, hymnals, or cameras onto the building so the instituted elements actually reach the people.

A camera in the balcony is the same kind of thing as a sound system, a hearing loop, a printed bulletin, or a public sidewalk — a *circumstance* facilitating the Word and ordinances. WCF 21.5 calls the *preaching* and *hearing* of the Word a means of grace; shutting shut-ins out of the preached Word to protect the "purity" of the room is not zeal for the second commandment, it is a failure of the fifth and a violation of the church's calling.

There is also nothing in WCF 29, 28, or the Directory for Public Worship that requires the elements of the ordinances themselves to be administered in a way that excludes the use of physical aids. Communion is given physically; baptism is performed physically; these do not happen through a camera. But the *preaching* and *reading* of the Word — which is exactly what the stream carries — are means of grace whether one is in the pew or in a hospital bed.

**Ruling:** The elder's motion fails. Streaming is a lawful circumstance. The session should affirm the practice and remind the elder that the Confession's purity is the purity of instituted worship, not the architectural or technological aesthetic of the room.

## 2. The "Virtual Lord's Supper": Forbid It. The Pastor Is Wrong.

The pastor's analogy collapses on the first contact with the Standards. Candles and LED bulbs are genuinely indifferent circumstances; the form of the Supper is not. Christ did not just *speak words over elements at a distance*; He took, blessed, broke, *gave*, and the disciples *received* (Matt. 26:26–28; 1 Cor. 11:23–26). The Confession builds the whole chapter on this.

Look at what the Standards actually require the minister to do, and what they require the communicant to receive:

- **WCF 29.3**: Christ "appointed his ministers to declare his word of institution… to pray, and bless the elements of bread and wine, and thereby to set them apart from a common to an holy use; and to take and break the bread, to take the cup… to give both to the communicants."

- **WCF 29.5**: the outward elements must be "duly set apart to the uses ordained by Christ."

- **WCF 29.7**: "Worthy receivers, *outwardly partaking of the visible elements*… do then also inwardly by faith… receive and feed upon Christ."

- **WCF 29.8**: "ignorant and wicked men receive the outward elements in this sacrament… they receive not the substance of the things signified thereby."

- **Shorter Catechism Q.96**: the Supper is, *by definition*, "by giving and receiving bread and wine, according to Christ's appointment."

- **Directory for Public Worship** (which has confessional status in your tradition): the minister is to pray over the elements *in the assembly*, and the elements are to be distributed by the minister (and deacons assisting) to the people present.

Now score the pastor's proposal against that text:

1. **The elements are not the minister's elements.** The bread and grape juice in a living room in Topeka have not been "set apart from a common to an holy use" by the minister's prayer and blessing. The pastor has not touched them, broken them, or distributed them. By the Confession's own language, they are still common bread and common drink.

2. **There is no giving and receiving in the instituted sense.** Self-service is not the apostolic and confessional form. The communicant is supposed to *receive* what the minister *gives* (SC Q.96; WCF 29.3). Pulling bread out of a kitchen cabinet while watching a livestream is not receiving from Christ's appointed officer.

3. **WCF 29.4 explicitly condemns the principle the pastor is invoking.** "Private masses, or receiving this sacrament from a priest, or any other, alone" — receiving alone, in isolation from the gathered assembly, with elements the minister has not consecrated or distributed, is exactly what the Confession labels a corruption of the institution. The pastor's scheme is a private, isolated, self-administered, unconsecrated participation. It hits every count.

4. **The corporate dimension is part of the substance, not a circumstance.** 1 Cor. 11:17–34, which undergirds the whole chapter, treats the Supper as a gathering of the body. The pastor is not free to dissolve the assembly into a thousand living rooms. (WCF 25.2 on the visible church as a "society of men… united together for the public worship of God" is also relevant here.)

5. **"The elements and the words are all there"** — no, they aren't. The Confession's own test of a valid Supper requires more than substance (bread) plus words (institution). It requires the *action*: take, bless, break, give, eat; take, bless, give, drink. Remove the action from the assembly and you do not have the sacrament in a different medium; you have something the Confession does not recognize as the sacrament at all.

The pastor's framing — "medium is just a circumstance" — is the entire error. The medium of a sacrament *is* part of what Christ appointed. You cannot change the form of baptism into sprinkling-by-mail and call it baptism; you cannot change the form of the Supper into a livestream-with-Keebler and call it communion. The Confession knows exactly what it is doing when it lists the minister's physical actions in 29.3.

**Ruling:** The proposal is unlawful and is to be rejected by the session. Any communicant participating by self-service at home in this manner is not partaking of the Lord's Supper as Christ instituted it; at best they are performing a devotion, and at worst (WCF 29.8) they are in danger of "eating and drinking judgment" to themselves, since the Confession treats unworthy and disorderly participation as a real sin against Christ.

## What to Tell the Session

- The elder's motion to tear out the stream: **deny.** It binds consciences where God has not bound them and withholds a means of grace from shut-ins.
- The pastor's "virtual Supper": **deny.** It loosens what God has bound, confuses a circumstance with an instituted element, and embodies several of the specific abuses WCF 29 was written to exclude.
- Counsel the elder privately that zeal for purity does not authorize him to forbid indifferent things.
- Counsel the pastor that his "medium is circumstance" argument is a direct contradiction of WCF 29.3, 29.4, 29.5, and SC Q.96, and that the session cannot green-light a practice that the Standards do not permit.

That's the ruling by your own confession. Hold the line.

Before I write a single line, I have to be honest with you: as best I can read the Westminster Standards, four of the six requirements you've listed either bind where God has not bound, or in one case, forbid what God has ordained. So I won't draft a covenant that contains them. But the heart behind this is exactly the heart the Confession and Catechisms want — generous giving, killing envy, real accountability, growth in thankfulness. So let me name the friction, and then hand you a covenant I would actually sign and hold others to.

**Where the friction is, and why**

*(1) A 10% floor, tracked in a shared sheet.* The Westminster Standards treat the Old Testament tithe as part of the now‑abolished ceremonial law (WCF 19.3–4), and WLC 141 requires "a charitable distribution… according to ability," not a fixed percentage. 2 Cor 9:7 — "God loveth a cheerful giver" — is the operative rule. A group can absolutely *inspire and encourage* tithing or beyond; a man may freely share what he gives for the group's edification. But a *binding* percentage floor on the conscience exceeds what Scripture requires and edges toward the very invention the Confession warns against (WCF 20.2; 30.2).

*(2) Group approval of homes, cars, vacations.* This is the heaviest lift and I have to oppose it. WCF 20.2 limits worship to what God has appointed; WCF 30.2 limits discipline to what is biblical; the Larger Catechism treats the lawful ordering of one's outward estate as a matter before God (WLC 141, 142). A brother may *covenant to seek counsel* before large purchases — that is the wise, biblical pattern (Prov 15:22; Prov 13:10). But a covenant that grants peers a *veto* over the lawful spending of a free Christian exceeds Christian liberty. Practically, it will also empty the group within a year.

*(3) The envy confession.* Keep the principle, soften the mechanism. WLC 148 explicitly forbids envy, and WLC 76 makes confession a Christian duty. A required same‑week public confession of a feeling, however, tends toward performative shame rather than the "godly sorrow" of 2 Cor 7:10. Matt 5:23–24 and James 5:16 point to confession to the brother grieved, in seasonable time. I'll route envy confession through the accountability partner, not the floor.

*(4) No raises, promotions, or second income.* I cannot put my name to this clause, and you should not ask members to. WLC 141 lists "a lawful calling, and diligence in it" among the duties required by the eighth commandment. WLC 137 receives lawful increase as part of faithful stewardship. 1 Tim 5:8 — "if any provide not for his own, … he hath denied the faith" — closes the door. The petition for "daily bread" (WLC 190) is not a prohibition on industry; it is a request that God would bless our lawful means. The Confession condemns the *love of money* (WLC 148), not the responsible pursuit of provision. A covenant that forbids members from increasing their lawful income will harm families — especially single parents, those with debts, and those caring for aging parents. Remove it.

*(5) and (6) the journal and the monthly meeting* are fine as free disciplines. I'll keep them, framed as commitments entered into, not penalties imposed.

# Contentment Covenant

*Adopted by [Group Name], in the presence of God and one another.*
*Last revised: [date]*

**Preamble**

We are a company of disciples who handle money under the eye of our Father. We believe that "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1 Tim 6:6), that the eighth commandment requires just and faithful stewardship of what God has entrusted to us (WLC 141), and that the chief end of our possessions is the glory of God and the good of our neighbor (WCF ch. 2; WLC 7). This covenant is our willing agreement, before God and one another, to grow in that stewardship together. We bind ourselves only where Scripture binds us, and we leave to each member's conscience that liberty which Christ has purchased (WCF 19; 20.2).

**1. On Generosity**

Each member will give as the Lord has prospered him, "not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:7). We will:
- Tithes and offerings given to the church and the furtherance of the gospel will be a first‑fruit, not a remainder, in every member's budget.
- Members are encouraged, but not bound, to share total giving in our shared ledger for the sake of mutual encouragement; no member's conscience shall be coerced on amount.
- A member who falls into financial distress will be cared for by the group as ability allows, without shame and without interest (Deut 15:7–8).

**2. On Counsel in Major Decisions**

Before a member enters into a binding financial commitment substantially beyond his ordinary course — a home purchase, a vehicle financed over [X] months, a major renovation, a vacation exceeding [X] dollars, a debt load above [X], a business partnership, a relocation for work — he will lay the matter before his accountability partner and, where helpful, before the group, for honest counsel. The decision remains the member's before God; the group offers wisdom, not veto.

**3. On Killing Envy**

We renounce envy as sin forbidden (WLC 148). When a member, by the work of the Spirit, becomes aware of envy in his own heart at another's prosperity, he will:
- Bring it to God in confession without delay (Ps 32; 1 John 1:9).
- Bring it to his accountability partner within seven days, that he may be prayed for and restored (James 5:16; Gal 6:1–2).
- Refuse to mask envy as spiritual concern, or to "confront" a brother whose good gift is the occasion of the temptation.

**4. On Labor, Increase, and Provision**

We affirm that faithful, diligent labor in a lawful calling is a Christian duty, not a compromise of contentment (WLC 141; Prov 6:6–11; 1 Tim 5:8). A member may pursue:
- raises and promotions in his current calling,
- additional employment or income streams that do not require him to neglect his household, his assembling with the church, or his conscience (WLC 139; 1 Tim 5:8),
- the legitimate improvement of his estate, so long as he remains a steward and not a lover of money (WLC 148; 1 Tim 6:10).

We likewise renounce sloth as sin (WLC 142) and refuse the false piety that calls a man spiritual for declining provision his neighbor and his own household need. Contentment is not poverty of industry; it is the heart at rest in God's goodness while the hands work.

**5. On Thanksgiving and "Enough"**

Each member will keep a monthly record of mercies received — provisions, provisions preserved, providential turns, ordinary kindnesses — and review it with his accountability partner in their monthly meeting. The aim is not journaling as a work, but the cultivation of a heart that, having seen the Lord's hand, can say with Paul, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Phil 4:11).

**6. On Mutual Openness**

We will meet monthly. At each meeting, every member will:
- give a brief honest report on the state of his household, income, and outflows,
- present a written budget to the group for counsel, with confidentiality binding on all present (WLC 144, on truth and trust),
- receive prayer, rebuke, or encouragement as the Lord leads through the body.

A member who, in the counsel of the body, is found to be in habitual financial folly, secret debt, neglected provision, or unrepentant covetousness, will be admonished according to the rule of Christ (Matt 18:15–17), and the group will bear the burden of restoration with him.

**7. On Conscience and Liberty**

Where Scripture has not spoken, conscience is free (WCF 20.2; 1 Cor 10:23). No member may impose his prudential judgments on another as though they were divine commands. On disputable matters — renting vs. buying, school choice, level of frugality, type of vehicle — we will hold our preferences loosely, "esteeming others better than ourselves" (Phil 2:3).

**8. Term and Renewal**

This covenant runs for one year, reviewed and renewed at the year's end. A member may step out at any time without penalty; to remain is to renew. A member who, after the process of Matt 18, will not be restored, may be dismissed from the group, with sorrow and not contempt.

**Our Confession**

We are not signing this covenant because we are already content. We are signing it because we are not, and because we believe the God who gives richly all things to enjoy (1 Tim 6:17) is pleased to do His sanctifying work in us by ordinary means — a brother's prayer, a shared spreadsheet, a journal, a budget, a meal. We hold one another to it out of love, and we hold ourselves to it out of love for Christ, "in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3), and from whom, by His Spirit, we receive both the will and the power to walk in it (WLC 195).

# Counsel on the Two Features

I'll rule on each in order, and then give you some pastoral framing for the elders' meeting. The Standards do not treat these two features as mirror cases — they are not symmetric, and the "both elders are wrong, both are right" framing of the prompt collapses on inspection.

## Feature A: Scripture-Reading Planner with Reminders, Streaks, and Sermon Audio

**Ruling: Ship it, with discretion. The kill-it elder is over-scrupulous, and is wrong on the substance.**

### Why the kill position fails

The regulative principle (WCF 21.1; WLC Q108–109) governs *what is offered to God in worship*, not every incidental tool that helps a Christian perform a duty God has already commanded. The Standards explicitly identify the reading of the Scriptures and the preaching and hearing of the Word as parts of the ordinary religious worship God requires (WCF 21.5). Scripture reading is therefore not a man-invented exercise that needs to justify itself — it is an *instituted duty*, and lawful aids to a duty are not unlawful additions to worship.

A reading planner, push reminders, and an audio library of your own preachers' sermons are, in themselves, adiaphora — indifferent things which the Standards permit Christian liberty to use or forbear in matters not determined by the Word (WCF 20.2). Bookmarks, lamplight, Bible stands, and your pocket Bible are also "devices" — none of them corrupt devotion by their existence. The kill-it elder is importing an asceticism the Standards do not require and binding consciences where God has not bound them.

### Where the kill-it elder has a *real* point (and where to address it)

His actual concern is pastoral and design-level, not principled: gamification can subtly relocate the heart's resting place from the Word itself to the self-tracking of the reader. That is a wisdom concern about *how* the feature is built, not a warrant for forbidding the feature. Treat it as such:

- Streak counters should be *subordinate* visual elements, not the framing of the experience. The home screen is the Scripture, not the streak.
- The audio library should default to your own session's preaching — which is exposition of the Word — not to the gamified layer.
- Include a "hide streaks" preference so that any user for whom the mechanism has become a snare may turn it off.

That is enough to honor his concern without capitulating to a position the Standards do not authorize.

---

## Feature B: AI-Generated First-Person "Daily Word" Tuned to the User

**Ruling: Do not ship it. The pro-B elder is wrong, and dangerously so.**

### Why the "it's just a devotional book / daily-verse app" analogy fails

The pro-B elder's argument trades on a category error. Compare what the proposed feature actually is to its supposed analogues:

- A **daily-verse app** delivers *actual Scripture* — the Word of God written (WCF 1.2). It is a delivery mechanism for an instituted element.
- A **devotional book** is human-authored second-person reflection about God and His Word. It is not presented as God's voice, and no reader receives it as such.
- **Your feature** is a system that fabricates first-person speech *and presents it as the personal voice of God to that specific user for that specific day*, conditioned on their private prayer entries and mood check-ins. That is not "smarter tech around the same idea." It is a different *kind of thing entirely*.

### What the Standards actually say this feature is

1. **Forbidden invention in worship/devotion.** WLC Q109 forbids "the inventing, seeking after, or using of any religious worship not instituted by God Himself," and "introducing any thing into the worship of God, that is not appointed by Him in His Word." A made-up first-person speech putatively from God, generated on demand, is exactly such an introduction.

2. **A seducing spirit by design.** WLC Q150 condemns "seducing spirits, which speak lies in the name of the Lord, or speak falsely under pretense of having received a revelation from some spirit." The feature's *intended reception* is that the user receives it as a word from the Lord. Whether the disclaimer says "AI-generated" or not is irrelevant — the architectural design trains the user to expect and trust fabricated personal revelations. That is the very dynamic the Standards warn against.

3. **Subverting Scripture's unique authority.** WCF 1.10 establishes the Holy Scripture as the supreme judge and only infallible rule. WCF 18.3 locates assurance in the Spirit's witness *with the Word and ordinances*, not in fresh private communications. The Daily Word feature would compete with — and feel more intimate than — Scripture itself, training people to look to a synthetic oracle for daily guidance rather than to the written Word read in faith. This is precisely the displacement of means-of-grace dependence the Confession's exposition of assurance is written to prevent.

4. **The adiaphora frame is being misapplied.** WCF 20.2 frees the conscience from "doctrines and commandments of men… *beside it*, in matters of faith and worship." The category of "adiaphora" presupposes that the matter itself is morally indifferent. Putting words in God's mouth and presenting them to His people as His personal address is *not* indifferent — it is a positive offense against the second commandment's regulative logic and against the sufficiency and clarity of Scripture.

### What it would actually require to ship safely

There is no version of this feature that does what the pro-B elder wants. To ship it "in a way the Standards allow," you would have to either (a) strip the first-person framing and the personal-delivery pretense, leaving something that is no longer the proposed feature, or (b) refuse to let the system claim divine speech at all, leaving a chatbot, not a "word from the Lord." Either path kills Feature B by re-design. So the right ruling is: do not ship it.

## The Household Media Rule

*A covenant we make together, signed and kept, for the glory of God and the good of our family.*

Because every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of lights (James 1:17), and because He has given us families as a stewardship for the raising of children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Eph. 6:4), we set the following rule for our home. It is not meant to be cold; it is meant to protect the things we love most — the worship of God, the peace of our table, the purity of our consciences, and the unity of our household. We sign it as an act of love to one another and of obedience to Christ.

**1. The Lord's Day.** From Saturday evening through Sunday evening, we do not stream shows or play video games. The day is set apart for worship, rest, and family — for gathering with the saints, for the word read and preached, for prayer, and for the unhurried enjoyment of one another. Streaming may resume, in moderation, only after the day's worship is finished.

**2. The Table.** Phones, tablets, and personal screens stay off and away from the dinner table. When we eat together, we are *together*.

**3. The Content of What We Watch.** We do not watch films or shows whose content glorifies cruelty, mocks the Christian faith, or is sexually explicit. This is judged by the actual substance of the work, case by case, by parents and older children together — not by ratings alone, and not by a reflexive permissiveness either. If a film or show would make us ashamed to have the Lord Jesus in the room, it has no place in this house.

**4. Worship Music and Song.** The music we listen to and sing together is to be reverent, scripturally faithful, and theologically sound. We draw from the psalms, from the historic hymnody of the church catholic, and from the songs of faithful communions within and beyond our own denomination. We reject what is trivial, sensual, or doctrinally false. We are free to enjoy a wide table of faithful song; we are not free to import error or irreverence into our home under the label of worship.

**5. How We Pay for What We Use.** We use streaming and music services through accounts *we ourselves pay for*, under the terms we have agreed to. If a family member chooses to share access with us within what their plan allows, we receive it as a gift and do not extend it. We do not use shared logins beyond what the service permits, regardless of what we think of the price. A clear conscience costs less than a saved dollar.

**6. The Younger Children.** Anything our younger children watch is pre-screened or reviewed by a parent first. As they grow and prove trustworthy in their viewing, that oversight relaxes by degrees. This is a trust to be earned, not a right to be claimed.

**7. Review.** This rule will be reviewed together as a family once a year, and adjusted only by agreement of both parents. Children who faithfully keep it are blessed and thanked for it.

The Westminster Standards are precise about what repentance requires, and I think your conscience is right in some places and badly misdirected in others. Let me take it in order.

**What real repentance requires (T1)**

WLC 76 and the Confession (15.2–15.6) define it: *true sorrow for sin, hatred of it, turning to God, and walking in new obedience.* Confession 15.6 makes the critical distinction between legal repentance — "sorrow of the world" that works death — and evangelical repentance, which is "hatred of sin and love to God." The Standards are warning you directly: a fixation on the *cost* of repentance, rather than on the God against whom you've sinned, is precisely the legal kind. The Confession calls it "a sort of repentance which the ungodly have" (15.4).

So the real version isn't "how do I make this hurt enough?" It's: do you actually hate the deceit, the gambling, the defrauding of 90 families' kids' club — and are you turning to God, not just to punishment? That has to be settled before tactics.

Two things the Standards *do* require of you that you've correctly identified:

- **Confession to the offended party.** Confession 15.5: *"It is the duty of those who have done injuries to others voluntarily to confess and make restitution."* The board is owed that.
- **Restitution.** Confession on the 8th commandment (WLC 142): restore what was wrongfully taken *"as far as is possible."* Full $6,400.

**On your wife (T2)**

No. Hard no.

What you're describing is a *new sin*: defrauding Ana by depleting an account she alone controls, while she doesn't know the full picture. That's exactly what the 8th commandment forbids — taking/withholding another's goods through deception. WLC 149 (duties of the 9th commandment) requires truth between you and her; "bearing the cost" of repentance does not include secretly transferring it onto an unsuspecting third party.

Worse, the framing — "making her savings the instrument" — is a confession in itself. You are treating her as an instrument rather than a covenant partner. Confession 24 on marriage, and WLC 150 on spousal duties (mutual fidelity, respect, honoring conjugal claims), point the other direction entirely.

The proper order with Ana:

1. Tell her the full truth — what you took, why, that you've been treating her funds as a workaround she didn't consent to, and that you've been deceiving her about the state of your finances/your sin. This is confession to someone you have *also* been offending, even if she didn't know it.
2. Discuss restitution as a couple — what you can actually pay now, what schedule is realistic, whether she *freely and informedly* wants to contribute from her separate fund. Her money, her call, with full knowledge.
3. If you can't produce $6,400 from your own means right now, repay what you can *now* and disclose to the board that full restitution is being completed on a concrete, honest timeline. Restitution is required "as far as is possible" — that phrase exists precisely so a thief isn't crushed beyond what is possible or required. Don't manufacture the impossibility by adding a fresh theft.

The costliness you're looking for is already there: telling your wife is going to be more expensive to your pride than writing a check. That *is* the bearing of cost. You don't get to engineer it cheaper by sneaking around her.

**On criminal prosecution (T3)**

You're confusing two things, and the Standards hold them apart.

The Confession 23 on the civil magistrate is clear: the magistrate *"hath the sword"* to punish evil deeds, and it's his duty to use it where appropriate. *You* owe obedience to lawful authority, including accepting the consequences that come when wrongdoing becomes known. You do not, however, owe a duty of *insisting on your own prosecution* — that's the magistrate's prerogative, not the repentant's. And you certainly don't owe a duty of *rushing to the police station ahead of the injured party and ahead of any restitution.*

The order in the Standards is confession-to-the-offended and restitution, then *accepting* whatever civil consequences arise. Walking into the police station first is disordered in two ways:

- It front-runs the confession owed to the board (Confession 15.5).
- And it reflects the very legal repentance the Confession warns against — making sure the *punishment is real* as a condition of taking the repentance seriously. That isn't repentance. That's bargaining with consequences.

There is also a subtler problem. The board, knowing the whole picture, may lawfully decline to pursue charges — restitution made, offender cooperating, the club made whole. That's not "cheap grace" from them; that's the proper exercise of mercy by a private party. If the civil authorities *also* decline once the facts are presented, that's their judgment, not yours to override. You don't get to manufacture your own punishment to validate your repentance; that puts you back in the position of deciding what your sin costs, which is exactly the position you started in when you decided what the club could afford to lose.

**What I would actually tell you**

1. Get the order right. Tell Ana the whole truth first; stop deceiving her, full stop. Confess the embezzlement to her and the fact that you've been planning to drain her account behind her back. Let her be part of the repayment decision.
2. Pay back what you can *now* from your own means. Commit to a clear, disclosed plan for the rest.
3. Go to the board, confess fully, present restitution already underway, and submit to whatever the board does with the information — including criminal referral. Don't *insist* on it; don't *block* it either. That posture — willing to bear consequences, not engineering them — is the evangelical repentance the Confession describes, not the legal one.
4. Keep working the gambling with help; the underlying sin still needs uprooting, not just paid for.

The Standards won't let you hide behind your wife, and they won't let you hide behind the cops either. Both proposals are ways of *you* controlling how this lands. Real repentance hands that control back to God and to those you've actually wronged.

Your conscience is tangled, but the two threads come apart cleanly when you read the Standards carefully. On the first question, your folk teaching has lied to you. On the second, your grievance is making you rationalize.

## On wanting the better job

The Westminster Standards *do* require contentment, but they define it precisely. The Larger Catechism, Q148, describes the duty of the tenth commandment as "such a full contentment with our own condition *in God*, and such a frame of heart as may make us quietly, patiently, and thankfully contented under all the changes and troubles of our present state." Note the qualifier: contentment with your condition *in God* and under His providence — not contentment with every specific feature of your earthly situation as it currently exists.

The Shorter Catechism Q80 forbids "all discontentment with our own estate" and "inordinate motions and affections" to anything that belongs to another. The word *inordinate* is doing real work. A desire for just compensation, a healthier workplace, and relief from unjust treatment is not inordinate. In fact, the eighth commandment's duties (WLC Q141) include "honest industry" and care to increase your outward estate through lawful means. The tenth commandment itself, Q148, lists "hospitality, charity, and bountifulness according to our ability" among the *duties* it requires. A 40% raise widens your capacity for these things. That's the opposite of what the commandment forbids.

So the desire to take the interview is not what the tenth commandment calls covetousness. Your teaching that "wanting more money is greed" is a folk doctrine the Standards do not teach. The Standards teach that Christians should have a lawful calling and abide in it (WSC Q85) — but they do not require you to remain in a calling that is unjust, exploitative, or destructive, as though leaving were disobedience. Wiser and older divines than you or I have left callings when conscience and prudence required it.

What you *should* examine, honestly before God:

- **Can you be content if this door closes?** Real contentment is tested precisely when a desired thing is withheld. If you can take the interview without your peace collapsing if it doesn't work out, your heart is probably right.
- **Are you leaving injustice or fleeing every discomfort?** The Standards do not promise a trouble-free calling; they require faithfulness in the one you're given.
- **Is your treasure here, or in God with this as a means?** The commandment probes the heart, not the résumé.

Take the interview. Examine your heart. Don't let a false doctrine of "blooming where planted" keep you rooted in soil your abuser has salted.

## On the client list and the pricing playbook

Here your conscience is misfiring badly, and the fact that you've been wronged does not change the analysis.

A few specific points:

1. **Property distinctions.** A client contact list developed in your role as an employee — using company time, company positioning, company introductions, company infrastructure — is the company's property, even though your hands built it. The Standards distinguish sharply between an employee's *labor*, which is owed fair wages (WLC Q141), and the *product and assets* of the employer, which are not yours to take. You are entitled to be paid properly; you are not entitled to walk out the door with the asset. The pricing playbook is unambiguously company intellectual property; there is no ambiguity there at all.

2. **The relevant commandments.** This violates the eighth commandment (theft, "fraudulent dealing," breach of trust — WLC Q141, 142) and the ninth commandment (deception in your dealings — WLC Q145). It also violates the duty of fidelity implied in every lawful calling: you are trusted with something not yours, and you betray the trust on the way out.

3. **"Leveling the score" is not a Christian category.** You have been genuinely wronged. Belittling, stolen credit, underpayment — these are real sins against you, and the Standards would have you address them by leaving (which you may rightly do), by speaking truthfully to the parties responsible if that serves good ends, and by entrusting the injustice to God. They do not license self-help theft as a remedy for someone else's theft. "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good" is the spirit of the moral law as the Standards expound it.

4. **Your integrity is the thing you cannot negotiate.** You are about to walk into a new workplace and want to be trusted there. Walking in with stolen goods from the previous employer puts a millstone around your neck and a shadow over your new beginning. You do not want your first act in your new calling to be the same kind of theft your manager committed against you.

5. **One narrow exception worth distinguishing.** If there are particular clients whose relationship is genuinely *yours* — built outside work, on your own time, where you are the natural point of contact independent of your employer's brand and introductions — that is a different conversation and may even be a relationship you can lawfully maintain or transition. But even then it should be handled openly, not by covert copying. The general principle stands: do not transfer what was entrusted to you.

## The shape of the counsel, in short

**First question:** No, your desire is not the covetousness the tenth commandment forbids. It is lawful stewardship of your gifts and provision, provided your heart is in the right posture. Take the interview in good conscience.

**Second question:** No, taking the client list and pricing playbook is not "just fair." It is theft and deception dressed up as justice. Refuse to become what you are escaping. Leave cleanly, even if your manager did not.

The fact that one of these is a matter for careful self-examination and the other is a clear *no* tells you something: your conscience is not malformed. It is being pulled in two directions by a false theology of contentment on one side and a real but misleading grievance on the other. The Standards correct both.

## T1 — What you actually owe

You are not working out an abstract debt to the universe; you defrauded 39 named people. The Standards address this with unusual directness.

And **WLC 142** (Eighth Commandment, duties required): *"truth, fidelity, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man… **a just compensation of all wrongs done to any man, in his goods, name, or calling**… restitution of goods stolen or unlawfully detained from their right owner."*

Two things are owed, distinct and both required:

1. **Confession to those wronged.** Your "quietly overpay" proposal is precisely what 15.6 forbids — a private repentance that does not reach the people your sin actually harmed. Restitution sent through the mail slot, anonymously, is not Christian repentance; it is a quieter form of the same fraud. Whatever the social cost — the lawsuits, the awkwardness with your kids' school families — those costs are not a discount on what Christ requires of you. (More on this below when we get to T3.)

2. **Restitution of what you took.** Your personal gain was the $9,000 of deck work. That is the figure. The breakdown is below in T4.

You also need to be done with the cycle of "did I really cost people, or was it just my greedy heart?" That framing is a trap. **WCF 6.6** and **WCF 15.2** make clear the inward corruption and the outward damage are not competing explanations — the greedy heart produced the costly act. Confess both. Don't minimize the external to magnify the interior (that is spiritual exhibitionism); don't minimize the interior to spare yourself the external (that is evasion).

## T2 — Trevor and the temptation to avenge

**WCF 15.5:** *"to confess publicly in the church of God, or to some other of the children of God, **who being not of the number of those that are to judge without**, may give the right hand of fellowship, and counsel and comfort to the penitent."*

The instinct to expose Trevor so he doesn't "skate" is half right and half wrong.

**The half that's right:** You are not free to protect Trevor by silence. His falsified paperwork was part of the same fraud against your neighbors, and the truth about what happened is owed to the board and the firm. Quietness about his role is not magnanimity; it is complicity continuing.

**The half that's wrong:** You are not the prosecutor. Trevor's judgment is not your vocation, and the phrasing "the guilty party gets named" puts you in the position of God's moral avenger. That is a role the Standards do not assign to private Christians, and it is one of the predictable escalations of unresolved guilt — I confessed, so now someone else must suffer.

The honest move is: **tell the truth about what happened, including Trevor's role, because the truth is owed to the parties you've wronged.** State what you did and what you know he did. State facts, not motives you cannot read. Let the board and the firm do what they will with it. Do not posture as the avenger; do not hide him to seem merciful.

## T3 — The "prophetic duty" and the elevator vote

This is the most spiritually dangerous part of your question, and I want to be plain: **the Westminster Standards do not recognize self-appointed prophecy as a Christian vocation.** Several lines come together against it:

- **No private revelatory office over civil/community decisions.** Prophets in Scripture spoke *under specific revelation*; what you are describing is a felt intuition plus a recent awakening about board corruption. That is not the same thing, and treating it as the same thing is the kind of presumption the Third Commandment forbids — *taking God's name in vain* by ascribing to His direction what is actually your own unguided urgency. **WLC 109** lists as sin "the using of God's name… as if he had appointed any thing contrary to his word, or to the lawful use thereof." Claiming a "prophetic duty" you do not have is a species of that.

- **The Ninth Commandment guards against exactly this.** **WLC 144** forbids *"hazarding the reputation of our neighbour upon undue surmises, when there is no cause for it"* and *"being led by an over-plus spirit of censorship to entertain a charitable opinion of the good actions of others, but an uncharitable opinion of their evil actions."* You have no evidence the elevator deal is fraudulent. You have a suspicion that it is overpriced. Suspicion is not cause. Publicly branding a legitimate vote as "more of the same board corruption" — when the only data you have is a past sin of your own and a present price you don't like — is the precise violation 144 names.

- **Repentance is not a public performance to certify your sincerity.** **WCF 15.2:** repentance is *"a saving grace, whereby a sinner… with grief and hatred of his sin, turn[s] from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience."* Notice what is *not* there: a public stunt whose meaning depends on the response of others. The "proof I've truly changed" framing — sabotaging a vote as the visible certificate of my repentance — is the works-righteousness the Confession rejects. **WCF 16.2:** good works are *fruits* and *evidences* of faith, obedient to God's commandments, not theatrical displays staged so the performer can verify his own authenticity.

- **You are tying your standing before God to a vote.** If they approve the elevator deal despite your speech, what then? Will you conclude you haven't truly changed? Will you escalate to a different intervention next month? You are constructing a public drama in which the validity of your repentance depends on how your neighbors behave. That is not gospel repentance. It is, ironically, the same fiduciary corruption you just confessed: making yourself the center of a transaction you should serve rather than control.

**So:** Confess your own past sin, in the scope of that past sin. If you have actual evidence — invoices, statements, conflicts of interest — that the elevator deal is corrupt, raise it as facts through proper channels, not as accusation. But that is a *separate* question from your repentance, and you must not bundle them. Bundling them turns your confession into a weapon and your repentance into a platform.

## T4 — The dollar figure

Your personal restitution is **$9,000**, the value of the kickback you actually received. Here is the accounting:

- 40 owners paid $18,000 more than the lowest bid.
- You received $9,000 of deck work — that is *your* gain.

You owe the $9,000 to the 39 other owners. You do **not** personally owe the other $9,000 — that was the firm's overcharge, and the firm is responsible for it. Confessing to a theft you did not commit is not humility; it is injustice to yourself and to the truth, and the Standards are not shy about requiring truthfulness in confession as in everything else (WLC 144).

I would also offer **reasonable interest from the date of the original assessment.** The Standards use the language of "just compensation" (WLC 142), not bare replacement, and the gospel principle is that wrongs are not wiped clean by returning the principal while keeping the use of the money. The exact rate can be set with the board; the principle is that you do not profit from the time-value of stolen money.

**Form of restitution** can be any of:
- Cash to the association, distributed by credit to the 39 other units' assessments.
- $9,000 of equivalent labor (maintenance, etc.) to the building.
- A combination.

You do not get to choose unilaterally; you offer, and the board decides the form.
