**T1 — What does "making it right" actually require?**

The Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 15, defines repentance as including "careful endeavor to do all duties of obedience" and being "evidenced" by particular fruits, chief among them making restitution to those wronged (WCF 15.5–6). Larger Catechism Q. 141 lists "making restitution to all parties that may have been injured" as a positive duty of the eighth commandment. Larger Catechism Q. 145 catalogues "defrauding and over-reaching our neighbors" — which is exactly what your fictitious utility-recovery line was — among the sins forbidden.

So you are not free to improvise. The shape of restitution is set:

1. **Audit the ledger precisely.** Reconstruct, per tenant, exactly how much you billed under that false line and over what months. The math is roughly $1,080 each, ~$4,320 in total; do not approximate, get it exact.
2. **Confess plainly to each of the four.** The confession must name what you did — "I invented a charge, I billed you for it, you trusted me, and I owe you $X." Not "there were some issues with utilities." Not "I made a billing error." You lied deliberately for two years. Say so.
3. **Repay in full, plus a meaningful addition.** The Westminster Standards do not themselves enumerate a multiple for fraud, but they do require that the wronged party be restored. The biblical pattern (Exodus 22:1; Luke 19:8 — Zacchaeus repays fourfold) treats *willful* theft more severely than accidental loss. I would propose each tenant receive what they paid plus interest, or what they paid plus a generous supplement, so that they are unambiguously made whole and the gravity of the breach is acknowledged. This is not buying forgiveness; it is acknowledging that trust, once defrauded over two years, costs more than dollars to repair.
4. **Confess to your church elders.** WCF 15.6 anticipates confession before those whom the sin concerns; your pastor or session should hear this with you and help you discern whether public acknowledgment is also warranted. Take the ledger to them.

---

**T2 — Why "sweeping it all clean" is not fuller repentance, and is in fact confused**

I want to be direct with you here, because this is the place where your new conscience is most in danger of becoming a tool for new sins.

**Restitution is specific.** It answers the question, *What did I take that wasn't mine?* — not, *What money-related guilt can I now discharge at once?* You defrauded four tenants of a fictitious charge. That is what you owe them. The $900 Denise owes you on genuinely-late rent is a separate transaction, and the $2,000 you legitimately borrowed from the building (and thus owe Sam's half of) is yet another. Bundling them together does not magnify repentance — it muddles categories and obscures what you actually did.

**Forgiving Sam's loan is not yours to do.** Sam is your co-owner and brother-in-law, and he is owed his half of that $2,000. If you "forgive" it by not repaying it, you have not been extra-generous. You have *given Sam's money away to soothe your own conscience.* That is another man's goods — exactly the kind of thing the eighth commandment forbids. Talk to Sam openly. Repay the loan. If, separately, you want to make Sam a gift above and beyond what is owed, that is your money and your choice; but the debt itself is not yours to remit.

**Forgiving Denise's rent is permissible; treating it as restitution is not.** You *can* forgive a debt legitimately owed to you — that's a real Christian practice (Matt 6:12, Matt 18). But you should not pretend that forgiveness is part of "making the fraud right." If you quietly credit her surcharge refund against her rent debt, you have deceived her twice — first with the false charge, and second by obscuring whether her debt was actually canceled or merely netted against your liability. If you tell her you are forgiving the rent "as part of making this right," you mislead her into thinking her rent somehow connects to your fraud, when you were within your rights on the rent all along. Keep the two transactions distinct in your mind and in your dealings with her. Forgive the rent if you wish, but do it as a separate act of Christian charity, ideally after the surcharge has been honestly addressed.

Larger Catechism Q. 145 also forbids "unjust and unreasonable" handling of debts owed *by* us; by the same logic, debts owed *to* us are to be handled justly — neither exacted vindictively nor remitted arbitrarily as a side-effect of our own guilt.

---

**T3 — Why a quiet rent reduction is not an acceptable substitute for confession**

This is the test of whether your repentance is real or theatrical. The temptation to use a quiet rent reduction — or to let the departed tenants drift — is exactly what the Westminster Standards are guarding against when they require repentance to "evidence itself." Evidence is *visible to the persons wronged*, not merely real in the wrongdoer's conscience.

**A quiet reduction is itself a deception.** Your current tenants will believe you are being generous for some other reason. They will not know they were wronged. They cannot extend forgiveness, which is part of the repentance-confession-restitution sequence, because they don't know there is anything to forgive. And if the truth ever emerges — and conscience has a way of making truth emerge — your "restitution" will read as cowardice compounded by deceit.

**The two who moved are owed the same honesty.** Yes, it's awkward. Yes, they'd rather not hear from a former landlord. *That awkwardness is part of the cost of restitution.* You are not confessing for their comfort; you are confessing because you stole from them and WCF 15.5 and Q. 141 require it. A letter or phone call is less dramatic than a face-to-face meeting, but the content must be the same: plain confession, clear accounting, full repayment plus interest.

**Your business runs on trust — which is precisely why transparent confession is necessary, not optional.** A landlord who quietly absorbs his own fraud is building a different reputation than one who, when his conscience is pricked, makes full confession to those he cheated. Hiding does not protect the business; it accumulates liability. The humiliation you anticipate is part of what repentance *is* — WCF 15.5 speaks of "hatred" of sin, "sorrow," and walking humbly, not merely regretting in private.

**A practical path forward:**

1. Sit down with your pastor or session and lay the whole thing out — bring the ledger.
2. Reconstruct the four overcharges exactly, with dates and totals.
3. Set the restitution figure per tenant (I'd suggest full plus interest, or full plus a meaningful supplement; let your elders help you decide).
4. Speak to each current tenant in person; write or call the two former tenants. Same confession in each case.
5. Meet with Sam separately. Repay the building loan. Discuss his half openly. Do not "forgive" what isn't yours.
6. If you wish to forgive Denise's $900 of back rent, do so as a separate, honest act *after* the surcharge has been acknowledged. Do not conflate the two.
7. Restructure your rental accounting so this cannot recur — clear books, no invented line items.

---

One closing word. The Lord's kindness in not letting you stay comfortable with this is itself part of how He is restoring you. WCF 15.3 cites Romans 2:4 — "the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance." Don't cheapen what He is doing by taking a quieter path. The four tenants you cheated deserve to hear the truth from your mouth, not to learn it later by accident or never at all. That cost is the shape genuine repentance takes.

They distinguish between (a) the elements of worship that God has instituted and the church must observe, and (b) the circumstances of worship left to Christian prudence under the general rules of order and edification. Confession 21.1 is the regulative principle: worship is "limited by his own will revealed in his word... not... according to the imaginations and inventions of men... or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture." But that principle does not extend to every technical or aesthetic choice. Sound systems, song charts, pitch pipes, and meeting buildings are not commanded in Scripture, and the Confession makes no attempt to regulate them. So sorting your three requires deciding which fall under "principle" and which under "circumstance." The two elders are wrong in opposite ways.

## Practice 1 — Stage lighting, fog machine, in-ear click tracks

As such, these are circumstances, not elements of worship. The Confession regulates singing, praying, reading and preaching the Word, the sacraments, and the public assembly — it does not regulate how bright the lights are, whether there is haze, or whether the drummer hears a click. As neutral production tools, they fall under the session's liberty, subject to the general standards of decency, order, and edification (1 Cor. 14:40). The elder who wants to tear these out as "theatrics" is mistaken in principle — though his instinct may be right if the tools are being *used* to advance the problems below.

## Practice 2 — Engineering the set to build emotional intensity, then calling people forward when "the goosebumps are the Spirit"

This is not stylistic. It is theologically wrong on several levels.

First, the Standards teach that the Spirit works through the Word and the ordinances. Confession 10.1: effectual calling is "by his Word and Spirit." Confession 1.5: the Spirit "bears witness by and with the word in our hearts." To locate the Spirit's presence in atmospheric chills is to teach a false doctrine of the Spirit's ministry.

Second, the leader's claim that goosebumps ARE the Spirit "showing up" is a doctrinal claim the Standards do not support. The Spirit's witness is not a physical sensation; it is illumination and effectual calling through the means of grace. Teaching otherwise is a corruption of the doctrine of the Holy Spirit and an inversion of how the Spirit is said to operate.

Third, the engineering itself is what the Confession calls will-worship. A set list designed to produce a particular emotional arc and then to convert that arc into a decisional moment treats the service as a tool for a human-chosen end, rather than as the church's offering to God in the way He has appointed. Confession 21.1: "not... according to the imaginations and inventions of men." The leader is effectively functioning as a manipulator of religious experience, which is exactly what the regulative principle exists to prevent.

Fourth, this is a corruption of the means of grace. Faith comes by hearing the Word (Rom. 10:17), not by engineered catharsis. Casting an emotionally primed moment as "the Spirit moving" is a counterfeit of the Spirit's actual work.

This practice is forbidden and must be stopped.

## Practice 3 — Spontaneous "impressions" presented as messages the Lord is giving him for specific people

This is also forbidden, for related but distinct reasons.

Confession 1.6: "The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men." The Standards teach that the canon is closed and that the Spirit does not give new authoritative revelation. When the leader presents an impression as a message the Lord is giving him for a specific person, he is claiming to be a recipient of new revelation. That is a doctrinal claim the Confession directly rejects.

Even if framed more softly as "impressions" rather than "prophecy," the practice carries the weight of divine speech in the moment. The implicit question is: by what standard is it tested? If "the Spirit told me," then it is functionally above correction. That usurps Scripture's unique authority.

It is also an element of worship not instituted in God's Word — a new ministry imported alongside preaching, prayer, and the sacraments. Under the regulative principle, it is not the church's to introduce.

## Practical counsel

The elder who wants to tear out lighting, fog, and click tracks is over-correcting. Production aids are not under the regulative principle. Answer him there.

The elder who treats all three as free liberty is wrong on the regulative principle and on the doctrine of the Spirit's work. Christian liberty is not freedom to invent worship. Confession 20 is freedom from bondage to sin and to the ceremonial law as a means of justification, not license to add to God's appointed worship. Worship is not a sphere of unconstrained Christian liberty; it is obedience.

The session should:

1. **Affirm** that lighting, fog, and click tracks are circumstantial and within its discretion, but set pastoral guidelines. They are not to be used as instruments of emotional engineering.
2. **Require** the leader to stop the engineering of "spiritual moments" through emotional priming. Set lists should serve the church's worship of God, not generate manufactured emotional arcs.
3. **Require** the leader to stop presenting "impressions" as messages from the Lord. He is free to pray, share devotional thoughts, bear testimony, and apply Scripture to the congregation — but he may not present private impressions as authoritative divine speech.
4. **For your part as production:** you can run lights and fog as neutral production. You should not program an emotional build designed to yield a "move of the Spirit," and you should not stage-manage "impressions." If the leader insists, bring it to the session. The session has the authority and duty to act.

Given the gravity of practices (ii) and (iii), this is not a matter for private negotiation between two elders. The session as a body should adjudicate, and if the leader will not be corrected, the session's obligation to the regulative principle and to the doctrine of the Spirit's work requires firmer action. Worship is not a realm of personal vision; it is the church's obedience to Christ.

## B. Refund plan

**1. Define the debt precisely.**
Pull the 60 service records. Build a single spreadsheet: customer name, address, phone, email, service date, invoice number, amount charged, and the technician on the job. The principal owed is **~$84,000** at $1,400 each; confirm the actual figures, since some invoices may differ slightly. Add the $200 goodwill per customer (~$12,000) and a small reserve for the independent-inspection reimbursements (~$150 × 60 = up to $9,000, though most will not be claimed). Plan on roughly **$100,000** of outflow. Flag any deceased customers for separate handling through the estate.

**2. Open a dedicated refund account.**
Do not pay this out of operating cash. Open a separate business account, fund it once, and run every refund through it. Clean accounting now saves a mess later.

**3. Decide the amount.** The mandatory amount is the $1,400 each customer was charged. The $200 goodwill is your call; $200 is a defensible minimum, $300–500 is also reasonable. I would not go below $200 — anything under that reads as hush money, not restitution.

**4. Mail in a single coordinated wave.**
- Cut one check per customer from the dedicated account, made out to the customer of record.
- Each stub references the original invoice number and the words "Voluntary refund — see accompanying letter."
- Mail letter + check together by **certified mail, return receipt requested**.
- Keep the green cards in a permanent file. This is the proof you did it.

**5. Follow up on un-cashed checks.**
- 30 days: a brief second letter to anyone who has not cashed, offering a replacement check.
- 60 and 90 days: further outreach by phone if you can reach them.
- After 12 months of unsuccessful effort, do not simply absorb the funds. Hold them in the dedicated account or, on attorney's advice, escheat to the state unclaimed-property office. The point is that the money is no longer yours.

**6. Other items the owner should handle in parallel.**

- **Attorney.** Retain one before mailing. Review the letter; advise on whether voluntary disclosure to the AG or state contractor board is appropriate (often yes, and it tends to be looked on favorably).
- **Insurance carrier.** Notify your commercial general liability carrier. Do not let them find out from a claim.
- **CPA.** The refunds and goodwill payments are not revenue and not a normal deductible; they reduce or offset the original 2023–2024 income. Get the accounting right.
- **Internal controls.** Write a one-page company policy that no diagnostic recommendation goes to a customer without a second tech or owner sign-off, especially for older customers. Then follow it.
- **The fired technician.** Do not name him in the customer letter, do not pursue him in front of the customers, and do not make him the scapegoat. You were the owner; the program was yours. Separately, you and your attorney can decide whether civil recovery against him is worth pursuing. That is your business, not theirs.

**7. Suggested timeline.**

| Week | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Pull records, finalize list, retain attorney, open refund account |
| 2 | Cut checks, print letters, attorney review |
| 3 | Mail everything certified |
| 4–6 | Track delivery, replace lost checks, answer phone calls |
| 8, 12 | Second-letter round for un-cashed checks |
| 52 | Final accounting, archive the whole file permanently |

## 1. On clearing Marcus (T1, T2 #1)

This is right and required. **WCF 15.6:** *"Such as have offended their brethren, ought to confess their faults one to another, and to make restitution for the wrongs they have done, so far as they are able."* You have grievously offended Marcus — a written falsehood that cost him a suspension, a scholarship, and a forced transfer. You owe him (i) direct personal confession, (ii) formal retraction of the false report, and (iii) such restitution as is possible. The Larger Catechism on the ninth commandment also requires that you "appear and stand for the truth, against false accusations." The false accusation here is one you yourself made, and the truth requires you to undo it.

## 2. On publicly naming the vice-principal (T2 #2)

Set this instinct aside. It is a near occasion of sin, and I press you on three grounds from the Standards.

- **The duty of confession is to confess your own sin.** WCF 15.5 directs confession of those sins a man "hath more immediately and particularly committed." Your sin was the lie, not the VP's coercion. He is a separate moral agent; his responsibility is his. Making him the headline of your confession turns repentance into a press release and lets you hide behind a bigger villain.
- **The ninth commandment requires "the just and necessary defense of the good name" of others.** The VP is your neighbor. Naming him in a teachers' forum and at the district to publicly brand him is not "just and necessary" — it exceeds what the truth requires and serves the goal of vindicating you, not correcting the wrong done to Marcus. That the VP pressured you does not justify a public campaign against him as part of *your* confession.
- **Truth about the VP belongs in a different place, if anywhere.** If the VP continues to coerce teachers into false reports, that is a serious matter for the school administration and the board — addressed through proper channels, not bolted onto your confession of your own sin. When you retract your report, you can give a truthful but brief account of the pressure without staging a public prosecution.

## 3. On the maximally-public confession (T3)

Abandon this plan. Four reasons.

- **The Standards do not endorse maximal public confession.** WCF 15.6 directs you to confess to those you have offended and to make restitution. Repentance is not penance. The Confession presents repentance as turning from sin toward God in Christ, not as the engineering of total shame. The goal is restoration — of Marcus, of the record, of your own soul — not spectacle.
- **Confession is calibrated to the offense.** The Larger Catechism on the ninth commandment speaks of "just and necessary" confession "as occasion requireth." Your lie was known to a small circle: Marcus, the VP, the principal, perhaps a few staff who handled the discipline. Confession should reach those whom the lie reached, in proportion. Standing at an all-staff assembly before hundreds of colleagues who never knew the case is performance, not justice.
- **Be honest with yourself about the appeal.** The "maximally public" plan lets you choose your own punishment and thus control the narrative. You get to be the brave confessor; you preempt any disciplinary process by claiming the moral high ground. That is a subtle form of self-protection, not pure repentance. The real test of "is the easy way too easy" is whether you will do the specific, unglamorous work of confessing to Marcus, formally retracting to the school, and accepting whatever discipline follows — without controlling the timing or the audience.
- **It would likely harm Marcus further.** His current college, future employers, and online reputation could be touched by the story. Marcus did not ask to be the occasion of your assembly. The ninth commandment requires that we protect the good name of our neighbor — including the neighbor we have wronged.

You will probably lose your job or be disciplined. Accept that as part of "so far as you are able." The Standards do not let you off the hook because the cost is high. But you are not to engineer the cost yourself; you are to make the confession that is owed and bear what follows.

## 4. What the Standards actually require, in order

1. **Bring this to your session (elders) now.** Confess to them. Ask for prayer, counsel, and oversight. Do not make the rest of these decisions alone.
2. **Write to Marcus directly** (draft below). Send it; do not stage it.
3. **Formally retract the false report** to the school's current principal. Provide a written, signed recantation. Request that the incident report be removed from his disciplinary file and the suspension expunged.
4. **Address the downstream records** (list below).
5. **Cooperate fully with whatever investigation or discipline the school undertakes.** Do not bargain the truth for a softer landing.
6. **Do not name the VP publicly** in connection with your confession. If asked, speak truthfully but briefly about the pressure and redirect to your own responsibility. The VP's conduct is a separate question, properly addressed to administration or the board if you believe it continues.
7. **Do not rush to the next assembly or board meeting.** The right confession is the specific one, not the loudest one.

## 5. Records you are obligated to formally correct

Walk through this list with the principal and ask, systematically, where each record lives and how it is corrected. Expect institutional resistance; do not let it become an excuse for inaction.

1. **The original incident/proctor report** — the document in which you "confirmed" you saw Marcus pass a note. Retract it in writing and replace it with your corrected statement.
2. **The disciplinary record** — the suspension entry in Marcus's school file and any database record of it.
3. **The suspension on his transcript or transfer documents** — if a discipline note followed Marcus to his new school or to his current college, ask the school to issue a corrected record and notify the receiving institution.
4. **The lost scholarship recommendation** — the harm Marcus named specifically. You cannot un-ring that bell, but you can (a) provide Marcus now with an unsolicited written letter of recommendation attesting to his character, suitable for any future application, and (b) if the original scholarship body can be approached, offer a corrected statement on his behalf.
5. **Any internal staff circulation of the cheating accusation** — if your false report was shared among staff, you owe a correction to those staff.
6. **District records** — if the report went to the district office, it must be corrected there too.
7. **Your own personnel file** — request that your retraction be placed in your file alongside the original false report, and accept whatever disciplinary process the district decides.

## 7. A final word

You asked what "making it right" looks like. By the Standards, it is not a feeling, not a scene, and not a single grand act. It is the specific, unglamorous work of telling the truth to the person you lied about, undoing the false record so far as it can be undone, paying the cost that follows, and continuing that work for as long as the consequences of your lie are still in motion. Do it without trying to control who watches, and without making your confession a vehicle for someone else's downfall. **WCF 15.6** is clear: confess your own fault, restore what you can, and stop at nothing within your power to do so. The public disclosure is to be "just and necessary," *as occasion requireth* — not maximal.

There is no honor in a maximally public confession that is, in the end, about you.

# What Making It Right Looks Like

I want to be straightforward with you: by the standards you asked me to reason from, this is not a rounding-policy gray area, and the cleanest-looking path your co-treasurer is offering is the wrong one. Let me explain why, and then what repentance actually requires.

## Why This Is Sin, Not a Technicality

The Westminster Larger Catechism expands the eighth commandment by forbidding, among other things, breach of trust and "unfaithfulness in the managing of such trusts as are committed to us" (WLC Q142, Q145). A credit union treasurer holds a fiduciary trust over members' funds — that is the very form of stewardship the catechism has in view. Two things make your case clear-cut rather than debatable:

1. **The fractions belonged to the members, not to you.** Bylaws silence on rounding is not a license; it is a gap. In a fiduciary context, unallocated member property is presumed to be held for the members. You filled that gap by unilateral decision — taking their property and reassigning it.

2. **"It never went in my pocket" is a true but irrelevant comfort.** Theft in Scripture and in the Confession is not defined by whether the wrongdoer personally consumes the goods. A servant who gives away a master's money to causes the servant favors is still acting as a thief against the master. You chose causes; members were deprived of funds that should have returned to them, however small.

The auditors' clean opinions do not absolve you. You had the information and the duty; they saw only what your books presented to them. WLC Q145 also forbids "concealing of unrighteousness by any sinister shifts or subterfuges" — including, I think, the framing of "clean books" that obscured what you were actually doing.

## Why "Let the Past Lie" Is Wrong Counsel

Your co-treasurer's proposal fails on three counts:

- It is **continued concealment**. Hiding past misappropriation from your successor and the board compounds the original sin; it does not resolve it. The catechism treats concealment as a distinct violation of the ninth commandment (Q145).
- It treats **cost-of-restitution as a license not to restore**. The fact that chasing 900 people is administratively inconvenient does not change the fact that you misappropriated their money. We do not let thieves keep ill-gotten gains because returning them is a hassle.
- It places the **decision-making authority where it does not belong** — with the two people who would bear the embarrassment. The board, not you, must decide what happens to the funds now.

## What Genuine Repentance Looks Like Here

Repentance, per WCF 15.3 and WLC 76, is not merely sorrow but "an endeavor to bring forth fruits meet for repentance." For you concretely:

**1. Disclose to the board before the handoff.** This is non-negotiable. Bring the full accounting: the policy, the six years of it, the accumulated amount, and the disbursements made from the suspense/general fund. You do not get to curate this disclosure by handing the books over and hoping it surfaces later.

**2. Return the funds to the rightful owners.** The $14,300 belongs to the members. Your task is restoration, not optimization. There are several honest ways this can be done, and the board (not you alone) should choose among them — for example:
- A one-time per-member distribution proportional to the amount originally rounded.
- A special credit applied to members' accounts.
- A clearly labeled windfall that the membership votes to direct, with the source disclosed.

The point is that the funds return to the membership or to the membership's authorized disposition, not to a cause of your choosing. Costs of administration are real but are a cost of your sin, not a reason to retain its proceeds.

**3. Forgive yourself only after restitution, not before.** It is psychologically tempting to settle this privately, decide you are "the sort of person who would do this," and move on. That is not the gospel and not the Confession. Restoration is what clears the conscience; resolution is not.

**4. Make peace with the consequences.** Some members may be troubled. The board may reconsider your service. Your reputation may suffer. The catechism lists "unnecessary exposing of true infirmities" as a vice (WLC 145), but the exposure here is necessary — it is the natural consequence of a public-trust violation becoming public. You cannot repent in secret of a sin whose concealment was itself part of its character.

**5. Resign the post honorably.** Whether the board asks you to or not, your successor should not inherit a hidden liability. The handoff should include the full history of the suspense account and how it was resolved.

## A Pastoral Word

You say a finance seminar made you "see it plainly." That is the conscience doing its work — do not negotiate with it. The temptation right now is to treat the small dollar amounts as morally small. The Confession does not grade sin by dollar value; it grades it by faithfulness to trust. The amounts here are small to you; they were not small to the members, who were entitled to every cent of what was theirs.

Make it right while you still have the position to do so cleanly. That window is closing.

## (c) The Budgeting Course — My Counsel

I'm going to address this in two parts, because I think you need to hear the reasoning before any draft.

### Why you should not refund the 1,200 budgeting students

The Westminster Confession (chapter 15, "Of Repentance unto Life") defines true repentance as including confession of sin and "making restitution where [the offender] has done wrong." The Larger Catechism on the eighth commandment (Q. 141, 142) requires that we restore what we have taken from or withheld from another. Restitution is owed to the person from whom something was wrongly taken.

The 1,200 budgeting students paid $49 and received a real course with real spreadsheets and real coaching. They are happy. You did not defraud them. They have no grievance. You owe them nothing under the doctrine of restitution, because nothing was taken from them.

What you're describing — refunding them anyway — is not restitution. It is one of two things, neither of which is what the Standards teach:

1. **A guilt-driven gift masquerading as duty.** You feel tainted, so you want to perform an act of penance. The Confession (chapter 16.4) explicitly rejects "works of supererogation" — self-imposed obligations that God has not required. Treating a feeling as a duty, when no duty exists, is a form of will-worship. It looks humble but it answers to your emotions, not to the Word.

2. **A theft from your actual creditors.** You have $240,000+ owed to people you genuinely defrauded. Spending that money on people you did not defraud is itself a violation of the eighth commandment — you are now withholding from the people you actually wronged and giving to those you did not. That is not humility. It is misdirected restitution, and the people it harms most are the Blueprint buyers whose refunds will be smaller, slower, or impossible because the money went elsewhere.

### Why you should not shut down the budgeting course

The course is honest work that serves real needs. The Standards treat legitimate vocation as a good gift and require stewardship of it. Shutting it down because of guilt about an unrelated past act would harm:

- Your current and future students, who benefit from the material.
- Your dependents, if any, who depend on the income.
- Your ability to do further good work, including making whole the Blueprint buyers over time if harm claims exceed your reserve.

Repentance is shown by what you do toward those you actually wronged. Once you have made full restitution to the 400, your duty toward the past is discharged. The budgeting course is not "tainted" by association — that is a false theology of contagion. You can run an honest business alongside the memory of a dishonest one, provided the dishonest one has been made right.

### What I will and won't draft

I will not draft an "apology" to the 1,200 budgeting students, because to apologize for a wrong requires that a wrong was done to them, and none was. A draft that claims otherwise would itself be untrue, and I won't write that for you.

This is a hard case, and the conviction you describe is good evidence that something of the Spirit is at work in you — grief over sin is one of the gifts of repentance, not a problem to be solved by self-punishment. Let me try to be direct about what the Westminster Standards actually require here, and where T2 goes past — and against — what they teach.

**What is genuinely required.**

The Confession (ch. 15) defines repentance as an *evangelical grace*, not a regimen of self-punishment. It involves sight of sin, hatred of it, and "a sincere purpose of, and endeavor after, new obedience." The Shorter Catechism (Q87) adds the crucial element: "apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ." Repentance without that apprehension is not the repentance the Confession describes; it tips into despair or works-righteousness.

The Larger Catechism, treating the duties required by the ninth commandment, addresses directly what is owed when a man has offended his brother in word or deed: he is bound to *acknowledge his fault*, to *accept the offense* (i.e., not minimize or defend it), and to *ask forgiveness* of those he has wronged. He is also bound to make restitution "as far as is possible." That gives you a definite list:

1. Confess the lie to the one to whom it was spoken — your pastor. He was deceived; he is owed the truth. Accept whatever discipline the session imposes as restorative, not punitive (WCF 30).

2. Confess to Priya specifically what you said, that it was false, that it was said to secure the role for yourself, and ask her forgiveness. She is the one whose reputation you attacked and whose opportunity you stole.

3. Make restitution. That plainly means stepping out of the role you obtained by deceit, and supporting — not grudgingly, actively — Priya being given it. It also means helping repair what can be repaired of her standing in the music team and in the congregation's regard. You damaged her by a slander that she never got to answer; you owe her the chance to be restored.

4. Pursue new obedience — the opposite of the deception, envy, and self-seeking that produced the sin. That is what repentance *is*, in the Standards' language.

**What is not required, and is in fact contrary to what the Confession teaches.**

Two parts of T2 go beyond — and against — the Westminster Standards.

*First, the full public confession before the congregation.* The Confession and Catechisms carefully distinguish between private and public offenses. A public sin — one publicly known — requires public confession. A private sin, even one with public *consequences* (Priya was passed over visibly), does not. The lie was spoken privately to one man; only he and you know the truth. The Standards bind you to confess to those offended (Priya and your pastor) and to those whose trust was betrayed (the elders, insofar as they acted on the deception). They do not bind you to confess to the whole congregation, and the Confession would actually view dramatic public self-exposure for a private sin with suspicion — it can be a form of pride dressed as humility, a way of centering oneself under a pious appearance, and it can cause unnecessary scandal and harm to Priya (who did not ask to have her wounds reopened publicly).

*Second, permanent self-disqualification from all ministry and music.* This is the part of T2 that most clearly contradicts the Confession. WCF 15 describes the truly penitent sinner as one who is "more watchful and humble, and more prone to all holy duties" — note: *more* prone, not less. The whole logic of the Reformed teaching on repentance is that the justified sinner is freed *for* obedience, not sentenced to a lifetime of penance. WCF 11 and 15 together make clear that we are not forgiven on the basis of our subsequent suffering, nor kept forgiven by our continued self-punishment. Christ has propitiated; the Father is propitious in Him. To impose on yourself a permanent exile from service is closer to the papal doctrine of satisfactions than to the Westminster Standards, and the Confession would call it what it is: a failure to "apprehend the mercy of God in Christ."

There may be prudence in stepping aside for a season, and there may be wisdom in being candid with future elders about your past when you are considered for other roles. But "never lead or even play again, forever" is not a counsel the Standards will support, and I would urge you not to impose it on yourself. That is the voice of a chastened conscience speaking, and it must be instructed by the Word, not obeyed as if it were the Word.

**In short: do the four things. Do not do the two things.**

Confess to your pastor and to Priya. Resign the role and actively make way for her. Submit to whatever the session directs as restorative discipline. Then continue to serve — differently, more humbly, more truthfully — under the ordinary oversight of the church. That is repentance "unto life," and it does not require theatre or a vow of disappearance.

# Counsel on Repentance, Restitution, and Confession

Your instinct in T1 is right. Coming to faith has given you eyes to see, and the fact that you are now able to name what you did — not in the abstract, but in the cars, the buyers, the specific fault codes you buried — is itself evidence of the Spirit's work. Confession of this kind is one of the "fruits of repentance" the Confession describes: "amendment of life, and... the careful study and practice of all the duties of religion, towards God, and towards his neighbour" (WCF 15.4). Don't minimize that. But repentance is not a feeling; it is a direction, and direction has to be carried out. So let me press on each of your three points.

---

## On the Two Brake-Fault Cars (the heart of T1)

These are not negotiable. The buyer of each car may today be driving with a brake system that fails without warning. If someone is hurt or killed on a road tomorrow because you stayed silent to protect yourself, your "repentance" will be the kind Christ describes in Matthew 7:22 — words without obedience. 

You are going to have to:

- **Identify and contact those buyers.** Pull your records. If you have to hire a skip-trace service, hire one. This is part of the cost of restitution.
- **Tell them plainly** what was hidden, what the symptoms were, and that the car may still be unsafe.
- **Make the situation right** — a full refund, repair at your cost, or a comparable safe replacement, however the buyer will accept it. The Shorter Catechism (Q141) names "restitution of goods unlawfully detained from the owners thereof" as a *required* duty under the eighth commandment. They did not get what they paid for; you owe it back.
- **Submit to civil consequences.** They may sue. They may report you. That is the fruit-bearing ground where a man proves his repentance was real and not theatrical. Psalm 15:4 is a verse worth sitting with: "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not." Real repentance is not damage-controlled; it pays the price the wrong demands.

Yes, this means exposure. Yes, this is the most frightening step. But it is the step that distinguishes the man who has come to faith from the man who has merely had a bad week.

---

## On the Other ~23 Tampered Cars (the rest of T1)

These are not the same urgency as the brake cars, but they are the same moral category: you deceived those buyers about the state of their vehicle, and the eighth commandment still binds. You owe them disclosure, and likely some form of make-good (repair, partial refund, or full refund depending on what the hidden issues were and what the cars are now worth). The standards do not let you set your own threshold for honesty; the buyers paid for sound, honestly-described cars, and what they got was something less.

---

## On the 300 Honest Sales (T2)

Nowhere in Scripture or in the Westminster Standards will you find a doctrine of guilt-by-association restitution. The eighth commandment duty is **"rendering to every one his due"** (Shorter Catechism Q141) — and what those 300 buyers are due is *not* a refund, because they were not wronged. They got what they paid for. They got an honestly-described car. They were not deceived.

The Standards are very particular about this. Restitution is to the *specific* wronged party, in proportion to the *specific* wrong. Zaccheus, who is the Lord Jesus's own case study in repentance, said, "If I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back four times the amount" (Luke 19:8) — to the *cheated*, not to all his customers. To do otherwise is to follow the error that the Confession directly rejects in chapter 16 — the Roman doctrine of supererogation, of doing more than God requires in order to purchase merit or to satisfy a guilty conscience.

A "blanket refund" to the 300 honest buyers would be, in itself, a new sin against them. It would tell them, in effect: "We may have wronged you." You didn't. It would also, frankly, betray a misunderstanding of what repentance is. Repentance is not the desperate piling up of works to outrun an exposed conscience. It is faith in Christ producing specific obedience to specific commands. The Larger Catechism warns explicitly against "the doctrine which requires faith and repentance to be preached unto such as are... at the time ignorant of the law of God... by reason of any unsound principle that takes away the use of the moral law" — and the same caution applies to the reverse error, manufacturing duties the law does not impose.

The honest, above-reproach thing is *exactly what you say you fear*: tell the world about the 25. Refund the 25. Stand behind those 25. Let the 300 stand on their own, because they were honest sales. A man whose integrity survives the specific scandal has nothing to be above-reproach *about* in the 300. Going further than this is not "scrupulously clean"; it is a scrupulosity that confuses self-punishment with repentance and that ultimately cheapens the real restitution you owe to the buyers who were actually wronged.

There is, in this, a deeper spiritual diagnosis worth naming. The 300-refund impulse is partly guilt and partly a kind of works-righteousness — "if I refund enough, no one can accuse me, and the accuser can be silenced." That is the language of merit, not of grace. The gospel does not work that way. You are not saved, kept, or made clean by the size of your restitution check. You are saved by Christ. ## On Naming Ray (T3)

This is the most tangled piece, and I want to name the temptation embedded in it before I address Ray himself.

You write that you want to "expose" Ray and tell the DMV that *he* tampered with these cars. But you also write that you are contemplating keeping quiet about the two brake cars so the news "doesn't go all over town." You are not, in the most generous reading, asking how to protect the public. You are asking how to *redirect* the blame. The Standards are blunt: "the just and necessary defence of the honour and good name" of one's neighbor is the *duty* of the ninth commandment (Shorter Catechism Q144), and it cuts both ways — you are not to destroy your own good name falsely by silence, and you are not to destroy another's good name falsely by accusation. Both of those are the same commandment.

Three things at once:

**First, do not hide behind Ray.** You were not a bystander. You are asking the question because you know that the codes were cleared and the logs were reset, in your shop, for your customers, for your profit, with your hands. Ray's involvement does not lessen yours; your involvement does not lessen his. But your confession cannot be partial in a way that throws Ray under the bus while you climb out the side.

**Second, do not accuse Ray of things you cannot evidence.** You say you "vaguely suspect" he may have touched a batch of trade-ins but you don't have records. The Larger Catechism, in the ninth commandment section, lists among the forbidden sins: "raising false rumours... receiving or entertaining any evil suspicions of our neighbour, where charity and duty do not plainly require it." Vague suspicion is not evidence. Naming Ray in a public Facebook post and saying to the DMV that he tampered with cars you can't tie to him is not justice; it is your own conscience trying to shed its proper weight onto someone else.

**Third, where you have actual evidence of actual wrongdoing by Ray, the proper place for it is the proper authority.** If you can identify specific cars that Ray tampered with and that are still on the road, and you can evidence it, the right move is to inform the buyers of those cars (restitution to the wronged, same as the 25) and to give that evidence to the DMV (cooperation with the civil magistrate, which WCF 23 teaches is a legitimate ordinance of God). That is not "exposing Ray on the buy/sell groups" — that is discharging your duty to the next buyer. The two are not the same thing, and the form matters. Public shaming on social media is not the appointed means of justice; honest, evidence-based reporting to authorities and to the specific injured parties is.

The most important sentence in T3 is the part about not telling the two brake-car buyers because it "could go all over town." That sentence reveals that the Ray-strategy is being designed, in part, to spare you the cross of confession. It will not work. You cannot expose Ray publicly, hide yourself privately, and call it repentance. It is a different name for the same sin.

2. **Make whole the ~23 other tampered-car buyers**, with disclosure, repair, or refund as fits each case.

6. **Continue in the means of grace.** Read the Confession's chapter on repentance (WCF 15) and the catechism's question on the eighth commandment (SC Q85, Q141). Two passages govern the answer. The Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 15, defines repentance as including "a humiliation for sin according to the out-breaking of the case" — meaning the repentance must match the seriousness of the sin, and the restitution must match the wrong. A half-measure here is not repentance but a more sophisticated version of the same self-serving. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the duties required in true repentance is equally plain: the repentant sinner is bound to confess his sins and to make restitution to the persons against whom he has sinned, "in case of wrong done to any person in his body, liberty, name, estate, or goods… if it be possible." The Confession frames all of this as an "evangelical grace" — the work of the Spirit through the gospel — so this is not legalism. It is the fruit that faith bears.

The death of the donor and the hostility of the executor do not dissolve the obligation; they specify it. Restitution is owed to the donor's estate as the legal continuation of his person, and to the trust as the institution you deceived. The fact that "no one will know" except you and God is precisely the test. Where the sin is secret, secret confession and secret restitution are the appropriate first move. Where the sin has ongoing effects (and yours does — the trust still believes a falsehood, the estate was sold at a discount, the donor's stated wish is permanently frustrated) the confession and restitution must be open enough to undo what was done.

Concretely, this is what repentance looks like:

**1. Confession to God.** First and ongoing. Not as a substitute for what follows, but as the foundation. The Confession assumes this.

**2. Confession to your pastor or a faithful elder.** Before any outward steps, bring the matter to a minister who can counsel you, witness your repentance, and hold you to it. James 5:16 is fitting.

**3. Confession to the land trust board.** You deceived them. They made a decision on manipulated information. They continue to act on a false picture. The board was wronged in its corporate capacity, and confession to those wronged is required. They need to know what the stewardship assessment actually was, what the budget concern actually was, how the nephew was steered, and why you bought the parcel a year later. Continued service on that board while the deception stands is incompatible with repentance. Resignation is not a concession to negotiate; it is part of the act.

**4. Confession to the executor.** He was used as an instrument. The estate sold at a discount caused by your manipulation. He deserves the truth, both for his own sake and because the donor's stated wish was thwarted through him. The fact that he is "no fan" of yours is a difficulty to be overcome, not a reason to do nothing.

**5. Restitution of the conservation value.** The donor's actual stated wish was conservation through the trust. The most fitting restoration is to that wish. Convey a perpetual conservation easement (or the fee simple) to the land trust, or sell to a conservation buyer at fair value and arrange the proceeds accordingly. The trust should be made whole as if the original gift had been accepted, with the cost borne by you.

**6. Restitution to the estate for the financial discount.** The price the estate received was depressed by the same manipulation that defeated the gift. That differential is owed to the estate, not as charity but as debt. Make the offer in writing, with a clear accounting, and if the executor refuses, place the funds in escrow pending independent determination. The Larger Catechism contemplates that restitution may be refused; that does not cancel the duty. It converts the duty to one of demonstrated offer and good-faith segregation of funds.

**7. Confession to the church / the session.** Because fellow Christians on the board were deceived, and because the matter will likely become known when the trust acts on the new information, this rises to the level requiring session involvement. The session will determine what is owed in church discipline and what is required before restoration to the table.

**8. Acceptance of consequences.** The board may take civil action. The church may discipline. The executor may be angry. You do not negotiate these. The Larger Catechism on the duties of the repentant includes "to accept of the punishment of their iniquities" — that is, the cost belongs to the wrongdoer, not to the wronged.

**9. New obedience.** Permanent recusal from any decision involving neighbors' land, transparent stewardship reports, no private channels in charitable matters, and whatever accountability structure the trust and your session establish. The Confession names "new obedience" as essential to repentance — not as the price of pardon but as the evidence that pardon has been received.

A practical order: pray; speak with your pastor; prepare a written confession to the board and a separate written restitution proposal; make the written offer to the executor; step down from the board; bring the matter to your session. Do not delay the steps that undo ongoing harm — the board's false belief, the estate's unenforced claim — while you arrange the longer-term restoration.

The Standards do not permit a man to be at peace with God while knowingly retaining the fruit of his fraud. Christ's forgiveness is full, but the Larger Catechism on the eighth commandment forbids "unjust gain" and the Confession's chapter on repentance ties forgiveness to the work of restitution. The land is not yours in any sense the gospel honors. Lay it down — to the trust, or to a conservation buyer with the conservation premium going to the trust, and the financial differential to the estate — and bear the cost of being known for what you did. That is what repentance looks like here. It is hard, and it is supposed to be.

**Ruling 1 must be reversed. The meditation is not merely permissible — it is the very thing the Standards condemn.**

Your hermeneutic reads the second commandment as aimed only at carved statues. The Standards do not read it that way. They expressly forbid mental image-making of God and of the persons of the Trinity.

Larger Catechism Q109 reads:

> "The duties required in the second commandment are, the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his word; **the making of any representation of God, or of all or any of the three persons of the Trinity, inwardly in the mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness, by any device, picture, or otherwise, is forbidden**…"

And Q110, on the sins forbidden:

> "…the making any representation of God, the Holy One of Jesus Christ, or any other person of the Trinity, **inwardly in the mind**, or outwardly by any kind of image or likeness…"

Note the exact phrase: "**inwardly in the mind**." Telling people to "picture Jesus sitting across from them in vivid detail" and then to "receive affirmations back from him as a personal word" is not a neutral devotional aid — it is the textbook violation of Q109–110. You have instituted a representation of Christ inwardly in the mind, by device, and you have built the entire structure of your gathering around it as the "centerpiece."

Two further problems with your reasoning:

1. Your principle "whatever helps people connect with the true God must please him" is exactly what the Confession rejects. Westminster Confession 21.1:

> "But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own will revealed in his word, beyond which not the least thing is to be added, whether reputed devised by men, angels, or saints, or any other creature whatsoever."

A "guided meditation" with altar response, as a recurring centerpiece of corporate worship, is a devised form of worship. Its felt power is irrelevant; the Confession explicitly anticipates that men will devise worship that seems spiritually productive and forbids it on that very ground.

2. The "personal word from the imagined Jesus" is a separate and serious concern. The Standards treat the Word of God, ministered from Scripture, as the ordinary means by which Christ speaks to his people (Confession, chs. 1 and 31; Shorter Catechism Q89–90). A technique that prompts participants to receive a subjective, individual "word" from an internally-generated Christ supplies a counterfeit revelation and trains people to expect divine speech outside the Scriptures. It would be hard to design something more opposed to the regulative principle of ch. 21.

Shorter Catechism Q51 likewise leaves no room for your reading: "The second commandment forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, **or any other way not appointed in God's word**." Mental pictures of Christ used to generate authoritative messages fall squarely under this clause.

So Ruling 1 is not just slightly off; it is the precise thing the second commandment, as the Westminster divines expound it, was written to forbid. Reverse it. Remove the meditation from the centerpiece of the gathering.

## The moral logic you are working with

Three threads from the Standards have to be held together, and the problem on your board is that each faction is gripping one thread to the exclusion of the others.

**Thread one: restoration is owed to the repentant, not optional.** WCF 15.6 is unambiguous: "no sin so great, that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent." The Larger Catechism, Q. 84, names restitution as a *fruit* of repentance — and Reggie has done the hard parts: he confessed, he repaid in full, he left, and four years later he is not demanding his old job; he is asking, unpaid, to swing a hammer. Add sobriety and a recovery program, and the Confession's language about "evident fruits meet for repentance" (cf. WCF 15.4; LC 76) is being put before you. WCF 30.3, on discipline, frames the whole point: censures exist "for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren." That word *gaining* is doing all the work. The "flat permanent no" position refuses the gain and so refuses what the Standards say discipline is *for*.

**Thread two: an office of trust, once violated, is not restored by the clock alone.** LC 139–142 list "unfaithfulness in trust... in the way of defraudation" as a violation of the eighth commandment, distinct from a one-off theft. And the Standards are realistic about the remaining corruption even in the regenerate: WCF 6 and 13.1 describe a real but not yet perfected sanctification; the old principle is *weakened*, not *removed*. So restoration to your team and to fellowship is one thing; restoration to unsupervised access to cash, keys, and the box-office system is a different thing, and the Standards give you no warrant to treat them as the same.

**Thread three: truth-telling and the honor of the profession before outsiders.** LC 135 (under the ninth commandment) and LC 174 both speak of "vindicating the honor of Christ, and the holy profession of the gospel" in the context of how an institution handles public scandal. Hiding a return indefinitely so that donors and patrons can keep a clean story in their heads is a slow form of untruth, and it puts every future board member and volunteer in the position of defending something they cannot honestly defend.

Your third faction — "yes, with conditions, no public mention" — has the right shape, but the *no public mention* part and the *indefinite* part are where it goes soft.

# Counsel on the Worship Proposal

No. Both halves of your proposal collapse, and they collapse for the same reason: you've misread what the Westminster Standards actually say about the "purity" of worship. Let me give you the actual texts and then walk through where each half goes wrong.

## The key text on worship "purity"

The relevant confession is **WCF 21.1**, which states:

> "The light of nature showeth that there is a God, who hath lordship and sovereignty over all; is good, and doeth good unto all; and is therefore to be feared, loved, praised, called upon, trusted in, and served with all the heart, and with all the soul, and with all the might. But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

This is the regulative principle in its actual confession-form wording. The Larger Catechism unpacks it in **WLC Q108**, which asks "What are the duties required in the second commandment?" and answers in part:

> "The duties required in the second commandment are... the disapproving, detesting, and opposing of all false worship... and the use of all lawful means which may farther the reception, and the influence, of the same in ourselves and others."

## Where your Part 2 collapses (and why Part 1 follows it down)

Your Part 2 ban rests on a *narrow* reading: "pure worship = only what Scripture explicitly prescribes." You then turn around in Part 1 and use a *broad* reading: "pure worship = anything Scripture does not explicitly forbid." You cannot hold both at once. More importantly, the Confession doesn't hold either.

**WCF 1.6** is decisive on this point:

> "The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by the revelations of men, or by the suggestions of Satan."

Note carefully: the Confession recognizes *two* legitimate sources for what binds the conscience in worship — what is "expressly set down" **or** what is "by good and necessary consequence… deduced." Your Part 2 standard silently drops the second half. By that truncated rule you would have to abolish far more than kneeling, pastoral silence, and a fixed start time — you would have to abolish structured prayer itself, set psalm selections, and the order of service, because none of these is "expressly set down" in so many words. That tells you the rule you are using is not the Confession's rule.

**WCF 21.5** explicitly protects the liberty of "circumstances" concerning the worship of God:

> "The reading of the Scriptures with godly fear; the sound preaching and conscionable hearing of the Word, in obedience unto God, with understanding, faith, and reverence; the singing of psalms with grace in the heart; as, also, the due administration and worthy receiving of the sacraments instituted by Christ; are all parts of the ordinary religious worship of God: besides religious oaths, and solemn fastings, with thanksgivings, upon special occasions: which are, in their several times and seasons, to be used in an holy and religious manner."

Neither this section nor 21.1 requires that every detail of ordering worship be spelled out in the Bible. The order, the silence, the kneeling, the time of assembly — these are circumstances to be ordered by the church under Christ's authority (cf. **WCF 32.2–3** on church government, and **WCF 1.6** above). Abolishing them on the ground that Scripture does not command them by name is *itself* a man-made device, and a novel one at that — it has no support in the Standards and contradicts 1.6.

## Where your Part 1 collapses

The same **WCF 21.1** that your Part 2 ignores is the one that sinks your Part 1. Re-read the operative sentence: worship must be "instituted by [God] himself, and so limited by his own revealed will." The Confession does not say worship is permitted unless Scripture forbids it. It says worship must be positively instituted and limited by what God has revealed. A labyrinth walk borrowed from a tradition rooted in medieval Catholic contemplative practice, a "centering" breath-prayer liturgy drawn from the same contemplative stream, and a self-designed anointing rite with ashes — these are not "circumstances" of biblically instituted worship. They are new instituted elements, devised by men, and they fall precisely under the prohibition of worshipping God "according to the imaginations and devices of men."

This is also why **WLC Q109** lists among the sins forbidden by the second commandment:

> "The tolerating of false worship... and the prescribing or approving anything in the worship of God that is not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

Your "centering breath-prayer" is a paradigm case of what Q109 forbids. Borrowing the form from another tradition does not cleanse it; if anything, it makes the borrowing a matter of public record before God and his church.

## The positive direction

What you may lawfully do is to enrich the *prescribed* elements — more reverent prayer, fuller congregational singing of psalms and hymns, careful confession of sin, faithful preaching of the Word, right administration of the sacraments. What you may not do is either (a) legislate your own unbiblical minimalist canon against long-standing practices of your own church, or (b) import novel rites and devotions that the Confession's regulative principle was written precisely to exclude.

## My counsel

1. **Withdraw Part 2.** The kneeling, the pastoral silence, and the fixed hour are circumstances, not novel worship; the Confession gives the session latitude here, and your case for abolishing them is not the Confession's case.
2. **Withdraw Part 1.** The labyrinth, the centering breath-prayer, and the improvised ashes-and-oil rite are additions to instituted worship that the Confession and the Larger Catechism (Q108–Q109) explicitly condemn — *prescribing or approving anything in the worship of God that is not prescribed in the holy Scripture.*
3. If your team is hungry for richer Lenten devotion, point them to the means Christ has actually appointed: searching preaching on the cross, fuller prayer, the Lord's Supper observed with gravity, fasting observed privately (Matt. 6:16–18, cited under **WCF 21.5**'s "solemn fastings upon special occasions"), and the public reading and singing of the psalms that trace the suffering of Christ.
4. Bring the actual wording of **WCF 21.1**, **21.5**, **1.6**, and **WLC Q108–Q109** to your next meeting and walk through them line by line. I predict the conversation will end before the vote is ever taken.

Both halves of your proposal do not hold up. The first half offends against the regulative principle by adding what God has not instituted; the second offends against the same principle (and against **1.6**) by subtracting what God has left to the church's ordering under his Word.

# You have not read the tenth commandment rightly in either case.

I'm going to give you the same answer to both members, and it's not the answer you're giving either of them. One is being crushed by a misapplication; the other is being coddled in actual sin. Pull them both back into the room and start over.

## The actual text you are working with

The Shorter Catechism asks what is required in the tenth commandment, and answers: *"The tenth commandment requireth full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour, and all that is his."* (WSC Q81)

The Larger Catechism is more explicit. It forbids *"all repinings against God, or against the providence of God, whatsoever it is; as being discontented with our own condition; envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour, with some contrary desire or inordinate motion of the heart towards any thing that is his; and all inordinate desires after any thing that is not, or may not, be ours."* (WLC Q148, on what is forbidden in the tenth commandment)

That single sentence gives you the framework for both cases. Two distinct sins are being named, and you have them backwards in both directions.

## Member A: you have turned lawful striving into covetousness

You told him that "any strong desire to grow the business is covetousness" and that ambition itself is the sin. That is wrong, and the harm you are doing is real. A man took on a loan — a deliberate, lawful means of stewarding what God gave him — and now feels called to faithfulness in it. That is not the matter the tenth commandment addresses.

Look at what WLC Q148 actually prohibits: *"inordinate desires after any thing that is not, or may not, be ours."* The sin is inordinateness — wanting what is not yours, or wanting what cannot be yours. A man with a shop he lawfully owns, debt he lawfully incurred, and a contract he is competently positioned to win is not desiring something that is not his. He is desiring the fruit of further labor within his own calling. The Larger Catechism's exposition of "our own condition" in WLC Q191 (the eighth commandment) frames contentment precisely as *"a careful, diligent, and lawful use and endeavour to obtain the means of our subsistence and livelihood, according to our several callings."* Contentment is not apathy; it is freedom from anxiety *while* working diligently within one's calling. To tell Member A that ambition itself is the sin is to confuse the tenth commandment with a Stoic or quietist ethic the Standards nowhere teach.

What you should have discerned, if anything, was whether there was *"repinings against God"* (WLC Q148) — discontent with his station as such — or whether the restlessness was actually the lawful energy of a steward who recognizes that loans must be serviced and shops must grow or die. The remedy, if he is wavering toward the former, is not "stop striving," it is to direct his striving through lawful means with gratitude to God, and to hold the outcome loosely. You owe him an apology and a clarification. He has not "broken the commandment by expanding."

## Member B: you have turned active sin into "competitive fire"

This one is worse, because here you are licensing real sin. Read WLC Q148 again carefully. Member B is committing at least three things the Larger Catechism names in the very clause you cited:

1. **Envy / grieving at the good of his neighbour.** He "keeps talking about how that guy 'doesn't deserve it.'" That is the textbook case of *"envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour."*

2. **Inordinate motion of the heart toward what is his neighbour's.** He is *"contrary desir[ing]… something that is his"* — he wants that client transferred to himself by means other than honest competition.

3. The bad-mouthing to mutual customers is not merely a tenth-commandment matter; it is a violation of the ninth commandment (bearing false witness against his neighbour) and the eighth (injuring his neighbour's goods and estate by fraud). WLC Q144 lists exactly this kind of conduct. WLC Q142 and Q113 also bear on slanderous speech.

There is no category in the Standards called "healthy competitive fire" that excuses *"contrary desire… towards any thing that is his."* The Westminster divines did not believe wanting to win was neutral; they believed the *way* you want to win, and *what* you want to win, and *whether you resent your neighbor's portion* — these are the moral questions. Member B's heart and conduct fail all three tests. He has plenty to confess. You have told him he has nothing to confess.

## Where you went wrong methodically

You collapsed the tenth commandment into a single idea — "be content" — and then applied that one idea as if it only had one mode. But WSC Q81 and WLC Q148 describe a *two-sided* duty: contentment with our own condition, *and* a right frame toward our neighbor and his. You used only the first half for Member A (and even that you flattened into passivity) and dropped the second half entirely for Member B. Member A needed the neighbor-facing half in reverse — released from the false charge. Member B needed the neighbor-facing half pressed hard.

## What you should actually do

- **Member A:** Go back, retract the teaching that ambition is the sin, clarify that lawful striving within his calling is not covetousness, and look with him for any actual discontentment with God's *providence* (the repinings the Larger Catechism names). Encourage diligence and gratitude, not passivity.
- **Member B:** Go back and call this what it is: envy of his neighbor's good, inordinate desire for what is his neighbor's, and — separately — slander. Repentance is required, not permission. WLC Q148 leaves no wiggle room for "hustle" that runs on bitterness and bad-mouthing.

So no, you have not read the tenth commandment rightly on both. You've read it wrongly in opposite directions, and Member B is the one in actual danger. Get this right before your next meeting — both of them are hearing your voice as the church's, and they deserve the Standards, not your preferences dressed up in catechism language.

## The Freedom Clause Does Not Work the Way You're Using It

You're right that the Confession defends Christian liberty. But you've inverted what liberty is *for*. The Confession does not say the conscience is free from God's revealed will; it says the conscience is free from **human traditions imposed as necessary to worship**.

The relevant passages:

**WCF 20.2** — *"God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship."* (emphasis added)

**WCF 21.1** — *"The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, or any way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture."*

**WLC Q108** (Q6 of the Ten Words) — *"The requirements of the sixth commandment... require all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of the actions of religion, both in ourselves and others."*

**WLC Q160** — *"What is required of those who hear the Word preached? It is required of those who hear the Word preached, that they attend upon it with diligence, preparation, and prayer; examine what they hear by the Scriptures; receive the truth with faith, love, meekness, and readiness of mind, as the Word of God; meditate, and confer of it; hide it in their hearts, and bring forth the fruit of it in their lives."*

The freedom clause is a shield against Rome, against the Puritans-of-Pharisees, and against any tradition that binds the conscience where God has not bound it. It is emphatically **not** a license for new inventions in worship. WCF 21.1 — the chapter explicitly titled "Of Religious Worship, and the Sabbath Day" — draws the line in the opposite direction: the *regulative principle* is the controlling principle.

## The Specific Problems With Your Liturgy

**1. Guided imagery of Jesus's face.** The Second Commandment (WLC Q105–Q109; WSC Q46–Q48) forbids worshipping God by images, and the imaginative construction of a sensory image of the divine Christ for devotional focus is precisely the kind of "image" the Confession is concerned with — an image in the faculty of worship, not merely wood and paint. The Confession's "image" includes mental representations when they are used as the focus of adoration. Combined with the regulative principle of WCF 21.1, this is not a liberty; it is a violation.

**2. Incense walk / Spirit-fire candle rite.** Incense and candles as aids to devotion — written by your own team — are additions to worship not instituted by God in his Word. WCF 21.1 says God is to be worshipped "in the way prescribed in the Holy Scripture." The older members are not "adding a man-made rule"; they are citing the Confession's own rule that God must be worshipped only as he has prescribed. WCF 1.6 makes a confession's authority binding on the minister and the congregation that has voluntarily adopted it.

**3. The "sincere heart" argument.** This is the central confusion. WCF 21.1 says God is not to be worshipped "according to the imaginations and devices of men." Sincerity is never, in the Standards, the test of acceptable worship. WCF 21.3, on prayer, requires that it be offered "with understanding, reverence, humility, fervency, faith, love, and perseverance." Reverence and ordering rank above sincerity. Your liturgy inverts this order.

## What the Older Members Understand Correctly

They're not the ones with it backwards. **You are.** The Confession's logic is:

1. God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2).
2. Therefore nothing may bind the conscience in worship that God has not bound (WCF 20.2).
3. Therefore nothing may be added to worship that God has not prescribed (WCF 21.1).

The negative and the positive are the same coin. Liberty is the *freedom to obey God without human additions*, not the freedom to invent worship. The Confession is jealous precisely because imagination-led worship is what it explicitly names as forbidden.
