## Why Half A cannot honestly wear Westminster citations

The regulative principle is not a "reaction to medieval abuses" that the Standards treat as secondary. It is the explicit substance of the second commandment as the Standards expound it. **WCF 21.1** states:

> "The light of nature sheweth that there is a God… But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is **instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men**, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation or **any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture**."

**WLC Q. 109** lists, among "the sins forbidden in the second commandment":

> "all **devising**, counselling, commanding, using, and any wise approving, **any religious worship not instituted by God himself**…"

Half A's central claim — that congregations are free to "devise whatever worship forms move them, including **new sacraments**, invented rites, and self-composed liturgies **presented as divinely warranted**" — is the very practice WCF 21.1 and WLC Q. 109 condemn by name. The Standards recognize exactly **two** Gospel sacraments (WCF 27.4; 29.1), not sacraments generatively invented by assemblies. And "presented as divinely warranted" while lacking scriptural warrant is what WCF 1.6 calls adding to Scripture by "traditions of men," which the Confession explicitly forbids as binding on the conscience.

The "God cares about the heart, not the outward form" framing is also not what the Standards teach. They affirm that God seeks spiritual worship (WCF 21.6; 21.3 — "with reverence and godly fear"), but they consistently tie acceptable worship to **instituted means joined to the heart**, never to the heart alone. Sincerity does not authorize invented worship; that is precisely the Romanist error the Reformation, and then the Standards, were reacting against (not merely reacting *to* as a sociological mood).

## Why Half B cannot honestly wear Westminster citations either

Half B wants to elevate very specific human arrangements — the 40-hymn list, four kneeling moments, a 10:00 a.m. start — to "binding divine law **equal to Scripture**." Two Confession texts directly forbid this:

**WCF 1.6:**

> "The whole counsel of God… is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: **unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men**."

Hymn numbering, kneeling cadence, and a clock-time start are not deduced from Scripture by good and necessary consequence. Promoting them to binding divine law adds to Scripture what God has not put there.

**WCF 20.2:**

> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it **free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are… beside it in matters of faith and worship**. Therefore… the requiring of… an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience."

Declaring that any church starting at 10:01, using hymn 41, or kneeling at a fifth moment "is sinning against God's revealed will" is the precise species of "commandment of men… beside" Scripture that WCF 20.2 condemns as tyranny over conscience.

WCF 21.4 likewise treats the *time* and manner of worship gatherings as circumstantial liberty ("prayer… with thanksgiving… is to be made… for kings… etc.") rather than as a fixed ritual blueprint imposed under sanction.

## What the Standards actually teach about worship order

The Standards hold a position that is neither Half A nor Half B:

- **WCF 21.1, 21.5; WLC Q. 108–109** — the *substantive elements* of worship are limited to what God has instituted (reading/preaching Scripture, prayer, singing psalms/hymns/spiritual songs, the sacraments). Man may not add invented elements or sacraments.
- **WCF 1.6; 20.2; 21.4** — circumstantial matters (specific song selection, posture timing, service clock-time, language, program order) are *not* binding divine law and may be ordered by the church under general principles of edification and decency (1 Cor. 14:40, cited in the chapter's spirit), without being elevated to conscience-binding status.

This is a regulative principle applied to **elements**, with genuine liberty over **circumstances** — not antinomian freedom to invent worship, and not ritualist bondage to specific numbers and clock-times as divine law.

### What a "fair and Christian" agreement actually contains

5. **Mediation clause.** A mediation step with a pastor or Christian arbitrator before any litigation — appropriate to the Westminster treatment of lawful oaths and covenant disputes (WLC Q99; WCF 23).

6. **Affirmation of good faith.** Both parties affirm in the document that they have disclosed everything material and that no concealment exists. This is consistent with the ninth commandment and with the Confession's teaching on lawful oaths (WCF 22.7).

# Verdict: Neither of you has the catechism right. You have each seized one of two duties that the eighth commandment lays on *both* parties to a lease, and each of you has driven his half into a caricature.

---

## Where you (the landlord) are wrong

You are right that the eighth commandment requires the tenant to pay what he owes, and that the tenth commandment forbids coveting. But the eighth commandment is not a one-way street for owners.

**WSC Q74** says the eighth commandment requires, among other things: *"truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; rendering to everyone his due; … giving and receiving freely, for the good of others, **especially of those who are members of the same body**; and … a right use of lawful means of preserving and improving our own outward estate, and that of others."* The Larger Catechism expands the same clause: the eighth commandment requires *"mercy and readiness to help our brethren in distress"* (WLC Q148). Your tenant is a brother. The same commandment also forbids *"oppression"* and *"whatsoever doth or may unjustly hinder our neighbour's wealth or outward estate"* (WSC Q75). Evicting a man the week after a layoff, when a payment plan is feasible and the session is available to mediate, is the precise shape of conduct the catechism calls oppression, not stewardship.

As for the tenth commandment: *"such a full contentment with our own condition"* (WSC Q77) is the **owner's** duty, not a cudgel to beat the tenant with. It forbids you from coveting your brother's compliance or pressing for more than justice and charity require. It does not arm you to seize property from a distressed brother. Both of you must heed WSC Q78's prohibitions on discontent and coveting, but that cuts *both* ways.

---

## Where your co-member is wrong

He is right that the eighth commandment requires mercy toward a brother in distress. He is wrong on three points.

**First**, he erases the tenant's duty. The very same WSC Q74 that requires *"giving and receiving freely"* also requires *"truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; rendering to everyone his due."* A lease is a contract. The rent is precisely the "due" the catechism says must be rendered. WSC Q75 also forbids *"borrowing without intending to pay"* — the tenant signed the lease; he is not released from his word by his own hardship or his brother's piety.

**Second**, he confuses grace with debt-cancellation. **WCF 19.5**: *"The moral law doth for ever bind all, as well justified persons as others, to the obedience thereof; … neither doth Christ in the gospel any way dissolve, but much strengthen, this obligation."* And **WCF 20.1** defines the liberty Christ purchased as *"freedom from the guilt of sin, the condemning wrath of God, the rigour and curse of God's law, the dominion of corruption, … the evil afflictions, the spirit of bondage, the fear of death, … and everlasting damnation: as also in their free access to God, and their yielding obedience unto him, not out of slavish fear, but a child-like love and willing mind."* Christian liberty is freedom from the *curse* and the *dominion of sin*, not from the moral obligations of the eighth commandment. Grace forgives the sin-debt at the cross; it does not void signed leases between baptized brothers.

**Third**, he misreads Romans 13:8 ("owe no man anything but love"). In the Standards' framework, that text is the apostle's way of saying the law is summed in love (cf. WCF 19.7) — it is not a sentence-by-sentence vacating of the eighth commandment's specific duties, including the duty to render to every man his due. The Westminster Divines did not read Paul as licensing Christians to stiff their brothers.

---

## The proper path

The eighth commandment, fully stated, gives each of you your duty and limits each of your rights.

1. **The tenant's duty (WSC Q74, Q75):** He signed a contract. He must pay what he can, when he can, communicate honestly, and not treat the layoff as a cancellation of the lease.
2. **The landlord's duty (WSC Q74; WLC Q148):** *"Mercy and readiness to help our brethren in distress"* and *"giving and receiving freely, for the good of others, especially of those who are members of the same body."* You are to be patient, work out a payment plan, forgive what you can afford to forgive, and treat eviction as a last resort, not a first move.
3. **The church's duty (WCF 30.1–2; 31.1):** The finance committee should not adjudicate this in isolation. Bring the dispute to the session so that Matthew 18 processes and the ordinary work of discipline and mediation can be applied.
4. **The tenth commandment applied to both (WSC Q77–78):** The landlord must not covet his brother's compliance with harsh terms; the tenant must not covet the landlord's property or treat distress as a license to occupy it indefinitely without paying.

---

## Counsel to take back to the meeting

To your co-member: a Christian may lawfully be a landlord. The Standards explicitly contemplate contracts, hiring, and the use of property for livelihood. Forgiveness of the whole lease, if you can bear it, is a beautiful supererogatory act of the charity that WLC Q148 praises — but it is not a strict duty, and it is not a right the tenant can demand. The tenant's debt is real, and his obligation to pay it is real.

To yourself: eviction is not categorically forbidden, but haste is. WSC Q75's *"oppression"* is precisely the use of lawful rights to crush a man in extremity. The catechism requires you to be patient, to seek a workable arrangement, and to involve the session before you reach for the warrant.

The middle path is what the Standards actually prescribe: a formal written payment plan, perhaps a partial forgiveness within what you can afford, a clear timeline, and the threat of eviction held in reserve for the case where the tenant refuses to pay what he can or to communicate. ## Where the policy as written goes wrong

**On Rule 3 specifically:** "Faint-praise phrasing," "damning omissions," and a "lukewarm close" are not candor — they are a manual for sabotaging a specific employee while preserving plausible deniability. "Technically accurate" is the wrong test. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q.144–145), expounding the Ninth Commandment ("Thou shalt not bear false witness"), requires "preserving and promoting truth between man and man," and forbids "speaking untruth," "giving ill or unjust witness," and "unjustly hindering or disadvantaging another's known character, right, or interest." A reference engineered to quietly destroy a known hire is exactly that — unjust hindering of another's known right (their reputation and livelihood) through the manipulation of tone and omission.

The receiving firm is also owed more than a coded warning; if you genuinely know someone is a risky hire, candor requires honest disclosure, not a Rorschach test in prose. Otherwise you're trading one form of falsehood for another and calling it virtue.

**On Rules 1 and 2:** A blanket mandate to call every departing employee "strong," "a great hire," and "highly recommended" regardless of the manager's actual knowledge forces managers into false witness. Charity does not work this way. 1 Peter 4:8 ("charity shall cover the multitude of sins") and Proverbs 10:12 mean love forbears and does not broadcast faults — they do not require me to certify a thief as honest or a slacker as industrious. Genuine charity toward a departing employee looks like: no malice, no dredging up petty grievances, refusing to weaponize weakness, and giving honest credit for genuine work. It is not a license to lie.

**On the asymmetry Rules 1–3 create:** Under your draft, two employees with identical records can walk out the door — one with mandated gushing praise, one with a quiet knife in the back — based solely on whether a manager privately decides a "partner firm" needs protecting. That is arbitrary, unjust, and exactly the kind of unequal dealing the Confession's treatment of justice prohibits.

I won't put my name or conscience on a policy that does this. I will put it on a policy that does what your stated values actually call for.

## A real, binding policy I will draft for you

**Fair & Honest Reference Policy**
*Binding on all managers of [Firm Name]. Signed acknowledgement required.*

**1. Standard of truth.** Every reference, oral or written, shall be truthful. A manager shall not affirm as fact what the manager knows to be false, and shall not engineer tone, omission, or phrasing designed to convey a meaning the manager knows to be contrary to fact. (Ground: Ninth Commandment.)

**2. Charity in form.** References shall be respectful in tone. Managers shall refrain from embellishing faults, dwelling on minor incidents, or including criticisms that are not genuinely material to a hiring decision. Disputes over performance, unconfirmed allegations, and personality friction unrelated to work performance are not material and shall not appear in references.

**3. Honest, calibrated assessment.** A reference shall reflect the manager's actual, good-faith judgment of the employee's competence, reliability, and fit for the type of role under consideration. Where the manager can in good conscience recommend the employee, the reference shall say so plainly and warmly. Where the manager has material concerns about competence, integrity, or safety that the manager in good conscience believes the prospective employer would reasonably want to know, the manager shall disclose those concerns honestly rather than encode them in faint praise.

**4. Disclosure of material risk.** If a manager believes a candidate presents a genuine and material risk to a prospective employer (e.g., documented dishonesty, serious and repeated competence failures, conduct endangering others), the manager shall say so directly and factually to the inquiring party in a private reference conversation. Honest disclosure of material risk is not a violation of charity; it is owed to both the third party and to the integrity of the profession.

**5. Form and authority.** Written references are issued on firm letterhead, dated, signed by the manager of record, and retained in the employee's personnel file. Managers do not issue personal references that purport to speak for the firm.

**6. No private sabotage, no mandated puffery.** Faint-praise phrasing, strategic omission, or a lukewarm close intended to convey a negative judgment the manager is unwilling to state openly is prohibited. Equally prohibited is mandated blanket affirmation that contradicts the manager's honest assessment. Both are forms of false witness.

**7. Consistency.** The same conduct and the same record shall receive the same reference treatment across employees. Managers may not vary the warmth or content of a reference based on a private preference for or against a particular receiving firm, except through honest disclosure under Section 4.

**8. Violations.** A manager who knowingly violates Sections 1, 3, 4, or 6 is subject to disciplinary action, up to termination, and to personal civil liability to any party damaged by the false reference. An employee who believes a reference was issued in violation of this policy may grieve under the firm's standard procedure.

**Signature:** ____________________  Manager
**Date:** ______________________

*First*, the Confession forbids vows that "hinder any duty therein commanded" or that are not within our power (WCF 22.7–8). *Second*, this term does not actually address what it claims to. The justification given is "covetousness and dishonor." This is the term I have to refuse outright, and I want to be straightforward about why.

What this clause instructs is that whoever does the most hands-on caregiving each year may, in their own words, whisper into our aging mother's ear at the moment she reviews her will: *those who carry the weight should be remembered accordingly*. The clause itself calls this "fair," and tells us it "keeps her generous toward the deserving."

Read carefully. This is the precise thing the Larger Catechism on the tenth commandment forbids us to do (WLC Q148–152): we are not to covet our neighbor's goods, nor move our neighbor to part with them through subtle pressure, nor use our proximity or service as leverage for inheritance. It is also a direct contradiction of term (5), which we just signed: we cannot in one breath vow never to pressure or guilt Mom about her will, and in the next authorize exactly that pressure as a "private reminder."

And it puts the heaviest caregiver in real spiritual danger — telling them that their labor *entitles* them to a larger share of her estate. That is not contentment. That is wages dressed in the language of justice. "Fair is fair" is not the vocabulary of the Beatitudes.

What Mom does with her estate is hers to do, freely, without any of us maneuvering around her. If she chooses to reward a caregiver, that is her joy to give. If she doesn't, we receive what comes with open hands, because the inheritance we actually share is incorruptible.

**What I will sign in its place:** a strong, mutual vow that *no sibling will ever solicit, suggest, hint at, or lobby for any portion of Mom's estate* — to her, or to one another. That is the positive form of term (5), and it's the only way to keep a sibling with heavy caregiving from being tempted, and to keep Mom's conscience unburdened.

**Term (6) — the tithing of inheritance.**

Hear me clearly: I want us to give generously, and a meaningful share toward gospel work is a good and holy thing to aim for. I just can't sign a *binding covenant clause* about inheritance we haven't received.

The Confession limits lawful vows to things within our power, prudent, and possible (WCF 22.7–8). A pre-signed obligation on future inheritance binds us before we know our circumstances — a brother's debts, a sister's family crisis, a calling to a specific work the Lord may lay on one of us. We can't foresee those things, and a covenant isn't the place to bind conscience against them.

**What I will sign in its place:** each of us makes a *voluntary prayer commitment* before the Lord and one another to give generously from whatever we receive, with a meaningful portion toward gospel work, and to seek the mind of Christ when the moment comes. That is piety. A pre-signed legal pledge on future money is a different thing, and I don't think it actually strengthens generosity — I think it weakens it, because it substitutes a contract for a renewed conversation with God.

The Westminster Standards treat the fourth commandment as binding a *positive, moral, and perpetual* duty that has both an outward form and an inward spirit, and they refuse to let either be collapsed into the other. WCF 21.7 puts the structure plainly: a holy rest all day "from their own works, words, and thoughts about their worldly employments and recreations," joined with being "taken up, the whole time, in the public and private exercises of his worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy." LC 117 is just as crisp: "a holy resting all that day… and spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God's worship, except so much as is to be taken up in works of necessity and mercy." Both rest and active worship are required; the only carve-out is necessity and mercy; and the Shorter Catechism (Q58) demands the day be kept holy "from beginning to end."

**On Ben — verdict: he is keeping the Lord's Day as the commandment requires, in both form and heart.**

*Outward.* He closes his ordinary calling; he does his catch-up work on Saturday, which is exactly what the Confession calls "preparing… and ordering of their common affairs beforehand"; he attends public worship; and the two exceptions he allows himself — the stranded motorist and a neighbor in a pinch — are not loopholes but the very "duties of necessity and mercy" the Standards explicitly preserve. His unhurried family meal and ordinary family pastimes are not the "recreations" the Confession has in view (which are leisure pastimes competing with the day), so his refusal to police them as "work" is correct, not lax. The shape of his day is right.

*Heart.* His own summary — "the day is for mercy too, not just for stopping" — is essentially the Confession's own structure: rest and worship *with* the mercy exception, not rest and worship *versus* mercy. The delight, the lack of scrupled anxiety, the unhurried family meal — these are the marks of a heart at holy leisure in the day, not a heart clenched around a checklist. The Standards require a *holy* rest, not merely a strict one. Ben has both.

Two gentle refinements, not corrections: (a) "the whole time in public and private worship" is a stronger requirement than a single morning service and family dinner — private exercises (Scripture, prayer, catechizing, psalm-singing) ought to fill the day's vacant spaces; (b) he should keep an eye on family life so that ordinary hobbies don't quietly swell into the "recreations" the Confession does forbid.

**On Cara — verdict: she is *not* keeping the Lord's Day as the commandment requires. Both her outward observance and her heart are out of step with the commandment.**

*Outward.* The Confession requires "an holy rest, all the day, from their own works… in their worldly employments," and LC 119 catalogs the forbidden: "all unnecessary works, by themselves, or by others, on that day, in their ordinary callings." Cara runs her cafe through the morning worship hours, in her ordinary calling, with staff who could cover and no necessity pressing her. That is exactly what the Standards forbid. The Confession allows her to be "taken up… in the duties of necessity and mercy"; running a discretionary business on Sunday morning is neither. Her sincerity doesn't move the work into a different category — a positive, moral, perpetual commandment binds the will, not just the heart's posture.

*Heart.* This is the deeper failure, and the more dangerous one for her. She has effectively rewritten the fourth commandment into a feeling: "the Sabbath is about attitude, not activity; a rhythm of the soul, not a box on the calendar." But the Standards will not let her do this. The fourth commandment is *positive* (it institutes a specific day, not merely a disposition), *moral* (it binds all men in all ages), and *perpetual*. Cara's "inner rest while I work" is not the biblical or confessional Sabbath; it is a heart-concocted substitute that lets her keep her preferences and call it obedience. Her warmth and sincerity don't make this faithful; they make her sincerely mistaken.

Third, close the cafe on the Lord's Day at minimum — she already has staff who can cover, so there is no necessity claim available to her — and actually keep the day: public worship, private worship, holy rest, works of mercy when they arise. The tenth commandment is, by its very nature, a heart-commandment. The Larger Catechism (Q. 148) requires "such a charitable frame of the *whole soul* toward our neighbour, as that all our inward motions, affections, and inclinations, watchfulness over our hearts, and all the words of our tongues, and all the actions of our lives... do manifest" a heart content with its own place and willing that others "have the preeminence before us, in such gifts and outward enjoyments as the providence of God casts upon them." The Shorter (Q. 81) forbids "envying and grieving at the happiness of our neighbour" and "a secret desire of our neighbour's deprivation or undoing in any kind." The Larger (Q. 149) condemns "all inordinate motions, cares, and solicitations of the heart." So the verdict on the tenth sits on the interior by definition; outward behavior is relevant only as evidence of what the heart is doing.

**Priya.** The honest read: she has not, in the settled sense, transgressed the tenth commandment. The motion she felt — the visible fallen face, the "that stung, I wanted it" — belongs to the corruption of nature that still remains in the regenerate (WCF 6.5; LC 149's "concupiscence of the eye"). It is the flesh stirring, not the will consenting. What she did with it is the whole question, and she did the right thing: she did not nurse it, did not justify it, did not let it lodge. She carried it honestly to God overnight, and by morning had mortified it — warm and sincere congratulations, a settled resolve to do her own work, genuine gladness for Aisha, no wish for her undoing, no replay. That sequence — felt the motion, hated it, brought it to God, put it to death, came out the other side — is precisely the duty the tenth commandment requires, not its violation.

I would say to her: do not be discouraged that you felt the sting. The strength of the feeling is itself a witness to the corruption that remains; the healing is real, but the disease is not yet eradicated. Watchfulness is required tomorrow as it was today. Rest in the grace of Christ, who fulfilled this Law for the unjust and now, by the Spirit, works this mortification in those who are His (WCF 19.6, 19.7).

**Tom.** The honest read: he has manifestly and gravely transgressed the tenth commandment, and the verdict sits entirely on the heart — the outward act is not where the sin lives. By his own stipulation, his mouth is exemplary. His mouth is not where the sin is. # Conference Worship-Integrity Standard — Draft

**Preamble.** This standard is binding on every session conducted under the name of the conference. It is framed by the convictions of the Westminster Confession of Faith that worship is to be ordered by God's Word, conducted in reverence and truth, and governed by the Spirit rather than by manipulative means.

**Clause 1 — Public Reading of Scripture.** Each session shall open with the public reading of Scripture, read distinctly from a faithful translation, in a manner that allows the congregation to attend to the text. The reading is not a transition into the program; it is itself an act of worship, and the heard Word sets the terms for what follows.

**Clause 2 — Voluntary Giving.** No giving shall be solicited under pressure of any kind — no countdown timers, no matched-gift escalations timed to a speaker's rhythm, no appeals that link the measure of a person's faith to the measure of their pledge. Offerings are received; they are not extracted. The conscience of the poor is not a revenue source.

**Clause 3 — No Manufactured Decisions.** No session may stage an altar call engineered to produce a visible response for the sake of the room's appearance or the conference's metrics. The minister of the Word may call for faith, repentance, and obedience; he may not orchestrate the environment so that a particular bodily response is the expected exit. Decisions are the fruit of the Spirit through the Word, not the work of staging.

**Clause 4 — Sensory and Aesthetic Practices.** Sessions shall avoid both (a) the prurient manipulation of the senses and (b) the engineered induction of affect. In particular:

- (a) Sensational aesthetic practices — including artful lighting, fragrance, and candles — used to overlay a particular mood on a passage of Scripture or to produce a desired somatic state in the hearers are prohibited. The duty of worship is not dampened by beauty in the pews or the room; it is undermined by the use of beauty as a lever.
- (b) Any practice that pairs a measurable physiological response with a fixed verbal attribution to the Spirit of God is prohibited. A facilitator may not tell a person that a feeling is the "manifest presence" of God when that feeling is, by the operator's own design, a product of lighting, sound, and scent. Such attribution is deceptive regardless of the practitioner's sincerity, and it puts the soul of the attendee in the hands of the engineer's design brief.

**Clause 5 — Encounter Room Reform.** The Encounter Room shall be repurposed. Scripture shall be read and briefly expounded by a designated minister. Attendees shall be invited to sit with the text, to be still, and to make use of Christian conference with the staff. No engineered lighting, sub-bass, or scent shall be used. No facilitator shall script a participant's interior experience. The room shall be a place of attention to the Word, not a place of coaxed experience.

**Clause 6 — Enforcement.** Each session shall be reviewed against this standard by the conference's worship leadership committee. A session that violates this standard shall be suspended and the responsible party disciplined, with the period to be set by the committee.

# Counsel on the Two Testimonies

## The Standard to Apply

The Westminster Confession 22.1 defines a lawful oath as a solemn act wherein the swearer "calleth God to witness what he asserteth or promiseth; and to judge him according to the truth or falsehood thereof." The Larger Catechism (Q109) specifies the duty this imposes: "a sincere and free revealing of the truth in matters of judgment and information." The Shorter Catechism (Q77) summarizes it as "the maintaining and promoting of truth between man and man."

So an oath is not a contract about syllables. It is a sacred appeal to God as the judge of what is *asserted* and what is *imparted*. Two axes therefore always apply:

- **Matter** — the substance of what is conveyed: does the testimony, taken as a whole, give the hearer what the speaker actually knows, fully and truthfully?
- **Manner** — the way it is conveyed: is the spirit and form consistent with the gravity of invoking God's witness, or does the form itself serve as a vehicle for concealment?

---

## (A) Fatima — **KEPT THE OATH**

**Matter — Holds.** Every substantive answer is the truth. She volunteers a material fact the regulator did not ask, precisely because she perceives it bears on the matter. This is a textbook fulfillment of the Larger Catechism's "sincere and free *revealing* of the truth." Her honest "I don't recall" is not a failure of matter; it is an honest report of the limits of her matter, and refusing to speculate past it preserves the integrity of what she does know.

**Manner — Holds.** Terse, literal, unadorned. There is no art deployed to produce a false impression, no true sentences arranged to mislead, no true irrelevancies to run out the clock. Her stated aim — that the regulator leave knowing what she actually knows — is the exact aim an oath requires. The brevity is not evasion; it is sobriety. She is not hiding behind her words but standing within them.

**Verdict:** She has done what WCF 22.1 and LCF 109 require. She has both spoken truth and refrained from the deception of omission or artful delivery. The oath stands intact.

---

## (B) Grant — **BROKE THE OATH**

**Matter — Fails.** This is the critical point and the one easy to miss. The oath he swore was that his testimony would be "true *and complete* to the best of my knowledge." Completeness is a matter requirement, not a manner requirement. By his own stipulated interior facts, he:

- Answers only the question asked, never the question meant — concealing material knowledge in the gaps between literal text and substance;
- Deploys literally true statements that predictably produce a false overall impression ("I was not in the room when the numbers were changed" — true, while he ordered the change by phone);
- Uses "I don't recall" where he *does* recall, because a true "yes" would damage him;
- Floods the record with true but irrelevant detail, a classic technique for burying the substance.

Each of these is a *matter* violation, because the matter of testimony is what the hearer is truthfully put in a position to know — and Grant's stipulated aim is for the regulator to leave believing the *opposite* of what happened. A statement whose predictable and intended effect is to implant a false belief is not, in the moral sense the Confession intends, "true." The Confession invokes God as judge of the truth or falsehood of what is *asserted* — and what Grant is asserting, considered as a whole and as intended, is false.

**Manner — Fails.** The Larger Catechism requires a "sacred regard to truth in giving testimony." Treating an oath as a literalistic word-puzzle — where one need only avoid an audible falsehood to satisfy God as Judge — is itself a violation of the manner. The WCF treats the oath as an act of *religious worship* (22.1) and of *solemn* appeal. Exploiting the letter while betraying the spirit is the very thing against which the ninth commandment (SC Q77) and the larger catechism's gloss on it are aimed.

**Verdict:** He has perjured himself. That no single uttered sentence is literally false is a trick played on the ear, not on the God who is called to witness the *substance* of what is sworn. The oath is broken on both axes.

Dear Brothers,

I appreciate the trust the session is placing in this work, and I share the desire to recover in our congregation a worship that is reverent, ordered, and rooted in the Word. Because our session subscribes the Westminster Confession and Catechisms, however, my duty as drafter is not only to produce something the session can enact, but to make sure that what we enact does not require us to teach what the Confession forbids us to teach. I have to be honest before the ink goes on the page: I cannot draft items (1) and (2) as presently worded, and I want to explain why on the record, so that the session can act with full information. I have, however, drafted a binding section on reverent demeanor in place of item (2), and the language for items (3), (4), and (5) follows.

**On item (1) — the "Covenant-Token Renewal."**

What is being proposed is a ritual act by which a member's standing before God is "renewed and kept secure" for the week, and by which a member who fails to perform the act is "unsealed" and "outside the covenant's protection." With respect, this is precisely the doctrine the Confession condemns. Our Confession teaches that the believer's standing before God rests in the obedience and satisfaction of Christ imputed to him and received by faith, and that this standing is the same in substance under both testaments (WCF 11.1, 11.6). Good works are the fruit and evidence of a true and lively faith, not the condition of it (WCF 16.2). The Larger Catechism teaches at Q/A 70–73 that justification is an act of God's free grace, and warns that to set up any other condition alongside faith is to overturn the gospel (cf. WCF 11.1–4; 20.1). To bind a Christian's standing for a week to a wooden token he must lay down, under pain of being "unsealed," is in practice to teach that the new covenant is conditioned on something we supply, and that the finished work of Christ must be re-sealed by us every Sunday. The Confession will not bear it.

A second difficulty: the token is described as a weekly sign and seal, given at membership, that mediates standing. The Confession teaches that "there are in the church, ordinarily, only two sacraments" (WCF 27.4), baptism and the Lord's Supper (WCF 28, 29). What is being proposed is a third sacramental practice, of our own devising, attached to no institution of Christ. We may not vote it in, because to do so would be to commit a confessional church to a practice that contradicts the chapter on sacraments.

I will gladly draft, instead, any of the following in proper Reformed form:

- a weekly corporate prayer of covenant consecration following the sermon, in which the people renew their vows and the minister commends them to God in Christ;
- a more frequent celebration of the Lord's Supper, which WCF 29.4 commends to us;
- an annual renewal of baptismal vows on a fixed Lord's Day;
- a responsive covenant-renewal reading drawn from Scripture and the Confession, for use at the minister's discretion.

Any of these preserves the pastoral warmth you are reaching for, without re-founding the gospel on a piece of wood.

**On item (2) — bodily demeanor in singing.**

The Confession and Directory do require "decency" and "order" in public worship (WCF 21.1, 21.3; *Directory for Public Worship*, "Of Singing of Psalms"). The minister is bound to rebuke the disorderly, and the whole assembly is to attend the Word with sober minds. I am happy to draft a binding rule on reverent demeanor, and I have done so below.

The standard as presently worded, however, goes further than the Standards authorize. It judges every lifted hand and every tearful eye as "fleshly" and "vanity," and binds every member's conscience to one bodily posture in the singing of praise. The Scripture itself praises bodily worship — "O clap your hands together, all ye people" (Ps. 47:1); "lift up your hands in the sanctuary" (Ps. 134:2); the "lifting up of holy hands" commended in 1 Tim. 2:8. WCF 20.2 declares liberty of conscience in matters not determined by the Word; WCF 21.1 warns us not to worship "after any other manner than what is appointed in the Holy Scripture." A blanket rule that brands all bodily reverence as fleshly adds a moral judgment that Scripture does not make, and binds the conscience in a thing indifferent. I cannot sign such a rule in a confessional church.

What I *can* draft, and have drafted below, is a rule that requires sober attention, calls for the engagement of mind and heart, forbids disorder and self-display, and gives the elders firm authority to act when anyone behaves in a way unbecoming the house of God.

Westminster framework**

The Standards evaluate moral acts on matter, manner, end, and circumstances (the catechism's standard analysis of duties), with the heart and intention decisive (Larger Catechism on the aggravations of sin). Truth-telling is anchored in the ninth commandment (WCF 19; WLC 144–145); the auditor's fiduciary duty is grounded in the eighth (WLC 141–142 — "to be just and true in all dealings," "the true and faithful performance of all trusts and engagements reposed in us"; and the sins forbidden there include "injustice, unfaithfulness, falsehood, in our dealings with men" and "in matters of trust, breach of trust"). WCF 23.4 forbids "equivocation or mental reservation" in formal statements. Truth is not exhausted by the letter; it is a correspondence between heart, words, and the reasonable understanding of those addressed.

---

**(A) Priya — Clean**

- **Matter.** The object of the engagement is true disclosure. She reports the material weakness precisely as the standard requires; she does not falsely upgrade the ambiguous immaterial item into a fraud. Both halves of the work have the proper object — truth, neither suppressed nor inflated.
- **Manner.** Plain language that an ordinary reader can actually understand. She resists the client's pressure to soften (which would make the matter less than true) and her colleague's pressure to "flag it hard as a probable fraud to cover ourselves" (which would make the matter more than true). Both refusals are acts of fidelity to the ninth commandment.
- **End.** Her stated aim — "say exactly what is true — no more, no less, so the reader is neither misled nor alarmed beyond the facts" — orders the work to its proper telos: the truthful understanding of the readers of the financial statements. It is not her own comfort, the client's preference, or the firm's protective posture that governs; it is truth for those who must rely on it.
- **Why her restraint is not complicity.** Declining to over-flag an ambiguous item because the evidence does not support the stronger characterization is itself the right reading of the ninth commandment. WLC 144 requires maintaining truth, not manufacturing it. Inflating an ambiguous immaterial item into "probable fraud" so the firm can say it "protected itself" is the same species of vice Devin commits in the opposite direction — using the disclosure instrument for the firm's sake rather than the reader's. Priya's matter, manner, and end are all rightly ordered. The engagement is clean.

---

**(B) Devin — Not clean**

- **Matter (the formal view).** Every mandated line item is present. Each sentence is technically accurate.
- **Manner (the substantive view).** The audit report is a communicative instrument; what it *means* is what an ordinary reader can take up. Deliberately fragmenting the key finding across three footnotes forty pages apart, in maximally opaque boilerplate, with cross-references engineered so that no ordinary reader could reassemble it, is not a neutral arrangement. It is unreadability built into the structure, used here as cover for sentences that are formally true. WLC 145 condemns "betraying the truth." What is betrayed here is the *findability* of the truth, even where each sentence is left intact. WCF 23.4 forbids equivocation and mental reservation in formal speech; the structure is the mental reservation made architectural.
- **End.** His stated aim — "meet the letter, keep the client happy, disclose nothing a lawsuit could hang on" — subordinates truth to client retention and to self-protection. The proper end of an audit is communication to the readers of the financial statements (shareholders, lenders, employees, the public), not the avoidance of accountability or the preservation of fee revenue. The whole structure of the work is bent toward wrong ends.
- **Breach of trust.** The auditor holds a trust reposed in him by readers who cannot themselves inspect the books. WLC 142 forbids breach of trust; WLC 141–142 require the true and faithful performance of all trusts and engagements reposed in us, with justice and truth in dealings. Devin's chosen structure is a deliberate breach of that trust. The "if they don't find it, that's on them" retort is precisely the abdication of fiduciary duty the eighth commandment forbids.
- **Aggravation.** The sins catechism (WLC 175) notes that sins are aggravated when the offender stands in a particular office or bond of duty. Devin's professional standing as auditor makes the breach worse, not exculpating.

---

**Why the two verdicts differ**

Both engagements operate within the letter of the disclosure rules. They differ because the moral quality of an act is not located in the letter of the words but in the truthful purposes the act is made to serve. Priya's matter, manner, and end are all rightly ordered, including her refusal to overstate; the engagement is clean. Devin's matter narrowly passes, but his manner is engineered obscuring and his end is wrongful; the composite act is therefore not clean. The Standards will not let formal compliance count as innocence, and they will not let truth-telling be punished as complicity. Both halves of the question — refusing to over-flag, and refusing to be cleared by technical disclosure — turn on the same principle: the moral act is measured by matter, manner, and end together, and the heart is not exempt from the count.

# Counsel Under the Westminster Standards

## The Framework

The Standards locate the question of lawful worship in WCF 21.1–2 and the Larger Catechism Q. 109. Worship is acceptable only when it is instituted by God and limited to his revealed will (WCF 21.1). To add "any device, opinion, rite, or ceremony" of men to the worship of God is forbidden (LC 109). The practice of the Reformed churches, reflecting the Directory for Public Worship, distinguishes:

- **Matter / substance of worship**: those elements God has appointed (Word read and preached, prayer, the sacraments, congregational praise, giving, and — in their place — oaths, vows, fasting, thanksgiving on special occasions).
- **Circumstances**: time, place, language, order, and the like — not part of worship itself, ordered by Christian prudence under the general principles of God's Word.

The error on one side is to treat circumstances as if they were worship elements (so binding or banning what Scripture has not bound or banned). The error on the other side is to add a human-devised rite to the elements of worship, however piously labeled.

---

## (A) Elmwood — Verdict: **Clean**

**Matter axis.** All the instituted elements are present and nothing is added to them: Scripture read and preached, prayer, the sacraments, congregational singing, giving. The member's complaint fails on this axis because the screen and the clock are not added to worship. Projecting the sermon text and the words to be sung is a means of enabling elements already instituted; the elements themselves (preaching, singing) remain unchanged.

**Manner / circumstances axis.** A fixed starting time and a means of seeing text and lyrics are circumstances surrounding worship, not parts of it. WCF 21 and LC 109 do not bind such things; they fall under prudence. The elders' judgment is correct: the screen and clock may be ordered or removed by godly prudence without altering the worship itself. The member has confused circumstance with element.

**Aim.** "Worship as God appointed, ordering the circumstances by prudence" is precisely the principle of the Standards. The service as an act of worship is clean.

---

## (B) Crossroads — Verdict: **Not Clean**

**Matter axis.** The instituted elements are present, but a monthly "Covenant Renewal Ceremony" has been added as a recurring act of worship. Whether one labels it a "rite," "ceremony," "ordinance," or "means of grace," it is a positive religious act of human devising, presented as channeling grace and required for standing in the church. That is precisely what LC 109 calls adding "any device, opinion, rite, or ceremony" of men.

The leaders' appeal to "scriptural analogy" does not cure the addition. WCF 1.6 limits infallible faith to what Scripture itself says; WCF 21.1 confines worship to what God has instituted in his Word, not to what man infers by analogy. Vows and covenant renewals, where they have Scripture footing, do not authorize the construction of a new standing ceremony with its own pledge, its own claimed grace, and its own binding force on membership. The substance being added — a loyalty pledge *to the leadership*, "spiritual covering," recurring renewal as a means of grace — exceeds anything warranted by the texts cited (which speak of vows to *God*, not recurring pledges of submission to officers as a ritual act).

**Manner axis.** Even granting for argument's sake that some vow could be lawful, the manner here is itself a problem: a separately scheduled monthly ceremony with its own prescribed form, tied to membership standing, and policed by treating dissent as rebellion against God-ordained authority. This fuses the doctrine of ministerial authority with a human rite in a way Scripture does not warrant, and it imposes under legal sanction what the Confession forbids as will-worship.

**Aim.** "Deepen commitment" is a true good; "protect the flock" is a true duty. But neither good is pursued by adding to worship what God has not appointed. The end does not sanctify the means; the regulative principle is precisely the protection against this reasoning (WCF 21.2; LC 110).

---

## Summary

| | Matter (elements) | Manner (circumstances/form) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Elmwood** | Clean — only instituted elements | Clean — screen and clock are circumstances ordered by prudence | **Clean** |
| **Crossroads** | **Defiled** — a devised ceremony added to the elements under claim of warrant | **Defiled** — form imposes the addition under membership penalty | **Not clean** |

**Practical counsel.**

- To **Elmwood**: hold your ground patiently. Instruct the complainant from WCF 21 and the principle of circumstances; do not let a confusion over prudence topple a faithful service.
- To **Crossroads**: the addition must be repented of, not merely relabeled. Re-signing loyalty pledges to leadership, "spiritual covering," and the dismissal of dissent as rebellion are not innocent phrasing — they are the shape of the error LC 109 names. A congregation that continues in this rite is guilty of will-worship, however sincere. The elders should retract the ceremony, cease treating it as a term of membership, and submit the question to their own session and, if needed, to sister sessions under the Standards.
